* [`pca_chart`] — T² and SPE charts from a principal-components model, with contributions and a change point.
* [`monitoring_limits`] — environmental monitoring alert and action levels by location, with early-warning rules.
* [`multivariate_chart`] — Hotelling T², generalized variance and MEWMA charts of several columns.
* [`anom_analysis`] — analysis of means for means, proportions and rates, one- and two-way.
* [`stepwise_analysis`] — stepwise selection of linear-model effects.
* [`mixture_analysis`] — Scheffé mixture models, blending tests and ternary contour plots.
* [`survival`] — Kaplan–Meier curves, log-rank test, Weibull and lognormal fits.
* [`reliability_growth`] — power-law (Crow–AMSAA) reliability growth, by phase.
* [`recurrence`] — repairable systems: mean cumulative function, process fits, trend tests.
* [`competing_risks`] — competing risks: cumulative incidence, Gray's test, Fine–Gray regression,
  failure modes combined into a series system.
* [`warranty`] — warranty returns: counts to censored life data, fits and return forecasts.
* [`time_series_data`] — equally spaced series from a table: rows, time stamps, seasonal period.
* [`series_explore`] — Series and Signals ▸ Explore: series description (ACF, PACF, unit-root tests,
  spectrum), decomposition, trend models and cross-correlation.
* [`signal_analysis`] — Series and Signals ▸ Signals and spectra: Fourier spectra, digital filters, convolution and
  correlation, and wavelets, on evenly spaced signals (resampled when uneven) by group.
* [`intensity_map`] — time–frequency maps (spectrograms, scalograms) as coloured cells.
* [`functional_analysis`] — functional data: curves from long data smoothed in a basis, registration,
  functional principal components and a model of the scores with a predicted-curve profiler.
* [`forecasting`] — shared parts of the time-series forecasting reports: the series and its time
  stamps, forecast plot and table, residual diagnostics, accuracy, the saved forecast table.
* [`arima_analysis`] — seasonal ARIMA, orders chosen or searched by AICc, optional Box–Cox.
* [`smoothing_analysis`] — exponential smoothing (ETS) models, chosen or selected by AICc.
* [`test_plan`] — demonstration, estimation and accelerated life test plans.
* [`proportional_hazards_analysis`] — Cox proportional hazards regression with strata, hazard ratios,
  Schoenfeld-residual checks and predicted survival.
* [`survival_regression_analysis`] — accelerated failure time models with censored and interval data.
* [`time_weighted_chart`] — EWMA and CUSUM control charts of one column.
* [`surface_analysis`] — second-order response surfaces: stationary point, canonical and ridge analysis, contours.
* [`compare`] — one-sample, independent-group and paired comparisons, from
  stacked (value + group column) or side-by-side data.
* [`counts`] — proportion and event-rate tests.
* [`goodness_analysis`] — chi-square goodness of fit of counts to given proportions or a Poisson distribution.
* [`multiple_response_analysis`] — check-all-that-apply columns: item frequencies, cross-tab by group and per-item tests.
* [`crossover_analysis`] — 2×2 crossover trials: treatment, period and carryover effects and equivalence.
* [`factorial_repeated`] — two- and three-way repeated-measures ANOVA with sphericity corrections and simple effects.
* [`nested_analysis`] — nested t test and nested one-way ANOVA (REML with Satterthwaite DF, classical nested ANOVA).
* [`distribution_calculator`] — probabilities, quantiles and random draws for any catalogued distribution.
* [`power_analysis`] — power, sample size and detectable difference.
* [`prediction`] — validation roles, fit measures by role and saved prediction columns for predictive models.
* [`forest_analysis`] — random forests with out-of-bag error and permutation importance.
* [`pls_analysis`] — partial least squares regression and discriminant analysis.
* [`mars_analysis`] — multivariate adaptive regression splines.
* [`neural_analysis`] — neural networks with one or two hidden layers.
* [`gaussian_process_analysis`] — Gaussian-process regression with
  prediction intervals.
* [`sequential_optimization`] — the next runs of an experiment by
  expected improvement or an upper confidence bound.
* [`model_search`] — every applicable predictive model fitted and ranked.
* [`svm_analysis`] — support vector classification and regression.
* [`boost_analysis`] — gradient-boosted trees with early stopping on validation rows.
* [`model_comparison`] — fit measures, ROC, lift, gains and calibration of saved prediction columns.
* [`tree_analysis`] — classification and regression trees with pruning chosen on held-out rows.
* [`report_run`] — run a saved report request: its title and sections (shared by
  the GUI, projects and scripts).
* [`report`] — GUI-independent report content: formatted tables and plot data
  whose points carry their dataset row.
* [`brushing`] — convert box and click gestures into changes to the shared
  [`stat_data::RowStateManager`].
* [`axis_settings`] — user settings for plot axes, tick positions and labels.
* [`plot_style`] — plot styles (settings a user sets on one plot) in saved files.
* [`bayes_analysis`], [`bayes_models`] — Bayesian estimation, Bayes factor tests, Bayesian
  linear models and ANOVA, and Bayesian generalized linear and hierarchical models.
* [`signal_curves`] — smoothing filters, derivatives and integrals of x–y data, and
  spectrum analysis (baseline correction, peak finding and multi-peak fitting).
* [`plot_view`] — plot limits and the axis-drag gestures (rescale / shift).
* [`doe`] — create designed experiments as data tables.
* [`editing`] — data edits (cells, rows, columns, types) with undo/redo.
* [`external`] — tables from SQL databases and the web, with refresh; credentials never saved.
* [`file_formats`] — the file types the application opens and exports.
* `format` — number formatting for reports.
* [`project`] — project files: a dataset with its row states and saved
  analyses, which re-run identically when the project is reopened.
* [`sample`] — built-in sample datasets.
* [`recode`] — mapping a column's distinct values to new ones.
* [`search`] — finding text in the data grid's cells.
* [`settings`] — user preferences (light/dark appearance, text size) stored between sessions.

Keeping this logic out of the `egui` crate means it is unit tested, and the
GUI layer stays thin.

### `crates/app-model/src/life_distribution.rs`

Life distributions bound to a dataset ([`stat_reliability::censored_fit`]
and [`stat_reliability::life_data`]): maximum-likelihood fits of the
chosen families to exact, right-, left- and interval-censored failure
times, compared by log-likelihood, AIC, BIC and a censoring-adjusted
Anderson–Darling distance, with likelihood-ratio tests of nested forms;
Turnbull's nonparametric estimate; for one family (chosen, or the best by
AIC) a probability plot with a confidence band, parameter estimates with
Wald and likelihood-ratio intervals, percentiles and failure
probabilities, survival and hazard plots; and optionally the Weibull with
a known shape for data with few or no failures.

**Layouts:** one time column with an optional censor column (a censored
row is still running at its time), or start and end columns of the
interval in which each unit failed: an empty start means the unit had
failed by the end (left-censored), an empty end that it was still running
at the start (right-censored), equal values an exact failure. An optional
frequency column counts units per row; an optional group column fits each
group separately. Excluded rows and rows without usable values are left
out.

- `enum LifeDataLayout`: Where the failure times come from.
- `struct LifeDistributionRequest`: Columns and settings of a life-distribution analysis.
- `struct FamilyResult`: One family's fit to one group.
- `struct LifeGroup`: One group's data and fits.
- `struct LifeDistributionAnalysis`: A computed life-distribution analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/life_stress.rs`

Life–stress models (accelerated life tests) bound to a dataset
([`stat_reliability::life_stress`]): a Weibull, lognormal, log-logistic
or exponential life distribution whose location depends on one or two
stress columns through Arrhenius, Eyring, inverse-power or exponential
relationships, fitted to censored failure times; activation energies and
power exponents, acceleration factors, the life distribution at use
conditions, a life–stress plot, a probability plot per stress level with
the fitted lines, and likelihood-ratio checks against per-level fits.

**Layouts** are those of life distributions ([`LifeDataLayout`]): a time
column with an optional censor column, or start and end columns of the
interval in which each unit failed; an optional frequency column counts
units per row. Excluded rows and rows without usable times or stresses
are left out.

- `struct StressColumn`: One stress column and how it acts on life.
- `struct LifeStressRequest`: Columns and settings of a life–stress analysis.
- `struct LifeStressAnalysis`: A computed life–stress analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/linear_analysis.rs`

A linear-model analysis bound to a dataset and its row state.

[`LinearModelAnalysis::run`] fits ordinary least squares to the rows that are
complete (no missing value in the model's columns) and not excluded, and keeps
everything a report needs. It records the row state's exclusion revision, so a
view can call `is_stale` each frame and refit
when the user excludes or re-includes rows.

Predictors may be continuous or categorical. Text columns, and numeric
columns whose measurement level is nominal or ordinal, enter as categorical
terms with indicator coding ([`stat_linear::design`]); a model with both kinds
is an analysis of covariance. Each term gets a partial F-test.

[`LinearModelAnalysis::profile`] computes the Response Explorer: for each
term, the predicted response (with confidence band) as that term varies and
the others stay at chosen settings.

- `const STUDENTIZED_LIMIT`: Studentized residuals larger than this (in absolute value) are flagged.
- `struct LinearModelSpec`: Which columns enter the model.
- `enum ProfilePanel`: One factor's panel in the Response Explorer.
- `struct Profile`: The Response Explorer at one setting of every term.
- `struct LinearModelAnalysis`: A fitted linear model plus the data needed to report and plot it.
- `fn normal_quantile_points`: Points of a normal quantile plot for `(row, value)` pairs sorted by value: x is the standard normal quantile of the plotting position `(i − 3/8)/(n + 1/4)` (Blom 1958), y the value.

### `crates/app-model/src/manova_analysis.rs`

Multivariate analysis of variance bound to the row state
([`stat_linear::manova`]).

Several continuous responses are modelled on the same effects, coded as
in the linear model report (categorical predictors as indicators, or
sum-to-zero in models with interactions; continuous predictors centred
in higher-order effects). The rows used are those not excluded with
every response and predictor present.

The report gives each effect's Wilks, Pillai, Hotelling–Lawley and Roy
tests, an Effect Pareto by the chosen statistic, univariate F-tests of
each response, any contrasts among the levels of a categorical factor,
the canonical analysis of each effect (eigenvalues of `E⁻¹H`, canonical
correlations, standardized coefficients), a canonical plot of the rows
for one categorical main effect, the residual (partial) correlations of
the responses, and Box's M test of equal covariance matrices across the
cells of the categorical factors when every predictor is categorical.

- `struct ManovaContrast`: A contrast among the levels of one categorical factor: `Σ cⱼ μⱼ = 0`, the `μⱼ` being least-squares means (each level's mean with the other factors balanced).
- `struct ManovaRequest`: Responses, model and report settings.
- `struct ManovaAnalysis`: A computed MANOVA report.

### `crates/app-model/src/many_tests.rs`

Many two-group tests at once: the same test of two groups applied to each
of many variables (columns), with the p-values adjusted for multiple
testing ([`stat_inference::pvalues`]) and a volcano plot of each
variable's difference against `−log₁₀ p`.

The grouping column must have exactly two values among the rows used;
the first in natural order is the first group, so differences are
first − second. Each variable uses the rows (not excluded) that have
both a value and a group. The tests are the pooled or Welch two-sample t
test ([`stat_inference::means::two_sample_t`], difference of means) or the
Wilcoxon rank-sum test ([`stat_inference::nonparametric::rank_sum_test`],
Hodges–Lehmann shift), two-sided.

- `enum ManyTestKind`: Which test is applied to every variable.
- `enum ManyTestsOrder`: Order of the rows of the results table.
- `struct ManyTestsRequest`: Settings of a many-tests report.
- `struct VariableTest`: The test of one variable.
- `struct ManyTestsAnalysis`: A computed many-tests report.

### `crates/app-model/src/marginal_sections.rs`

Report sections for comparisons within the slices of an interaction and
for comparing slopes across groups ([`stat_linear::marginal`]), shared by
the linear model, GLM and mixed model reports.

- `fn sections`: The sections for every two-factor interaction of categorical predictors (`slices`) and every `factor × continuous` effect (`slopes`) of `design`; `PairAdjust::None` leaves out the pairwise tables.
- `fn spline_knots_section`: The knots of each spline term of `design`, or `None` without splines.

### `crates/app-model/src/mars_analysis.rs`

Multivariate adaptive regression splines bound to a dataset
([`stat_predictive::mars`]): a continuous response modelled as a sum of
hinge functions `max(0, x − t)`, `max(0, t − x)` and their products.
Uses the shared predictive-model sections ([`crate::prediction`]).

**Rows.** Excluded rows and rows missing the response take no role.
The model is fitted to the training rows that have every predictor;
rows missing a predictor the final model uses get no prediction.

**Size.** The forward pass builds the largest model; the backward pass
gives the best subset of each size. The size is chosen by the smallest
GCV when every row trains, by the smallest error on the validation rows
when there are any, or by the smallest k-fold cross-validated error
(each fold repeats both passes without its rows; the fit table then
shows each row's prediction from the fold that held it out).

**Predictors.** Continuous predictors enter through hinges, or only
linearly when listed as linear; a categorical predictor enters through
indicators of its levels other than the first.

- `struct MarsRequest`: Columns and settings of a MARS model.
- `struct MarsAnalysis`: A fitted MARS model.
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response` and `predictors`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry (missing members take their defaults).

### `crates/app-model/src/method_comparison_analysis.rs`

Method comparison bound to the row state
([`stat_linear::method_comparison`]): Deming and Passing–Bablok
regression of a test method on a comparison method, with a scatter plot
against the line of identity and a difference (Bland–Altman) plot.

Rows that are excluded or miss either measurement are left out.

- `struct MethodComparisonRequest`: What to analyse.
- `struct MethodComparisonAnalysis`: A computed method comparison.

### `crates/app-model/src/mixed_analysis.rs`

Linear and generalized linear mixed models bound to a dataset
([`stat_mixed`]).

Fixed effects are coded as in the linear model (continuous predictors as
they are, categorical ones as indicators, interactions and powers when
asked for). Each random-effects term names a grouping column, optionally
nested within other columns (its levels are then the combinations), with a
random intercept and/or random slopes on continuous columns. A binomial
response is either a two-valued column (the second value in sorted order is
the event) or a count of successes with a column of numbers of trials.
An ordinal response is a column of ordered categories (natural order
unless `order` says otherwise), fitted by the cumulative logit model.

A frequency column repeats each row that many times (whole numbers; 0
drops the row). A weight column gives prior weights: the residual
variance of a normal response (or the dispersion of a Gamma one) is
divided by the weight, and the log-likelihood contributions of Poisson,
negative binomial and ordinal responses are multiplied by it.

- `struct RandomEffectSpec`: One random-effects term.
- `struct MixedRequest`: Columns, family and options of a mixed model.
- `struct MixedAnalysis`: A fitted mixed model and what its report needs.

### `crates/app-model/src/mixture_analysis.rs`

Mixture-model analysis: Scheffé canonical polynomials fitted to blends
whose component proportions sum to one ([`stat_doe::ScheffeModel`];
Cornell, *Experiments with Mixtures*, 3rd ed., ch. 2–3).

Rows with a response and every component are used (excluded rows are left
out). Component values are rescaled to proportions of their row total, so
amounts or percentages work as well as fractions; rows whose total differs
from that of the first row by more than 1% are reported.

The model has no intercept (the proportions sum to one), so R² and the
ANOVA use the total sum of squares about the mean (Cornell §2.8), with
`q − 1` model degrees of freedom for the linear blending part. The test of
**nonlinear blending** compares the fitted model with the linear one;
each nonlinear term also gets a partial F-test. For three components the
fitted surface is drawn as a contour plot on the simplex (a ternary plot).

- `struct MixtureRequest`: What to fit.
- `struct MixtureAnalysis`: A fitted mixture model.

### `crates/app-model/src/model_comparison.rs`

Comparing predictive models through the prediction columns they saved.

Each model is a column: predicted values for a continuous response, or
the probability of one **event** class for a categorical response (other
classes count as non-events, so a model of several classes is compared
one class against the rest). Models are compared on the same rows: those
not excluded with the response and every model's prediction present.
An optional validation column (0/1/2 or Training/Validation/Test) splits
the measures by role.

**Measures.** Continuous: RMSE, mean absolute error and R²
([`ContinuousFit`]). Categorical: misclassification at probability 0.5,
log loss and the area under the ROC curve ([`ClassFit`] of the event
against the rest), and the Brier score `Σ(p̂ − y)²/n` (Brier, *Monthly
Weather Review* 78, 1950).

**Plots** (on test rows when there are any, else validation rows, else
every row): for a categorical response, ROC curves, lift and cumulative
gains by depth (the share of rows ranked highest by the model; Berry &
Linoff, *Data Mining Techniques*, 2004, ch. 5) and a calibration plot of
observed event rate against mean predicted probability in tenths of the
predictions; for a continuous response, actual by predicted and residual
by predicted. Every point is a dataset row (a row appears once per model),
so brushing works as elsewhere.

- `struct ModelComparisonRequest`: Columns compared.
- `struct ModelComparison`: A model comparison.
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry.

### `crates/app-model/src/model_data.rs`

Shared preparation of a response and predictors for model fitting: picks
the complete, included rows and codes continuous and categorical
predictors with [`stat_linear::ModelDesign`].

### `crates/app-model/src/model_search.rs`

Automated model search: every applicable predictive model fitted to one
response with its default settings and the same validation roles, ranked
by its error on rows it was not fitted to.

**Models.** Decision tree, random forest, boosted trees, neural network,
support vector machine, multivariate adaptive regression splines
(continuous response only), partial least squares, and discriminant
analysis (categorical response and numeric predictors only). Each runs
exactly as its own report would with default settings, the search's
validation roles and the search's seed, so its row in the ranking matches
the report it opens. A model that cannot be fitted to the data (for
example discriminant analysis with a text predictor) is listed with the
reason and left out of the ranking.

**Ranking.** Models are ranked by the held-out error that tunes them: on
the validation rows, or, with k-fold roles, from the predictions of each
row by the model fitted without its fold. With every row training the
search uses 5-fold cross-validation (seeded), since a ranking on the
training rows would favour the most flexible model. The measure is the
root mean square error for a continuous response, and the log loss
(mean −ln p̂ of the observed class) for a categorical one, a proper
scoring rule that rewards well-calibrated probabilities and separates
models that the coarser misclassification rate ties (ties broken by the
misclassification rate, then by the menu order of the models). Test rows, used by no model
for fitting or tuning, give an honest estimate for the winner.

**Repeated and nested cross-validation.** With `repeats` above one and
k-fold roles (or every row training), every model is cross-validated again
with each repeat's folds (seeds `seed`, `seed + 1`, …), and the report
lists each model's held-out RMSE (or misclassification rate) across the
repeats as a mean with a t interval, drawn as a forest plot (Kim 2009).
A single split's ranking can turn on how the rows happened to fall; the
spread across repeats shows how much. With `nested`, each repeat instead
holds out one outer fold at a time, lets the model tune itself by k-fold
cross-validation on the remaining rows only, and measures it on the
held-out fold: since tuning never sees the rows it is scored on, the
error is not biased by the tuning (Varma & Simon 2006).

**Reproducibility.** Every model is seeded from the request's seed and
the models are fitted in parallel with results combined in a fixed
order, so a search repeats exactly.

- `const DEFAULT_FOLDS`: Folds used when every row trains.
- `enum ModelKind`: A kind of predictive model the search can fit.
- `struct ModelSearchRequest`: Columns and settings of a model search.
- `type RepeatedErrors`: Each model's held-out error in every repeat of k-fold cross-validation.
- `struct ModelSearch`: A finished model search.
- `const MAX_REPEATS`: Most repeats of cross-validation.
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response` and `predictors`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry (missing members take their defaults).

### `crates/app-model/src/monitoring_limits.rs`

Environmental monitoring limits, bound to the row state
([`stat_quality::monitoring_limits`]): alert and action levels for colony
counts, positive samples or continuous readings, set per limit group
(all locations together, each location, or the levels of a grouping column
such as a room grade) from the best-fitting distribution, from the mean
and standard deviation, typed in, or read from columns; each location
charted against its levels in time order with the early-warning rules; and
a summary of excursions by location.

Rows missing the reading (or, for positives, the number of samples taken)
and excluded rows are left out. A missing location or limit-group value
is a level of its own, "(missing)". Each chart point is one dataset row,
so brushing links the charts with every other view.

- `const MISSING_LEVEL`: Name of the level a missing location or group value forms.
- `const ANY_GROUP`: The level used for every group without its own typed levels.
- `fn reading_kind_key`: What the readings are, with stable keys.
- `fn reading_kind_label`: Display name of a reading kind.
- `const READING_KINDS`: Every reading kind, in menu order.
- `fn families`: The families a reading kind can use: `(key, label)`.
- `enum LimitsBy`: Which rows share one set of levels.
- `struct TypedLevels`: Levels typed in for one limit group.
- `enum LevelMethod`: How the alert and action levels are set.
- `struct MonitoringRequest`: What to analyse.
- `struct MonitoringAnalysis`: A computed environmental monitoring study.

### `crates/app-model/src/multi_vari.rs`

Multi-vari chart (Seder 1950) bound to the row state
([`stat_quality::multivari`]).

The response is plotted against one to four factors, outermost first. Each
innermost cell (a combination of levels that occurs in the data) gets a
position along the horizontal axis; the outermost factor's levels become
side-by-side panes. Individual values are plotted at their cell, each
factor's level means are marked with their own colour and marker shape,
and the means are joined within each level of the factor above (the
outermost factor's means are joined across the panes).

By default the values of each innermost cell are spread a little to the
left and right of the cell's position in their row order and joined by a
thin line, so each cell reads as a short run chart and a trend or a jump
within a cell shows (the chart as drawn by Seder 1950 and Snee 2001,
"Graphical analysis of process variation studies", *Journal of Quality
Technology* 33(4)). [`ReplicateLayout::Stacked`] draws them on one
vertical line at the cell instead. A ranges view
charts the range within each cell against 3-sigma limits, and a table
gives the spread of each factor's means (Seder's families of variation).

Plotted values carry their rows and each cell's range carries its cell's
rows, so brushing either view selects rows everywhere.

- `struct MultiVariRequest`: What to chart.
- `enum ReplicateLayout`: How the individual values of a cell are placed.
- `const REPLICATE_HALF_WIDTH`: Half the width (in cell spacings) over which a cell's values are spread in [`ReplicateLayout::InOrder`].
- `struct MultiVariOptions`: Display options of a multi-vari report.
- `struct MultiVariAnalysis`: A computed multi-vari breakdown.

### `crates/app-model/src/multiple_imputation.rs`

Multiple imputation of table columns ([`stat_multivariate::multiple_imputation`]),
bound to the row state, and the stacked table it saves.

The columns to impute may be continuous (numeric, continuous level) or
categorical (text, or numbers marked nominal or ordinal; their levels in
natural order). Rows that are not excluded take part; excluded rows keep
their missing values. The result is `m` completed copies of those
columns, and the **stacked table** holds them as rows: an `Imputation`
column (0 for the original data, with its missing values, then 1 to `m`),
a `Row` column (the source row number) and every column of the source
table, the imputed columns filled in from imputation 1 on (the long form
of van Buuren 2018, §5.1.2). Analyses of that table can then be pooled
across imputations ([`crate::pooling`]).

- `const IMPUTATION_COLUMN`: Name of the stacked table's imputation-number column.
- `const ROW_COLUMN`: Name of the stacked table's source-row column.
- `enum MiEngine`: Which model draws the imputations.
- `fn method_label`: Label of a chained-equations method.
- `const METHODS`: Every chained-equations method, in menu order.
- `struct MiSettings`: Settings of a multiple imputation.
- `struct MiColumn`: One imputed column.
- `struct MiRun`: A computed multiple imputation of table columns.
- `const PLOTTED_COLUMNS`: Most imputed columns given trace, strip and density plots.
- `fn imputation_column`: The column of `table` holding imputation numbers: a numeric column named [`IMPUTATION_COLUMN`] whose values are whole numbers from 0 with at least two imputations (values ≥ 1).

### `crates/app-model/src/multiple_response_analysis.rs`

Multiple-response (check-all-that-apply) frequencies
([`stat_discrete::multiple_response`]).

The answers come in one of the two usual layouts:

* **one text column of lists** — each cell holds the items a case picked,
  separated by a delimiter (`"Price; Quality"`); spaces around items are
  ignored and an item listed twice in one cell counts once;
* **one indicator column per item** — a cell counts as picked when it is
  a number other than 0, or text such as `yes`, `y`, `true`, `x`,
  `checked` or `1` (any case); the column name is the item.

Excluded rows are left out; so is a case with no pick (counted as "no
response"). An optional group column adds a cross-tabulation and each
item's test of independence from the group, with a Bonferroni overall
test. The frequency chart's bars hold the rows of the cases picking each
item, so clicking a bar selects them everywhere.

- `enum ResponseSource`: Where the answers are.
- `enum ItemOrder`: The order of the items in the tables and chart.
- `struct MultipleResponseRequest`: Settings of a multiple-response report.
- `fn split_items`: The items in one list cell: split at `delimiter`, trimmed, empty pieces and repeats dropped (first occurrence kept).
- `struct MultipleResponseAnalysis`: A computed multiple-response report.

### `crates/app-model/src/multiple_responses.rs`

Several responses modelled on the same factors, explored and optimized
together: linked Response Explorer rows, desirability, a search for the
best settings, and simulation of factor variation and response noise.

Each response gets an ordinary least-squares model of the same form
(main effects, plus two-factor interactions, plus squares of continuous
factors) on the same predictors, fitted to the rows where that response
and the predictors are present and not excluded.

* **Term selection** ([`MultipleResponsesRequest::selection`]): instead
  of fitting every term, each response's terms are chosen by its own
  stepwise search ([`crate::stepwise_analysis`], Efroymson 1960; Draper &
  Smith 1998, ch. 15) among the same candidates (the model form's terms,
  or a list chosen in the stepwise dialog), with the same direction,
  criterion and heredity. Every selected model keeps all the factors, so
  the linked explorer, desirability, best settings and simulation work
  on the selected models unchanged; a factor no selected term of a
  response uses is flat in that response's row. A response for which no
  term is selected is predicted by its mean (with the interval
  `ȳ ± t₀.₉₇₅,ₙ₋₁ s/√n`), constant in every factor.

* **Linked profiles** ([`MultipleResponsesAnalysis::profiles`]): one
  Response Explorer row per response over the same factor settings, the
  factors' ranges being the union over the models; then a row of the
  overall desirability `D` as each factor moves.
* **Desirability** (Derringer & Suich 1980; [`stat_doe::desirability`]):
  each response maximized, minimized or held near a target between
  limits; `D` is the importance-weighted geometric mean. By default each
  response is maximized between its smallest and largest observed value.
* **Best settings** ([`MultipleResponsesAnalysis::best_settings`]):
  maximize `D` over the factor box by Nelder–Mead from a Latin hypercube
  of starts plus the current settings, for every combination of
  categorical levels (up to 64 combinations; beyond that the categorical
  factors stay at their current levels). Where `D = 0` the search climbs
  the mean of the individual desirabilities instead, so it can leave a
  region where some response is unacceptable.
* **Simulation** ([`MultipleResponsesAnalysis::simulate`]): each
  continuous factor varies around its setting (fixed, normal with a given
  SD, uniform or triangular over ± a half-width); each response gets
  normal noise with a given SD; `runs` runs are drawn from a seeded
  generator. Reported: each response's simulated mean and SD, and the
  share of runs outside its specification limits, with a 95% Wilson
  score interval; overall, the share of runs with any response outside.
  [`MultipleResponsesAnalysis::robust_settings`] searches the factor box
  for the settings with the lowest overall defect rate, using the same
  random draws at every candidate (common random numbers).
* **Constraints** ([`MultipleResponsesRequest::constraints`]): linear
  limits and disallowed combinations on the continuous factors, written
  in their units as for designs ([`stat_doe::Region::parse`]). The
  best-settings and robust-settings searches only return settings that
  satisfy them: a violated constraint adds a penalty of 2 plus the
  violation (in coded units) to the objective, which lies in [−1, 1]
  otherwise, and infeasible end points are dropped.
* **Specification region** ([`SimulationSetup::region`]): a box of
  continuous-factor settings (an operating window). At every corner the
  probability that all responses meet their specification limits is
  `Πᵢ [Φ((Uᵢ − ŷᵢ)/σᵢ) − Φ((Lᵢ − ŷᵢ)/σᵢ)]` with the noise SDs `σᵢ`
  (responses independent; a missing limit is ±∞; with `σᵢ = 0` the factor
  is 1 inside the limits and 0 outside), checked by simulating the noise
  (the same draws at every corner); the worst corner is the region's
  guaranteed probability (in the spirit of Peterson 2004, "A posterior
  predictive approach to multiple response surface optimization",
  *J. Quality Technology* 36(2), and del Castillo 2007, *Process
  Optimization: A Statistical Approach*, ch. 7, with the parameters taken
  as known). A contour plot over the first two varying factors shows each
  response's limits with the box drawn on it.

- `const MAX_RUNS`: Most runs a simulation may draw.
- `const MAX_REGION_FACTORS`: Most continuous factors that may vary over a specification region (`2^8 = 256` corners).
- `enum ModelForm`: The terms every response's model contains.
- `struct TermSelection`: Stepwise selection of each response's terms (see the module documentation).
- `enum FactorSetting`: A factor setting as stored in a request: a number, or a categorical factor's level by its label.
- `enum FactorVariation`: How a continuous factor varies around its setting in a simulation.
- `struct SimulationSetup`: Simulation settings.
- `struct MultipleResponsesRequest`: Several responses modelled on the same predictors.
- `struct Solution`: One point found by the best-settings search.
- `struct SimulatedResponse`: One response's simulation summary.
- `struct Simulation`: The result of a simulation.
- `struct RegionPoint`: One point of a specification region.
- `struct SpecRegionCheck`: The probability of meeting every specification over a box of settings.
- `fn wilson_interval`: `(rate, lower, upper)`: the share `x / n` with its 95% Wilson score interval (Wilson, *JASA* 22, 1927).
- `struct MeanOnly`: A response for which term selection kept no term: its mean, constant in every factor.
- `enum ResponseModel`: One response's model: the fitted linear model, or its mean when term selection kept no term.
- `struct MultipleResponsesAnalysis`: Fitted models of several responses and their joint exploration.
- `fn goal_text`: Goal name and target value.
- `fn effects`: The effects of `form` over predictors whose continuity is `continuous` (positions in the predictor list, as [`LinearModelSpec::effects`] takes them).
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members other than its columns, for project files: `"model"`, `"goals"`, `"settings"`, `"simulation"`, and when set `"constraints"` and `"selection"` (`direction`, `criterion`, `enter`, `remove`, `heredity` and, when chosen, `candidates` as lists of `[predictor position, power]`).
- `fn request_from_json`: The request from its project-file form, given its columns.

### `crates/app-model/src/multivariate.rs`

Multivariate analyses bound to a dataset: principal components and
clustering ([`stat_multivariate`]).

Both use the rows that have a value in every chosen column and are not
excluded. Score and cluster plots keep each point's dataset row, so they
take part in linked brushing like every other plot.

- `struct PcaRequest`: Columns and scaling for a principal component analysis.
- `enum ClusterMethod`: Clustering method.
- `struct ChooseClusters`: Settings of the "Number of Clusters" section of a k-means report: the gap statistic and average silhouette width for `k = 1, …, max_k`.
- `struct StartingCenters`: Starting centers given for k-means (Hartigan & Wong 1979), in the units of the data (standardized like the data when the request standardizes).
- `struct ClusterRequest`: Columns and method for a cluster analysis.
- `enum ClusterDistance`: How a cluster analysis measures the distance between rows.
- `struct PcaAnalysis`: A computed principal component analysis.
- `struct ClusterAnalysis`: A computed cluster analysis.
- `struct CorrespondenceRequest`: Two categorical columns for a correspondence analysis.
- `struct CorrespondenceReport`: A computed correspondence analysis of two columns' cross-tabulation.

### `crates/app-model/src/multivariate_chart.rs`

Multivariate control charts of several measurement columns, bound to the
row state ([`stat_quality::multivariate`]): Hotelling T² of individual
observations or subgroups, the generalized variance |S| of subgroups, and
the MEWMA chart of individual observations.

Rows are taken in table order, skipping excluded rows and rows missing a
value in any measurement column (or the subgroup ID). Subgroups are the
rows sharing a subgroup ID (in order of first appearance), or consecutive
runs of `subgroup_size` rows (an incomplete last run is left out). The
first `reference` points (all when `None`) estimate the mean vector and
covariance matrix; later points are monitored against them, with their
own (phase II) limits. Every plotted point records its dataset rows, so
brushing the chart selects them; for T² and MEWMA signals the report adds
each variable's contribution to the statistic.

- `const CONTRIBUTION_PLOT_POINTS`: Signals shown in the contribution plot (the largest statistics).
- `enum MultivariateChartKind`: Which multivariate chart.
- `struct MultivariateChartRequest`: What to chart.
- `struct MultivariateChartAnalysis`: A computed multivariate chart.

### `crates/app-model/src/multiway_table.rs`

The multi-way table report (Describe ▸ Multi-way table…): counts,
percentages and summary statistics of continuous columns, by several
nested row and column classifications ([`stat_discrete::tabulation`]).

The report runs through [`crate::ComparisonReport`], so front ends edit
its settings in place.

- `enum CellFrequency`: A frequency statistic shown in every cell.
- `enum CellSummary`: A summary statistic of a continuous column shown in every cell.
- `struct MultiwayTableRequest`: Settings of a multi-way table.
- `struct MultiwayTableAnalysis`: A computed multi-way table.

### `crates/app-model/src/nested_analysis.rs`

Nested comparison of groups bound to a dataset
([`stat_mixed::nested_comparison`]): groups, subjects nested in groups,
replicate measurements on each subject. With two groups this is the
nested t test; with more, a nested one-way ANOVA.

The data are stacked: one row per measurement, with response, group and
subject columns. Subjects are identified within their group, so subject
"1" in group A and subject "1" in group B are different subjects.

- `struct NestedRequest`: Settings of a nested comparison.
- `struct NestedReport`: A computed nested comparison.

### `crates/app-model/src/neural_analysis.rs`

Neural networks bound to a dataset ([`stat_predictive::neural`]): a fully
connected network with one or two hidden layers for a continuous
response (linear output) or a categorical one (logistic or softmax
output). Uses the shared predictive-model sections
([`crate::prediction`]).

**Inputs.** Continuous predictors are standardized with the training
rows' mean and standard deviation; each level of a categorical predictor
becomes a 0/1 indicator. Rows missing a predictor take no role. A
continuous response is standardized too, and predictions are returned in
its units.

**Tuning.** The weight-decay penalty α is chosen from 10⁻⁴, 10⁻³, …, 10
by the smallest held-out error (root mean square error in the response's
units, or log loss for classes): on the validation rows, or by k-fold
cross-validation (the request's folds, or 5 folds when every row trains).
Ties go to the larger penalty. α can be fixed instead. The final network
is fitted to the training rows; with k-fold roles the fit table shows each
row's prediction from the fold that held it out.

- `const PENALTIES`: Penalties tried when α is tuned.
- `struct NeuralRequest`: Columns and settings of a neural network.
- `struct NeuralAnalysis`: A fitted neural network.
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response` and `predictors`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry (missing members take their defaults).

### `crates/app-model/src/nonlinear_analysis/templates.rs`

Report sections of nonlinear regressions made from an assay curve
template ([`crate::curve_templates`]): the parameters' meanings, derived
quantities, standard-curve acceptance and quantitation range, the
inhibition-mechanism comparison, Schild analysis and relative potency.

### `crates/app-model/src/nonlinear_analysis.rs`

Nonlinear regression bound to the row state ([`stat_linear::nonlinear`]).

The model is one of:
* a library form in one predictor (exponential, logistic, dose–response,
  growth, segmented line, peaks…, with automatic starting values);
* a model formula with named parameters, written in the formula language
  ([`crate::formula`]) with the table's columns and the parameters as
  variables (a formula in two columns is a surface `z = f(x, y)`);
* a differential equation `dy/dx = g(x, y; θ)` with `y(x₀)` a parameter,
  solved at the observed `x` for each evaluation ([`stat_core::ode`]);
* an implicit curve `F(x, y; θ) = 0` fitted by orthogonal distance
  ([`stat_linear::nonlinear::implicit`]).

Options: a data-set column, with each parameter shared by every data set
or fitted to each ([`stat_linear::nonlinear::global`]); weights (`1/Y²`,
`1/Y` or a weight column); least squares, a robust (Cauchy-loss) fit, or
least squares after removing the outliers the robust fit identifies
([`stat_linear::nonlinear::robust`]); and comparisons by the extra
sum-of-squares F test and AICc ([`stat_linear::nonlinear::compare`]):
one curve for all data sets, each unshared parameter made common, and an
alternative library form. Rows with a response but no predictor value are
read off the fitted curve (inverse prediction,
[`stat_linear::nonlinear::inverse`]).

Excluded rows and rows missing the response, a predictor the model reads,
the data set or a valid weight are left out of the fit; predictions are
saved for every row the model can be computed on.

Project-file form (columns by name; a missing setting keeps its default):

```text
{"analysis": "nonlinear-regression", "response": "Rate", "form": "michaelis_menten",
 "predictor": "Conc", "parameters": [{"name": "Vmax", "start": 200, "lower": 0, "shared": true}],
 "level": 0.95, "profile": true, "max_iterations": 200, "group": "Batch",
 "weighting": "inverse_y2", "method": "outliers", "q": 0.01, "compare": "logistic3"}
{"analysis": "nonlinear-regression", "response": "Rate", "formula": "Vmax * Conc / (Km + Conc)",
 "parameters": [{"name": "Vmax", "start": 200}, {"name": "Km", "start": 0.1}]}
{"analysis": "nonlinear-regression", "response": "C", "rate": "-k * C", "predictor": "Time",
 "initial": "C0", "start_x": 0, "parameters": [{"name": "k", "start": 0.1}, {"name": "C0", "start": 10}]}
{"analysis": "nonlinear-regression", "response": "Y", "equation": "(X - a)**2 + (Y - b)**2 - r**2",
 "parameters": [...]}
```
`weighting` is `"equal"`, `"inverse_y2"`, `"inverse_y"` or a weight column
as `{"column": "W"}`; `method` is `"least_squares"`, `"robust"` or
`"outliers"`.

- `enum NonlinearModel`: The model of a nonlinear regression.
- `struct ParameterSetting`: Name, starting value, bounds and sharing of one parameter.
- `enum Weighting`: Observation weights.
- `enum FitMethod`: How the parameters are estimated.
- `struct NonlinearRequest`: What to fit.
- `struct NonlinearAnalysis`: A computed nonlinear regression.

### `crates/app-model/src/notebook.rs`

Script notebooks: a document of text cells and Rhai code cells with the
outputs of their last run (printed lines, errors, the cell's value shown
as text or as tables, and the reports it added), kept in a project.

The cells are run by `stat_script::NotebookSession`, which keeps the
variables and functions of earlier cells for later ones, as a single
script would. Running is the application's business; this module is the
document and its saved form.

#### Saved form
A project's `"notebooks"` member (optional; see [`crate::project`]):

```text
"notebooks": [
  { "name": "…",
    "cells": [
      { "kind": "text", "source": "…" },
      { "kind": "code", "source": "…", "run": 3,          (run: optional)
        "outputs": [                                      (optional)
          { "kind": "printed", "text": "…" },
          { "kind": "error", "text": "…", "line": 4 },    (line: optional)
          { "kind": "value", "text": "…" },
          { "kind": "table", "title": "…", "columns": ["…"], "rows": [["…"], …] },
          { "kind": "report", "table": "…", "title": "…" },
          { "kind": "note", "text": "…" } ] },
      … ] },
  … ]
```

- `enum CellKind`: What a cell holds.
- `enum CellOutput`: One output of a code cell's last run.
- `struct NotebookCell`: One cell.
- `struct Notebook`: A notebook: named cells.
- `fn read_notebooks`: The `"notebooks"` member of a project document (empty when absent).
- `fn notebooks_json`: The JSON form of a project's notebooks.

### `crates/app-model/src/open_data.rs`

Choosing which block of a sheet becomes a table, for the Open Data dialog,
file opening, web tables, pasted text and the script `open_table` options.

A file is first read as a [`RawSheet`]: every cell as text, rows and
columns numbered from 1 as in the dialog's preview, nothing taken as a
header yet. A [`Block`] then says where the table sits:

* **Header row** — the row holding the column names, or none (the columns
  are then called `Column 1`, `Column 2`, …).
* **Header rows** — how many rows, from the header row down, hold names.
  Their texts are joined with a space (`Temperature` over `Min` gives
  `Temperature Min`). A blank cell in an upper header row takes the text to
  its left, as a merged heading cell spans the columns under it.
* **Data starts on row** / **Data ends on row** — the rows read as values;
  blank rows among them are skipped.
* **First column** / **Last column** — the columns read; columns blank in
  every header and data row are dropped.

[`detect_block`] proposes a block: the largest run of consecutive non-blank
rows (runs above or below it of similar width join it; a narrow run such
as a title or a footnote does not), started at its first row that is at
least half as wide as the table. That row is the header unless it holds
numbers and no column has text in it above numbers below. The dialog shows
this as a starting point only.

[`ValueOptions`] add a decimal comma (`1,5` read as 1.5, and `1.234,5` as
1234.5, for a column whose every value reads that way) and extra missing
markers. Names are then made unique and non-blank
([`stat_data::unique_names`]) and the values typed exactly as delimited
text is ([`stat_data::table_from_records_with_notes`]).

- `struct RawSheet`: A sheet of cells as text, before any row is taken as the header: one workbook sheet, a text file split at its delimiter, a web-page table or pasted text.
- `enum CellRole`: What a cell of the preview is, under a [`Block`].
- `struct Block`: Where the table sits in a [`RawSheet`].
- `struct ValueOptions`: How values are read, beyond the standard rules.
- `struct OpenSettings`: Everything needed to read a table from a sheet: the block, the value options and, for text, the delimiter.
- `fn split_text`: Split `text` into a sheet at `delimiter` (detected when `None`; see [`stat_data::detect_delimiter`]), returning the delimiter used.
- `fn detect_decimal_comma`: Whether the sheet's numbers look written with a decimal comma: some cells read as such (`1,5`, `-0,25`) and none has a decimal point.
- `fn detect_block`: Propose where the table sits in `sheet` (see the module documentation).
- `fn detect_settings`: The settings [`detect_block`] and [`detect_decimal_comma`] propose for a sheet split at `delimiter` (`None` for a sheet that is not text).
- `type BlockText`: What [`read_block`] returns: the column names, the rows of values (as text) and notes on how they were read.
- `fn read_block`: The column names and rows of values the settings pick from `sheet` (names not yet made unique), with notes.
- `fn table_from_sheet`: The table `settings` pick from `sheet`, named `name`, with notes on how it was read.
- `fn stack_sheets`: One table from several sheets read with their own settings, stacked: a first column named `sheet_column` holds each row's sheet name, then every column any sheet has, matched by name, in the order first met (blank where a sheet lacks one).
- `fn use_row_as_names_edit`: The edit behind Data ▸ Use row as column names: the cells of `row` (0-based) become the column names (blank or repeated ones made unique as on import), the row is removed, and text columns whose remaining values are all numbers or dates are typed again, as one undoable step.

### `crates/app-model/src/outlier_analysis.rs`

Multivariate outlier distances of each row, bound to the row state
([`stat_multivariate::outliers`]).

The rows complete in every chosen column and not excluded give the mean
and covariance; each of them gets its Mahalanobis distance, jackknifed
distance and Hotelling T². The report plots the chosen distance by row
number against its reference limit (rows above it drawn as a distinct
shape and listed), and every point keeps its dataset row for brushing.
All three distances can be saved as columns.

- `enum OutlierDistance`: Which distance the report plots.
- `struct OutlierRequest`: Columns, plotted distance and α.
- `struct OutlierAnalysis`: Computed outlier distances.

### `crates/app-model/src/pareto_chart.rs`

Pareto chart of defect categories (Juran), bound to the row state
([`stat_quality::pareto`]).

Each row names a category; bars count rows, or add up a frequency column,
ranked largest first with a cumulative-percentage line. Categories below
a threshold share can be pooled into an "Other" bar, placed last. A
grouping column draws one Pareto chart per level side by side, each
ranked on its own (Juran's stratified Pareto). Every bar carries its
dataset rows, so clicking a bar selects them in every linked view.

- `struct ParetoRequest`: What to chart.
- `struct ParetoChartOptions`: Display options of a Pareto chart.
- `struct ParetoBar`: One bar of a [`ParetoChartSpec`].
- `struct ParetoPanel`: One panel (a level of the grouping column, or the whole data).
- `struct ParetoChartSpec`: Data for drawing a Pareto chart: bars at x = 1, 2, … within each panel, panels side by side with a gap of one bar.
- `const PARETO_BAR_WIDTH`: Width of a bar (bars sit one unit apart).
- `struct ParetoAnalysis`: A computed Pareto chart.

### `crates/app-model/src/pca_chart.rs`

A multivariate control chart from a principal-components model, bound to
the row state ([`stat_quality::pca_chart`]): T² on the retained component
scores and the squared prediction error (SPE) of what the model leaves
out, with variable contributions to every signal, a parallel-coordinates
view of the signalling rows, and a change-point estimate.

Rows are taken in table order, skipping excluded rows and rows missing a
value in any measurement column. The first `reference` rows (all when
`None`) fit the model; later rows are monitored against it. Every plotted
point is one dataset row, so brushing the charts selects it.

- `const PCA_PLOT_POINTS`: Signals shown in each contribution and parallel-coordinates plot (the largest statistics).
- `struct PcaChartRequest`: What to chart.
- `struct PcaChartAnalysis`: A computed principal-components monitoring chart.

### `crates/app-model/src/permutation_analysis.rs`

Permutation tests on table columns ([`stat_inference::permutation`]): two
independent groups (difference of means or of medians), paired columns
(sign-flip test of the mean difference) and the correlation of two
columns (Pearson or Spearman). Exact enumeration when the arrangements are
few, seeded Monte Carlo otherwise.

- `const MAX_RESAMPLES`: Most random arrangements a report may request.
- `enum PermutationDesign`: What is permuted.
- `struct PermutationRequest`: A permutation test request.
- `struct PermutationAnalysis`: A computed permutation test.

### `crates/app-model/src/pk_analysis.rs`

Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics bound to a dataset
([`stat_inference::nca`]): per subject (and treatment) the peak
concentration and its time, the areas under the concentration and first
moment curves to the last sample and to infinity, the terminal rate
constant with its regression, half-life, mean residence time, and, with
a dose, clearance and volume; then each parameter summarized by
treatment (geometric mean and coefficient of variation, arithmetic mean,
standard deviation, median and range), and the profiles on linear and
semi-logarithmic axes.

**Layout:** long data, one row per sample, with subject, time and
concentration columns, an optional treatment (or period) column whose
levels give separate profiles of the same subject, and an optional dose
column (the first value of each profile is used) or a single dose.
Concentrations below the limit of quantification should be entered as
0. Excluded rows and rows with a missing time or concentration are left
out.

- `enum PkDose`: Where the dose comes from.
- `struct PkRequest`: Columns and settings of a non-compartmental analysis.
- `struct PkAnalysis`: A computed non-compartmental analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/plot_breaks.rs`

Axis breaks on report plots.

Report scatter plots ([`PlotSpec`]) take the same breaks as graph
canvases ([`stat_viz::axis_breaks`]): several stretches left out of an
axis, each piece between them on its own scale and with its own share of
the axis, and slashes or a zigzag where the axis is cut. A plot's axes
are linear in data units, so the breaks are laid out on the linear scale,
with shares over the extent of everything the plot draws on that axis
([`data_extent`]).

An axis takes breaks when it is continuous: not labelled by categories,
a probability scale or dates, and not divided into panes; contour maps
and ternary plots take none ([`breakable`]). The view draws
[`broken_plot`] (every coordinate mapped, points inside a removed
stretch left out) and labels its ticks from the same maps, so box and
click selection, the screen and exported figures agree.

- `fn breakable`: Whether each axis of `spec` (`[x, y]`) can be broken.
- `fn data_extent`: The extent of everything `spec` draws on each axis (`[x, y]`): points, curves, bands, line work and annotations.
- `fn plot_breaks`: The maps of `spec`'s broken axes under `axes` (`[x, y]`; `None` for an axis without breaks or one that cannot take them).
- `fn broken_plot`: `spec` with every coordinate drawn through the broken axes `[x, y]`: points inside a removed stretch are left out (with their group memberships), curve vertices inside one are dropped and annotations in one are not drawn.
- `fn breaks_notes`: The note under a plot with points left out by a break, or whose broken axes mix scales.

### `crates/app-model/src/plot_style.rs`

Plot styles in project files, dashboards, scripts and graph files.

A [`PlotStyle`] (see `stat_viz::plot_style`) is written as one JSON object:

```text
{
  "x": {axis}, "y": {axis}, "y2": {axis},
  "equal_scale": false, "category_labels": "automatic",
  "hover_coordinates": true, "show_key": true,
  "title": "…" | null, "show_title": true,
  "scale_ratio": 1, "print_scale": millimetres | null,
  "export": {…}, "reference_lines": {"lines": [line, …], "bands": [band, …]},
  "annotations": {…}, "key": {…}
}
line = {"orientation": "horizontal" | "vertical", "value": value, "label": "…", "show_value": true,
        "color": "#rrggbb" | "#rrggbbaa" | null, "width": 1.5,
        "pattern": "solid" | "dashed" | "dotted" | "dash-dot", "scope": "whole" | "panel" | "group"}
band = {"orientation": …, "from": value, "to": value, "label": "…", "color": … | null,
        "opacity": 0.18, "edges": true, "edge_labels": true, "scope": …}
value = number | {"stat": "mean" | "median" | "quantile" | "mean-sd" | "individuals-centre"
                           | "individuals-upper" | "individuals-lower", "parameter": p or k}
axis = {"major": "auto" | interval, "minor": "none" | "auto" | {"subdivisions": n} | {"every": interval},
        "origin": 0, "grid": "major" | "major-and-minor" | "none",
        "tick_marks": true, "tick_labels": true,
        "format": "auto" | {"decimals": n} | {"scientific": n} | {"percent": n},
        "title": "…" | null, "show_title": true, "side": "standard" | "opposite",
        "break": [from, to] | null,
        "breaks": {"at": [[from, to], …], "mark": "slashes" | "zigzag",
                   "segments": [{"scale": "log10" | null, "share": percent | null}, …]},
        "tick_direction": "inside" | "outside" | "both",
        "major_mark": {"length": 5, "width": 1}, "minor_mark": {"length": 3, "width": 1},
        "offset": points, "extend_to_ticks": false,
        "custom_ticks": [{"value": v, "label": "\\pi"}, …], "range": [min, max] | null}
```

Every settings member is written, so a style read back is the style
written whatever the plot's own defaults are; members left out of a file
keep the value they have in the style the file is read onto. The four
formatting parts are written only when they differ from their defaults.
Graph canvases keep their titles and breaks in their own `"axes"` member,
so their style is written without them ([`StyleTitles::Without`]).

`"break"` is an axis's first break, kept for files read by earlier
versions; `"breaks"` (written when anything beyond one plain break is set)
holds every break, each piece's scale (`null`: the axis's own) and share
of the axis in percent (`null`: automatic), and the break-mark style, and
wins when both are present.

- `enum StyleTitles`: Whether titles and axis breaks are part of a written style.
- `fn plot_style_to_json`: The JSON form of `style` (see the module documentation).
- `fn plot_style_from_json`: Read [`plot_style_to_json`] onto `style`: members left out keep their value in `style`.
- `fn reference_to_json`: The JSON form of a plot's reference lines and bands.
- `fn reference_from_json`: Read [`reference_to_json`].

### `crates/app-model/src/plot_view.rs`

Plot view limits and the axis-drag gestures that change them.

Each axis behaves like a ruler the user can grab:

* **Near either end** (the outer [`END_HANDLE_FRACTION`] of its length) the
  axis is a *handle* for that limit: dragging moves only that limit while the
  opposite limit stays fixed, and the value that was under the pointer when
  the drag began stays under the pointer — so the axis stretches or
  compresses to follow it.
* **Anywhere else** dragging *shifts* the whole axis: both limits move
  together and the visible span is unchanged, again keeping the grabbed value
  under the pointer.

Positions are measured along the axis in screen units, from the end with the
smaller value: left-to-right for a horizontal axis and bottom-to-top for a
vertical one (callers convert from screen coordinates, whose y grows
downward).

- `const END_HANDLE_FRACTION`: Fraction of an axis's length, at each end, that acts as a limit handle.
- `const MIN_HANDLE_DISTANCE`: Closest the pointer may come to the fixed end while dragging a handle, in screen units; prevents division by (near) zero.
- `struct ViewBounds`: Visible data ranges of a plot.
- `enum Axis`: Which axis.
- `enum AxisHandle`: What dragging at a position on an axis does.
- `fn handle_at`: The handle under a position `along` an axis of screen length `length` (measured from the smaller-value end).
- `struct AxisDrag`: An axis drag in progress: the state captured when it began.
- `fn drag_range`: New `(lower, upper)` limits of one axis after a drag from `start_along` to `along`, for an axis of screen length `length` showing `[lower, upper]`.

### `crates/app-model/src/pls_analysis.rs`

Partial least squares regression bound to a dataset
([`stat_predictive::pls`]), with the shared predictive-model sections
([`crate::prediction`]).

**Responses.** A continuous response gives PLS regression. A categorical
response gives PLS discriminant analysis (PLS-DA): one 0/1 indicator per
class is modelled together, and a row is assigned the class with the
largest predicted indicator. For the fit measures, the predicted
indicators are clipped to [0, 1] and rescaled to sum to 1; they rank rows
like probabilities but are not calibrated.

**Rows.** Predictors must be numeric. Rows that are excluded, miss the
response or miss any predictor are left out (PLS has no rule for missing
values); their predictions are missing.

**Number of factors.** The fewest factors whose held-out mean squared
error is within one standard error of the smallest
([`stat_predictive::choose_factors`]): held out on the validation rows
when there are any, otherwise by k-fold cross-validation on the training
rows (the k-fold method's folds, or 10 folds). The predicted residual
sum of squares (PRESS) is shown factor by factor. A fixed number may be
set instead.

- `struct PlsRequest`: Columns and settings of a PLS model.
- `struct PlsAnalysis`: A fitted PLS model.
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response` and `predictors`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry (missing members take their defaults).

### `crates/app-model/src/pooling.rs`

Reports pooled across multiply imputed data sets.

A stacked imputation table ([`crate::multiple_imputation`]) holds the
original rows (imputation 0) and `m` completed copies. A report on it
whose scope pools by the imputation column ([`ReportScope::pool`]) is
fitted to each completed copy separately and the results are combined
by Rubin's rules ([`stat_inference::pooling`]): pooled estimates with
Barnard–Rubin degrees of freedom and their within/between variance
split, multi-parameter tests (D₁; for linear models also D₃), pooled R²
for linear models, and each imputation's own estimates. The report's
usual sections follow, computed from the original rows only
(imputation 0), which is the complete-case analysis.

Supported reports and what is pooled:

* linear models: coefficients (with one design, so centred terms and
  category levels mean the same in every imputation), D₁ and D₃ tests of
  each effect and of the whole model, R² and adjusted R² on Fisher's z
  scale (Harel 2009); complete-data degrees of freedom `n − p`;
* generalized linear and mixed models: coefficients and D₁ tests of each
  term, with `ν_com = n − p` (as R mice uses for these models);
* one-sample tests: the mean (`ν_com = n − 1`); two independent groups:
  the difference in means with the pooled variance (`ν_com = n₁ + n₂ − 2`),
  and with more groups each group's mean; two paired columns: the mean
  difference (`ν_com = n − 1`);
* correlations: each Pearson correlation on Fisher's z scale.

[`ReportScope::pool`]: crate::report_scope::ReportScope::pool

- `const TERMS_BY_IMPUTATION`: Most terms listed by imputation in the drill-down table.
- `fn can_pool`: Whether reports like `saved` can be pooled across imputations.
- `fn pooled_sections`: The pooled sections for `report` on `table`, whose column `column` numbers the imputations; `rows` are the table's row states narrowed by the report's own row filter.
- `fn imputation_count`: How many imputations a pooled report on `table` combines.

### `crates/app-model/src/power_analysis.rs`

Power and sample-size reports ([`stat_inference::power`]). These reports
do not read the data table: they describe a planned study.

One of three quantities is solved for, given the others: the power for a
sample size, the sample size for a target power, or the smallest effect
detectable with a sample size and target power. The report shows the
inputs, the answer, power against sample size, and power against the size
of the effect.

Besides tests of means, proportions, rates, standard deviations and
equivalence, the designs include margins of error (the answer is the
probability that the interval's half-width is at most a chosen `E`),
tolerance intervals (the probability that the interval's content stays
below a chosen limit), and two-level, screening and general factorial
experiments, where the sample size is the number of replicates.

- `enum PowerSolve`: What to solve for.
- `struct PowerRequest`: A power or sample-size question.
- `struct PowerAnalysis`: The answer to a [`PowerRequest`].
- `fn effect_name`: Name of the effect parameter of a design.
- `fn power_name`: Name of the probability a design reports: the power of a test, or for estimation designs the probability of the planned precision.
- `fn design_rows`: Labelled parameters of a design.

### `crates/app-model/src/prediction.rs`

The shared framework for predictive models (decision trees now; forests,
boosting and the others of the roadmap later): which rows train, tune and
test a model ([`ValidationMethod`], [`RoleAssignment`]), the response as a
model sees it ([`Response`]), predictions for every row
([`Predictions`]), and the report sections and saved columns every
predictive model shares ([`fit_measures_section`],
[`confusion_section`], [`prediction_columns`]) through the [`Predictor`]
interface. Fitted predictors also implement
[`crate::surface_profiler::SurfaceModel`], so they get the Response
Explorer, the 3-D profiler and several-responses desirability.

Fit measures are those of [`stat_predictive::measures`], reported for
each role: training rows show how well the model fits the data it learned
from (optimistic), validation rows the data that chose its size, and test
rows (used for neither) an honest estimate for new data.

- `enum ValidationMethod`: How rows are divided between training, validation and test.
- `enum Response`: The response as a predictive model sees it, for every table row.
- `struct PredictorInfo`: One predictor of a tree-based model.
- `struct FeatureSet`: The predictors of a tree-based model and their values for every row.
- `fn setting_value`: A profiler setting as a predictor value (missing when it does not fit the predictor).
- `struct RoleAssignment`: The role of every table row.
- `enum Predictions`: Predictions for every table row (NaN where the model cannot predict).
- `trait Predictor`: A fitted predictive model, as shared report sections see it.
- `fn fit_measures_section`: "Fit by Role": the fit measures of `model` on its training, validation and test rows, and from cross-validation when used.
- `fn confusion_section`: Confusion matrices (actual by predicted counts) of a categorical response, one block per role; `None` for a continuous response.
- `struct PredictionFormulas`: Formulas computing a model's predictions, for formula columns.
- `fn prediction_columns`: Columns a predictive model can save: predicted values (continuous), or each class's probability and the most probable class (categorical), as formula columns when `formulas` gives them; and the validation roles.

### `crates/app-model/src/prediction_formula.rs`

A fitted model's prediction equation written as a formula column
(see [`crate::formula`]), so the predictions follow later edits to the
data and can be computed for new rows.

The linear predictor `η = b₀ + Σ bⱼ xⱼ` is written effect by effect, the
way [`ModelDesign`] codes the design columns:

* a continuous main effect is `b * x`;
* a continuous factor inside an interaction or power is centred at its
  mean over the rows the model was fitted to: `b * (x - x̄) ** 2`;
* a spline term is one `natural_spline(x, [knots], k)` or
  `bspline(x, [knots], degree, k)` per basis column (boundary knots first
  and last; see [`crate::formula`]);
* an effect with categorical factors becomes a `switch` on the level (or,
  for several factors, on the levels joined by a tab), giving each level
  combination its effective coefficient `Σ bⱼ cⱼ` under the design's
  coding (reference or sum-to-zero), times the effect's continuous part.
  A level the model was not fitted to falls to `0.0 / 0.0` (NaN), which
  makes that row's prediction missing without an evaluation error.

Effects whose coefficients are all exactly zero (e.g. predictors a lasso
dropped) are left out. The mean is the inverse link of `η`: `logistic(η)`
for the logit link, `exp(η)` for the log link. Coefficients are written
with every digit needed to read back the same `f64`, so the formula
reproduces the model's predictions to rounding.

- `enum Link`: How the model maps its linear predictor `η` to the predicted mean.
- `struct FactorColumn`: A predictor column as the formula reads it.
- `fn factor_columns`: The predictor columns `indices` of `table`, in order (skipping unknown indices, which a fit would already have refused).
- `fn prediction_formula`: The formula predicting the response of a model with design `design` (predictors read from `factors`, one per design term), intercept `intercept`, one coefficient per design column in `slopes`, and link `link`.

### `crates/app-model/src/project/folders.rs`

Folders the user makes in a project's tree, to group its tables,
reports (graph canvases included), dashboards and notebooks.

A folder has a name, folders of its own and a set of items. Each item is
in at most one folder; items in no folder stay at the top of the project.
Folders change nothing about the items themselves: a report in a folder
still belongs to its table and re-runs with it.

Folders are saved in the version-3 form as the optional member
`"folders"`:

```text
"folders": [
  { "name": "…",
    "items": [ {"table": "table-1"}
             | {"table": "table-1", "report": index}   (index in that table's "reports")
             | {"dashboard": "dashboard-1"}
             | {"notebook": "…"}, … ],                 (optional)
    "folders": [ … ] },                                (optional; folders inside)
  …
]
```

On reading, items that name a table, report, dashboard or notebook the
project does not have are left out, as is a second mention of an item
already placed; report indices follow reports left out on reading.

- `const MAX_FOLDER_DEPTH`: Deepest nesting of folders read from a file (deeper ones are an error, so a malformed file cannot exhaust the stack).
- `enum FolderItem`: Something a folder can hold.
- `struct ProjectFolder`: A folder of a project's tree.

### `crates/app-model/src/project/tables.rs`

Project files holding several tables, with derived-table lineage and a
window layout (format version 3; see the parent module for the
JSON form).

A [`ProjectFile`] is a list of [`ProjectTable`]s, each with a stable
[`TableId`], plus the project's scripts and an optional
[`ProjectLayout`]. A table made by a table operation keeps a
[`TableLineage`]: the operation ([`TableOrigin`]), the ids of its source
tables within the project, and a [`DataFingerprint`] of each source as it
was when the table was made. Comparing those fingerprints with the
sources' current data ([`ProjectFile::origin_is_stale`]) tells whether a
source changed since; [`ProjectFile::rerun_origin`] re-runs the stored
operation on the current sources through [`TableOperation::run`].

[`save_project_file`] writes a project with exactly one table, an empty
layout and no dashboards in the single-table form of [`save_project`] (byte for byte), so
builds that predate version 3 still open it; anything else is written in
the version-3 form. [`load_project_file`] reads both.

- `const PROJECT_FILE_VERSION`: Version written for project files in the several-table form.
- `struct TableId`: A table's identifier within a project file: stable across saves and independent of the table's (editable) name.
- `struct DataFingerprint`: A 64-bit FNV-1a hash of a source table's contents, with the row states the operation reads (see [`DataFingerprint::of_source`]).
- `struct SourceSnapshot`: One source of a derived table, as it was when the table was made.
- `struct TableLineage`: How a table in a project was made: the operation and, for each of its sources, where that source is in the project and what it held.
- `struct ProjectTable`: One table in a project file, with everything kept alongside it.
- `enum ViewMode`: How a table's document is shown.
- `struct TableView`: A table's view mode in the layout.
- `enum WindowContent`: What a popped-out window shows.
- `struct PoppedOutWindow`: A window popped out of the main window.
- `struct DashboardWindow`: A dashboard shown in a window of its own.
- `struct ProjectLayout`: Plain data describing how the application had the project laid out.
- `struct ProjectFile`: A project: several tables, their scripts, dashboards and layout.
- `struct Rerun`: The result of [`ProjectFile::rerun_origin`].
- `fn save_project_file`: Serialize a project file to JSON text.
- `fn load_project_file`: Parse a project file in either form: a version 1 or 2 single-table project (which becomes a one-table [`ProjectFile`] whose table has the id `table-1`), or a version-3 file written by [`save_project_file`].
- `fn load_project_file_noting`: [`load_project_file`], also returning notes on what could not be restored: reports and dashboard tiles that cannot be read are left out, and formula columns on a cycle or that no longer compile keep their saved values, each with a note naming it and why (see [`load_project_noting`](super::load_pr…

### `crates/app-model/src/project.rs`

Project files: a dataset together with its row states and the analyses run
on it, so that reopening the file brings every report back.

#### Format
A project is a UTF-8 JSON document (extension `.acraft`):

```text
{
  "format": "statistical-engine-project",
  "version": 1 | 2,
  "table": {
    "name": "…",
    "columns": [ {"name": "…", "type": "numeric" | "text" | "datetime",
                  "level": "continuous" | "nominal" | "ordinal",
                  "value_labels": [["1", "Treatment"], …],     (optional)
                  "hover": true,                                (optional)
                  "values": [ … ]}, … ]
  },
  "rows": { "excluded": [row, …], "hidden": [row, …], "selected": [row, …],
            "colors": [[row, "#rrggbb"], …],
            "markers": [[row, "square"], …],                   (optional)
            "style_column": "…",                               (optional)
            "subsets": [{"name": "…", "rows": [row, …]}, …],   (optional)
            "active_subset": "…" },                            (optional)
  "reports": [ {"analysis": "linear-model", "response": "y", …,
                "options": {…}}, … ],
  "origin": {"operation": "stack", "sources": ["…"], …}   (optional)
  "scripts": [ {"name": "…", "source": "…", "run_on_open": true}, … ]
                                                          (optional)
}
```

Numbers are written in shortest round-trip form and missing numeric values
as `null`, so the data reload bit for bit.

A `"datetime"` column (version 2) stores its values as numbers of seconds
since 1970-01-01T00:00:00 UTC (`null` when missing), exactly like a numeric
column, plus how they are shown: `"format"` (`"date"`, `"datetime"`,
`"time"` or `"duration"`), `"fraction_digits"` (0–6) and `"offset_minutes"`
(the display offset from UTC). A project is written as version 1 unless it
has a date-time column, so files without dates still open in builds that
predate version 2; version 1 files always load. Reports store what was asked for
(columns by name, settings, display options), not results: on loading, each
analysis is re-run on the restored data and row states, which reproduces the
report exactly because every analysis is deterministic.

`"origin"`, present only for a table made by a table operation, records
the operation and its options ([`crate::table_ops::TableOrigin`]). It is
optional, so it does not change the format version.

`"external_source"`, present only for a table read from a database or the
web, records the connection and query, or the URL and headers, so the
table can be refreshed ([`crate::external::ExternalSource`]). It never
holds a password or a secret header value. Also optional.

`"scripts"`, present only when the project carries scripts, holds Rhai
scripts ([`ProjectScript`]) kept with the data. Those marked
`"run_on_open"` are offered to run when the project is opened; the
application asks before running them. Also optional.

#### Several tables (version 3)
A project holding more than one table, dashboards or a window layout is written by
[`save_project_file`] in a second form, version 3:

```text
{
  "format": "statistical-engine-project",
  "version": 3,
  "tables": [
    { "id": "table-1",
      "table": {…}, "rows": {…}, "reports": [ … ],   (as in the single-table form)
      "origin": {…},                                 (optional, as above)
      "source_tables": [ {"id": "table-2", "fingerprint": "89ab…"} | null, … ],
                                                     (with "origin" only)
      "external_source": {…} },                      (optional, as above)
    …
  ],
  "scripts": [ … ],                                  (optional, as above)
  "name": "…",                                       (optional: the name the user gave the
                                                     project, shown instead of the file's)
  "notebooks": [                                     (optional; crate::notebook)
    { "name": "…",
      "cells": [ {"kind": "text" | "code", "source": "…",
                  "run": n,                          (optional: run number)
                  "outputs": [ {"kind": "printed" | "value" | "note", "text": "…"}
                             | {"kind": "error", "text": "…", "line": n}
                             | {"kind": "table", "title": "…", "columns": […], "rows": [[…], …]}
                             | {"kind": "report", "table": "…", "title": "…"}, … ]}, … ]},
    … ],
  "folders": [                                       (optional; folders::ProjectFolder)
    { "name": "…",
      "items": [ {"table": "table-1"} | {"table": "table-1", "report": index}
               | {"dashboard": "dashboard-1"} | {"notebook": "…"}, … ],
      "folders": [ … ] }, … ],                       (both optional)
  "dashboards": [                                    (optional)
    { "id": "dashboard-1", "name": "…",
      "grid_columns": 12,                            (optional; default 12)
      "filters": [ {"column": "…", "levels": ["…", …]}
                 | {"column": "…", "min": x, "max": y}, … ],   (optional)
      "tiles": [                                     (optional)
        { "id": 1, "column": 0, "row": 0, "width": 6, "height": 4,
          "table": "table-1", "report": {…} },        (a report tile)
        { "id": 2, "column": 6, "row": 0, "width": 6, "height": 1,
          "text": "…", "style": "heading" | "body" }, (a text tile; style optional)
        … ] },
    …
  ],
  "layout": {                                        (optional; every member optional)
    "active_table": "table-1",
    "views": [ {"table": "table-1", "mode": "data" | "results" | "side-by-side"}, … ],
    "windows": [ {"table": "table-2", "view": "data" | "results" | {"report": index},
```
