- `enum CorrelationStatistic`: Correlation coefficient tested for independence.
- `struct PermutationOptions`: How a permutation test is carried out.
- `struct PermutationTest`: Result of a permutation test.
- `fn two_groups`: Permutation test comparing two independent samples `first` and `second` by `statistic` (first − second).
- `fn paired`: Permutation (sign-flip) test of paired differences `differences` (e.g.
- `fn correlation`: Permutation test of independence of paired values `x` and `y` by their correlation (`Greater`: positive association).

### `crates/stat-inference/src/pooling.rs`

Combining analyses of multiply imputed data sets (Rubin's rules).

After `m` completed data sets have each been analysed, every parameter
has `m` estimates `Q̂ₗ` and squared standard errors `Uₗ`. Rubin (1987,
*Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys*, §3.1) combines them as

```text
Q̄ = (1/m) Σ Q̂ₗ                       pooled estimate
Ū = (1/m) Σ Uₗ                       within-imputation variance
B = Σ (Q̂ₗ − Q̄)² / (m − 1)            between-imputation variance
T = Ū + (1 + 1/m) B                  total variance
```

with the relative increase in variance `r = (1 + 1/m) B / Ū`, the share of
the variance due to the missing values `λ = (1 + 1/m) B / T`, and the
fraction of missing information `γ = (r + 2/(ν + 3)) / (r + 1)`. The
reference distribution is Student's t with the Barnard & Rubin (1999,
*Biometrika* 86) small-sample degrees of freedom

```text
ν_old = (m − 1) / λ²
ν_obs = (ν_com + 1)/(ν_com + 3) · ν_com · (1 − λ)
ν     = ν_old ν_obs / (ν_old + ν_obs)        (ν = ν_old when ν_com = ∞)
```

where `ν_com` is the degrees of freedom the analysis would have with no
missing values (`n − p` for a regression; infinite for large-sample
tests). As in van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn (2011, *J. Stat. Softw.*
45(3)) `λ` is floored at 10⁻⁴ inside `ν_old`, so a parameter the missing
values do not affect gets a large but finite `ν`.

#### Several parameters at once
[`pool_wald`] is the D₁ statistic of Li, Raghunathan & Rubin (1991,
*JASA* 86): for `k` parameters with pooled estimate `Q̄`, average
covariance `Ū` and between-imputation covariance `B`,

```text
r₁ = (1 + 1/m) tr(B Ū⁻¹) / k,     D₁ = (Q̄ − Q₀)ᵀ Ū⁻¹ (Q̄ − Q₀) / (k (1 + r₁)),
```

referred to F(k, ν₁). With `a = k(m − 1)`, `ν₁ = 4 + (a − 4)(1 + (1 − 2/a)/r₁)²`
when `a > 4`, else `a (1 + 1/k)(1 + 1/r₁)² / 2`; with complete-data
degrees of freedom `ν_com` the small-sample form of Reiter (2007,
*Biometrika* 94) is used instead.

[`pool_likelihood_ratio`] is the D₃ statistic of Meng & Rubin (1992,
*Biometrika* 79): with `dₗ` the likelihood-ratio statistic of data set `l`
at its own estimates and `d̃ₗ` the same statistic with both models' parameters
held at their pooled values,

```text
r₃ = (m + 1) / (k (m − 1)) · (d̄ − d̃̄),       D₃ = d̃̄ / (k (1 + r₃)),
```

referred to F(k, ν₃) with `ν₃` from the large-sample formula for `ν₁` (`r₃` in
place of `r₁`).

#### R² and correlations
[`pool_correlation`] pools correlations on Fisher's z scale
(`z = atanh r`, variance `1/(n − 3)`, `ν_com = ∞`) and transforms the
pooled value and its interval back; [`pool_r_squared`] does the same with
`√R²` (Harel 2009, *J. Appl. Stat.* 36).

- `struct PooledEstimate`: One parameter pooled across imputations by Rubin's rules.
- `fn barnard_rubin_df`: Barnard–Rubin degrees of freedom for `m` imputations with between-imputation variance `b`, total variance `t` and complete-data degrees of freedom `df_complete` (`f64::INFINITY` for large-sample analyses).
- `fn pool_scalar`: Pool one parameter's estimates `estimates[l]` and squared standard errors `variances[l]` from `m ≥ 2` imputations by Rubin's rules, testing `Q = null` and giving a two-sided interval at `level`.
- `struct PooledTest`: A test of several parameters at once, combined across imputations.
- `fn pool_wald`: The D₁ (pooled Wald) test that `k` parameters equal `null` jointly.
- `fn pool_likelihood_ratio`: The D₃ (pooled likelihood-ratio) test of a model against a model with `k` fewer parameters.
- `struct PooledCorrelation`: A correlation (or `√R²`) pooled on Fisher's z scale.
- `fn pool_correlation`: Pool correlations `r[l]`, each from `n[l]` rows (`n > 3`), on Fisher's z scale with variance `1/(n − 3)` and no complete-data degrees of freedom; the interval is `z̄ ± z_{1−α/2} √T` transformed back.
- `fn pool_r_squared`: Pool coefficients of determination `r_squared[l]`, each from `n[l]` rows, as `√R²` on Fisher's z scale (Harel 2009), squaring the pooled value and interval ends back (an interval end below zero becomes 0).

### `crates/stat-inference/src/power.rs`

Power, sample size and detectable difference.

Power is the probability that a test at level `α` rejects `H₀` when a
specified alternative is true. Each design below has a power function of
the sample size `n` (per group; the second group has `round(r·n)` units for
an allocation ratio `r`):

| Test | Power (one-sided `>` shown; two-sided adds the other tail) |
|---|---|
| One-sample / paired t | `P(T'_{n−1,δ√n/σ} > t_{1−α})` — noncentral t |
| Two-sample t (pooled) | `P(T'_{n₁+n₂−2, δ/(σ√(1/n₁+1/n₂))} > t_{1−α})` |
| One-way ANOVA, `k` groups | `P(F'_{k−1, k(n−1), λ} > F_{1−α})`, `λ = nD²/(2σ²)` for a largest difference `D` between means (the least favourable spread: two means `D` apart, the rest midway) |
| One proportion (score test) | `Φ((p₁ − p₀ − z_{1−α}√(p₀q₀/n)) / √(p₁q₁/n))` |
| Two proportions (pooled z) | `Φ((p₁ − p₂ − z_{1−α}σ₀)/σ₁)`, `σ₀² = p̄q̄(1/n₁+1/n₂)`, `σ₁² = p₁q₁/n₁ + p₂q₂/n₂` |
| One standard deviation (χ²) | `P(χ²_{n−1} > χ²_{1−α}σ₀²/σ₁²)` |
| Two variances (F) | `P(F_{n₁−1,n₂−1} > F_{1−α}/ρ)`, `ρ = σ₁²/σ₂²` |
| Equivalence (TOST) | exact: `∫ f_{χ²_ν}(v) [Φ((U − cŝ − δ)/s) − Φ((L + cŝ − δ)/s)]₊ dv`, `ŝ = s√(v/ν)`, `c = t_{1−α,ν}` |
| One-sample z (σ known) | `Φ(δ√n/σ − z_{1−α})` |
| Paired t from the two SDs | as one-sample t with `σ_d = σ√(2(1 − ρ))`, `ρ` the correlation of the pair |
| One Poisson rate (score z) | `Φ((λ₁ − λ₀ − z_{1−α}√(λ₀/t))/√(λ₁/t))`, exposure `t = n·e` |
| Two Poisson rates (z) | `Φ((λ₁ − λ₂ − z_{1−α}σ₀)/σ₁)`, `σ₀² = λ̄(1/t₁ + 1/t₂)`, `σ₁² = λ₁/t₁ + λ₂/t₂`, `λ̄` the exposure-weighted mean |
| Two-level factorial or screening design, one effect `Δ` (high − low) | `P(F'_{1, ν_E, λ} > F_{1−α})`, `λ = r·m·Δ²/(4σ²)` for `r` replicates of `m` runs; `ν_E = rm + c − 1 − p` with `c` centre points and `p` model terms |
| General full factorial, one factor with `L` levels, largest difference `D` | `P(F'_{L−1, LC(r−1), λ} > F_{1−α})`, `λ = rCD²/(2σ²)`, `C` the cells of the other factors (full model) |

**Estimation.** For a planned confidence interval the "power" is the
probability that the interval's margin of error (half-width, or the
distance from the estimate to the farther limit) is at most `E` (Kupper &
Hafner 1989, *Am. Statistician* 43; Beal 1989, *Biometrics* 45):

| Interval | `P(margin ≤ E)` |
|---|---|
| Mean, `x̄ ± t_{1−α/2} s/√n` | `P(χ²_{n−1} ≤ (n−1)nE²/(t²σ²))` |
| Standard deviation, `s√((n−1)/χ²_{1−α/2})` to `s√((n−1)/χ²_{α/2})` | `P(χ²_{n−1} ≤ (n−1)(E/((b − 1)σ))²)`, `b = √((n−1)/χ²_{α/2})` |
| Proportion (Wilson score interval) | `Σₓ b(x; n, p)·[h(x) ≤ E]`, `h` the Wilson half-width at `x` |
| Poisson rate (score interval, exposure `t = n·e`) | `P(X ≤ (Et/z)² − z²/4)`, `X ~ Poisson(λt)`, half-width `z√(X + z²/4)/t` |

**Tolerance intervals** (normal, factor `k` for content `P` with
confidence `γ`): the "power" is the probability that the interval does
not contain more than `P′ > P` of the population, `1 −
P(content ≥ P′)` (Faulkenberry & Weeks 1968, *Technometrics* 10; Odeh &
Owen, *Tables for Normal Tolerance Limits, Sampling Plans and
Screening*, 1980), computed exactly from
[`crate::tolerance::tolerance_content_probability`]. At `P′ = P` it is
`1 − γ`.

**Distribution-free tolerance intervals** (Wilks 1941, *Ann. Math.
Statist.* 12; Guenther 1977, *Sampling Inspection in Statistical Quality
Control*, ch. 6): the interval from the `r`-th smallest to the `s`-th
largest of `n` values (any continuous population) leaves `m = r + s` order
statistics outside it, and its content is `Beta(n − m + 1, m)`. The
"power" is the confidence `P(content ≥ P) = P(Bin(n, P) ≤ n − m) =
Σ_{j=0}^{n−m} C(n, j) Pʲ(1 − P)^{n−j}`; the extremes give `1 − Pⁿ` for
one limit (`m = 1`) and `1 − nPⁿ⁻¹ + (n − 1)Pⁿ` for two (`m = 2`). The
sample size is the smallest `n` reaching the target confidence, and the
"effect" is `P` (the largest content reached with that confidence).

(Cohen, *Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences*, 2nd ed.;
Chow, Shao & Wang, *Sample Size Calculations in Clinical Research*, 2nd ed.,
§§3.1–4.2, 10.3; Fleiss, Levin & Paik, *Statistical Methods for Rates and
Proportions*, 3rd ed., §4.2; Phillips 1990, *J. Pharmacokinet. Biopharm.*
18:137 for TOST.) The proportion formulas are the usual normal
approximations.

The required sample size is the smallest `n` whose power reaches the
target (found by doubling then bisection); the detectable difference is the
smallest effect, in the direction of the alternative, with that power.

- `enum PowerDesign`: A design whose power is to be computed.
- `struct SampleSize`: Result of a sample-size search.

### `crates/stat-inference/src/proportions.rs`

Tests and intervals for proportions (Agresti, *Categorical Data Analysis*,
3rd ed., §§1.4, 3.1, 3.5, 11.1; Newcombe 1998, *Stat. Med.* 17:873).

* **Exact binomial test** of `p = p₀`: one-sided tails of Binomial(`n`,
  `p₀`); the two-sided p-value sums the probabilities of every outcome no
  more likely than the one observed (relative tolerance 10⁻⁷). Interval:
  Clopper–Pearson, `B(α/2; x, n − x + 1)` to `B(1 − α/2; x + 1, n − x)`.
* **Score test:** `z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n)` with the Wilson interval
  `[p̂ + z²/2n ± z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/4n²)] / (1 + z²/n)`.
* **Two proportions:** pooled z test
  `z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̄(1 − p̄)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂))`; interval for `p₁ − p₂` by
  Newcombe's hybrid score method (from the two Wilson intervals).
* **Fisher's exact test** conditions on the margins (hypergeometric); the
  two-sided p-value sums tables no more likely than the observed one.
* **Relative risk** `p̂₁/p̂₂` and **odds ratio** with log-scale (Katz,
  Woolf) two-sided intervals. For the odds ratio ½ is added to every cell
  when any cell is zero; for the relative risk only when a group has no
  successes (each group's total then grows by 1), since `p̂₁/p̂₂` and its
  log-scale variance stay finite when a group has no failures. The Fisher result's interval is the
  Woolf interval at the test's level and alternative (one-sided: `z_{1−α}`,
  with the unbounded side `[0, …` or `…, ∞)`).
* **McNemar's test** for paired binary outcomes uses only the discordant
  counts `b, c`: `χ² = (|b − c| − 1)²/(b + c)` on 1 df (continuity
  corrected), and the exact binomial test of `b` out of `b + c` at ½.

- `fn newcombe_difference`: Difference of two independent proportions `x₁/n₁ − x₂/n₂` with Newcombe's hybrid score interval (Newcombe, *Stat.
- `fn exact_binomial_test`: Exact binomial test of `p = p0` with the Clopper–Pearson interval.
- `fn score_test`: Score (z) test of `p = p0` with the Wilson interval.
- `struct RatioEstimate`: A ratio estimate with confidence limits.
- `struct TwoProportions`: Comparison of two independent proportions.
- `fn two_proportions`: Compare `x1` of `n1` with `x2` of `n2`.
- `struct McNemarTest`: McNemar's test for a paired 2×2 table `[[both, first only], [second only, neither]]` (`n12` = yes then no, `n21` = no then yes).
- `fn mcnemar_test`: McNemar's test.

### `crates/stat-inference/src/pvalues.rs`

Multiple-testing adjustment and combination of p-values.

**Adjustment.** For `m` p-values with ordered values
`p₍₁₎ ≤ … ≤ p₍ₘ₎`, each method returns adjusted p-values `p̃ᵢ`: rejecting
every hypothesis with `p̃ᵢ ≤ α` controls the stated error rate at `α`.

* **Bonferroni:** `p̃ᵢ = min(1, m pᵢ)` (familywise error rate, FWER).
* **Šidák** (1967): `p̃ᵢ = 1 − (1 − pᵢ)ᵐ` (FWER for independent tests).
* **Holm** (1979) step-down: `p̃₍ᵢ₎ = maxⱼ≤ᵢ min(1, (m − j + 1) p₍ⱼ₎)` (FWER).
* **Hochberg** (1988) step-up: `p̃₍ᵢ₎ = minⱼ≥ᵢ min(1, (m − j + 1) p₍ⱼ₎)`
  (FWER under independence or positive dependence).
* **Benjamini–Hochberg** (1995): `p̃₍ᵢ₎ = minⱼ≥ᵢ min(1, m p₍ⱼ₎ / j)`
  (false discovery rate, FDR, under independence or positive dependence).
* **Benjamini–Yekutieli** (2001): as Benjamini–Hochberg multiplied by
  `c(m) = Σₖ₌₁ᵐ 1/k` (FDR under any dependence).
* **Storey q-values** (Storey 2002, *JRSS B* 64; Storey & Tibshirani
  2003, *PNAS* 100): the proportion of true null hypotheses is estimated
  as `π̂₀(λ) = #{pᵢ > λ} / (m(1 − λ))` (capped at 1; `λ = ½` by default),
  and `q₍ᵢ₎ = minⱼ≥ᵢ min(1, π̂₀ m p₍ⱼ₎ / j)` — Benjamini–Hochberg scaled by
  `π̂₀`.

Missing (NaN) p-values are left out: `m` counts the others and their
adjusted values stay NaN, as R's `p.adjust` does.

**Combination** of `k` independent p-values for one overall hypothesis:

* **Fisher** (1932): `X² = −2 Σ ln pᵢ`, χ² on `2k` df under the null.
* **Stouffer** (1949), optionally weighted (Liptak 1958):
  `Z = Σ wᵢ Φ⁻¹(1 − pᵢ) / √(Σ wᵢ²)`, standard normal under the null; the
  combined p-value is `1 − Φ(Z)`. The inputs are read as one-sided
  p-values (all in the same direction).

- `enum AdjustMethod`: How to adjust p-values for multiple testing.
- `fn adjust_p_values`: Adjust `p` by `method`.
- `struct QValues`: Storey's q-values with the estimated proportion of true nulls.
- `fn storey_q_values`: Storey's (2002) q-values with `π̂₀(λ) = #{p > λ}/(m(1 − λ))`.
- `struct CombinedTest`: A combined test of several p-values.
- `fn fisher_combined`: Fisher's combined test `X² = −2 Σ ln pᵢ` on `2k` df (NaN p-values left out).
- `fn stouffer_combined`: Stouffer's (weighted) Z: `Σ wᵢ Φ⁻¹(1 − pᵢ) / √(Σ wᵢ²)`, p-value `1 − Φ(Z)`.

### `crates/stat-inference/src/rates.rs`

Exact tests for Poisson event rates (counts per unit of exposure such as
time, area or units inspected).

* **One rate:** with `x` events in exposure `T`, `X ~ Poisson(λT)`; the test
  of `λ = λ₀` uses the Poisson tails at mean `λ₀T` (two-sided: total
  probability of counts no more likely than `x`). The Garwood (1936)
  interval is `(χ²_{α/2}(2x)/2T, χ²_{1−α/2}(2x + 2)/2T)`.
* **Rate ratio** `λ₁/λ₂`: conditional on `x₁ + x₂`, `x₁` is
  Binomial(`x₁ + x₂`, `π`), `π = ρT₁/(ρT₁ + T₂)`, so the exact binomial test
  of `π = π₀` tests `ρ = ρ₀`; the Clopper–Pearson limits `(π_L, π_U)` give
  `ρ = π/(1 − π)·T₂/T₁` (Przyborowski & Wilenski 1940; Lehmann & Romano,
  *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, §4.6).

- `fn one_rate_test`: Exact test that the event rate equals `rate0`, with the Garwood interval.
- `fn rate_ratio_test`: Exact conditional test that the rate ratio `λ₁/λ₂` equals `ratio0`.

### `crates/stat-inference/src/repeated.rs`

Repeated-measures (within-subject) analysis of variance.

With `n` subjects each measured under `k` conditions (`yᵢⱼ`), the total sum
of squares splits into conditions `SS_C = nΣ(ȳ·ⱼ − ȳ)²`, subjects
`SS_S = kΣ(ȳᵢ· − ȳ)²` and error `SS_E` (the subject × condition
interaction). `F = (SS_C/(k−1)) / (SS_E/((n−1)(k−1)))`.

The F test assumes sphericity: equal variances of every difference between
conditions. Mauchly's (1940) test checks it, and two estimates of the
departure `ε` multiply both degrees of freedom: Greenhouse–Geisser (1959)
`ε̂ = tr(E)² / (d · tr(E²))`, from the error sums of squares and products
`E` of `d` orthonormal contrasts among the conditions (`ε̂ = 1` under
sphericity and `1/d` at worst), and Huynh–Feldt (1976) with Lecoutre's
(1991) correction, `ε̃ = ((ν + 1) d ε̂ − 2) / (d (ν − d ε̂))` for `ν` error
degrees of freedom, used capped at 1 (Maxwell & Delaney, *Designing
Experiments and Analyzing Data*, 2nd ed., ch. 11–12).

[`factorial_repeated_measures`] handles several within-subject factors
and between-subject factors by the multivariate formulation of the
univariate tests (O'Brien & Kaiser 1985, *Psychol. Bull.* 97): each
within-subject effect `W` turns every subject's cells into `d_W`
orthonormal contrast scores `Z = Y C_W`; a linear model of `Z` on the
between-subject factors (effect coding, Type III hypotheses) gives each
between term's hypothesis matrix `H` and the residual matrix `E`, and the
univariate test is `F = (tr H / (q d_W)) / (tr E / (ν d_W))` on
`(q d_W, ν d_W)` degrees of freedom, with `ν = n − p` and `q` the term's
columns. The empty within effect (`C` = the normalised sum) tests the
between-subject terms against subjects within groups.

- `struct Sphericity`: Mauchly's test of sphericity and the two estimates of `ε` for one within-subject effect with `d ≥ 2` contrast dimensions.
- `fn sphericity`: Sphericity statistics of an error sums-of-squares-and-products matrix `e` (`d × d`, from orthonormal contrasts) on `nu` degrees of freedom; `None` for `d < 2` or a matrix without positive trace.
- `fn orthonormal_contrasts`: Orthonormal (normalised Helmert) contrasts among `l` levels: an `l × (l − 1)` matrix whose columns are orthogonal to the constant and to each other.
- `struct RepeatedMeasuresAnova`: Result of a repeated-measures ANOVA.
- `fn repeated_measures_anova`: Repeated-measures ANOVA of `data` (one row per subject, one column per condition; no missing values).
- `struct BetweenFactor`: A between-subject factor: its name, number of levels and each subject's level.
- `struct RepeatedEffect`: One row of a factorial repeated-measures ANOVA table.
- `struct FactorialRepeatedMeasures`: Result of a factorial repeated-measures ANOVA.
- `fn factorial_repeated_measures`: Factorial repeated-measures ANOVA.

### `crates/stat-inference/src/runs.rs`

Mood's median test and tests of randomness based on runs (Conover,
*Practical Nonparametric Statistics*, 3rd ed., 1999, §4.3 and §3.5;
Bradley, *Distribution-Free Statistical Tests*, 1968, ch. 11).

* **Mood's median test** for `k` groups: each value is classed as above the
  grand median or not (values equal to it count as not above by default,
  as in Conover; they may instead count as above or be left out). The
  2 × k table of counts gives Pearson's
  `χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E` on `k − 1` df.
* **Runs above and below a reference** (Wald & Wolfowitz 1940): values
  equal to the reference are dropped; with `n₁` above, `n₂` below and `R`
  runs, the exact null distribution is
  `P(R = 2s) = 2·C(n₁−1, s−1)C(n₂−1, s−1)/C(n, n₁)` and
  `P(R = 2s+1) = [C(n₁−1, s)C(n₂−1, s−1) + C(n₁−1, s−1)C(n₂−1, s)]/C(n, n₁)`,
  with mean `1 + 2n₁n₂/n` and variance `2n₁n₂(2n₁n₂ − n)/(n²(n − 1))`.
  Too few runs means clustering; too many, mixing.
* **Runs up and down** (Levene & Wolfowitz 1944; Edgington 1961): the
  number `V` of runs of increases and decreases among successive values
  (repeats of the previous value dropped). For `n` distinct values in
  random order, the probabilities follow the recursion
  `P(n, v) = [v·P(n−1, v) + 2·P(n−1, v−1) + (n − v)·P(n−1, v−2)]/n`
  from `P(2, 1) = 1`; the mean is `(2n − 1)/3` and the variance
  `(16n − 29)/90`. Exact for up to [`UP_DOWN_EXACT_LIMIT`] values, normal
  (with a continuity correction) beyond. Too few runs means a trend; too
  many, oscillation.

- `enum MedianTies`: How values equal to the grand median are counted in [`median_test`].
- `struct MedianTest`: Result of Mood's median test.
- `fn median_test`: Mood's median test that `groups` share one median.
- `struct RunsTest`: A runs test.
- `fn two_symbol_runs_distribution`: Exact null probabilities `P(R = r)`, `r = 0, …, n`, of the number of runs of `n1` and `n2` symbols in random order.
- `fn runs_test`: Runs of values above and below `reference` (the sample median when `None`).
- `const UP_DOWN_EXACT_LIMIT`: Largest number of values for the exact distribution of runs up and down.
- `fn up_down_runs_distribution`: Exact null probabilities `P(V = v)`, `v = 0, …, n − 1`, of the number of runs up and down in a random ordering of `n ≥ 2` distinct values.
- `fn up_down_runs_test`: Runs up and down among successive values of `x` (a value equal to the one before it is dropped).
- `struct RunChartTests`: The four run-chart tests of a sequence: runs about the median (too few: clustering; too many: mixing) and runs up and down (too few: a trend; too many: oscillation), each as a one-sided p-value.
- `fn run_chart_tests`: Both runs tests of a run chart's sequence `x`.

### `crates/stat-inference/src/tolerance.rs`

Tolerance intervals: limits that contain at least a proportion `p` of the
population with confidence `γ` (Krishnamoorthy & Mathew, *Statistical
Tolerance Regions*, 2009, chs. 2 and 8; NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook §7.2.6).

**Normal population**, from the sample mean `x̄` and standard deviation `s`
of `n` values, limits `x̄ ± k·s`:

* **One-sided** (a lower bound `x̄ − k₁s` or an upper bound `x̄ + k₁s`): the
  exact factor is `k₁ = t′_γ(n − 1, δ)/√n`, the `γ` quantile of the
  noncentral t with `n − 1` df and noncentrality `δ = z_p√n` (Owen 1963;
  K&M §2.2).
* **Two-sided** (`x̄ ± k₂s` covering a central-or-not proportion `p`): the
  exact factor solves (Wald & Wolfowitz 1946; K&M eq. 2.3.5)

  ```text
  √(2n/π) ∫₀^∞ P(χ²_{n−1} > (n−1)·r(z)²/k²) e^{−nz²/2} dz = γ,
  ```

  where `r(z)` solves `Φ(z + r) − Φ(z − r) = p`. The integral is evaluated
  by composite Gauss–Legendre quadrature over `[0, 12/√n]` and the factor
  by root finding.

**Distribution-free** (Wilks 1941; K&M ch. 8): for continuous data the
content of `[x₍ᵣ₎, x₍ₙ₊₁₋ₛ₎]` has a Beta(`n − m + 1`, `m`) distribution,
`m = r + s`, so the interval covers at least `p` with confidence
`P(Binomial(n, p) ≤ n − m)`. The interval uses the largest `m` reaching
`γ` (split as evenly as possible between the two ends, or entirely on the
bounded end of a one-sided interval). When even the sample extremes do not
reach `γ`, the extremes are returned with the confidence they do achieve.

- `enum ToleranceSides`: Which limits a tolerance interval has.
- `struct ToleranceInterval`: A tolerance interval.
- `fn one_sided_tolerance_factor`: Exact one-sided normal tolerance factor `k₁` for `n` values: a bound `x̄ − k₁s` (or `x̄ + k₁s`) exceeded by (or exceeding) at least `proportion` of the population with confidence `confidence`.
- `fn two_sided_tolerance_factor`: Exact two-sided normal tolerance factor `k₂` for `n` values: `x̄ ± k₂s` contains at least `proportion` of the population with confidence `confidence`.
- `fn tolerance_content_probability`: The probability, over samples of `n` normal values, that the limits `x̄ ± k·s` (two-sided) or the one limit `x̄ − k·s` (or `x̄ + k·s`) contain at least `proportion` of the population — the confidence of a tolerance interval with factor `k` (inverting it gives the factors above).
- `fn normal_tolerance_interval`: Normal-theory tolerance interval for the population sampled by `x`.
- `fn nonparametric_tolerance_interval`: Distribution-free tolerance interval from order statistics (Wilks 1941).

### `crates/stat-inference/src/variances.rs`

Tests of one standard deviation and of a ratio of two variances, assuming
normal data (Montgomery & Runger, §§9-4, 10-5).

* **One standard deviation:** `χ² = (n − 1)s²/σ₀²` on `n − 1` df; the
  interval for `σ` is `(√((n−1)s²/χ²_{1−α/2}), √((n−1)s²/χ²_{α/2}))`.
* **Variance ratio:** `F = (s₁²/s₂²)/ρ₀` on `(n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1)` df; the
  interval for `σ₁²/σ₂²` is `(F̂/F_{1−α/2}, F̂/F_{α/2})` with `F̂ = s₁²/s₂²`.

Both are sensitive to non-normality; the Levene and Brown–Forsythe tests in
`stat-linear` are the robust alternatives for comparing groups.

- `fn one_sample_std_dev`: Chi-square test that the standard deviation equals `sigma0`; the estimate and interval are for the standard deviation.
- `fn variance_ratio_test`: F test that `var(a)/var(b) = ratio0`; the estimate and interval are for the variance ratio.

Test files: `pooling/tests.rs`.

Integration tests: `nca_reference.rs`, `resampling.rs`.

## Crate `stat-linear` (`crates/stat-linear`)

Linear models for the statistical engine: ordinary least squares with full inference and diagnostics.

Dependencies: `stat-core`, `stat-data`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/anova.rs`

One-way analysis of variance.

#### Model
`y_ij = μ + τ_i + ε_ij`, `ε ~ N(0, σ²)`, for `k` groups of sizes `n_i`
(balanced or not). The decomposition is the textbook one (e.g. NIST/SEMATECH
e-Handbook §7.4.3; Montgomery, *Design and Analysis of Experiments*, ch. 3):

```text
SS_between = Σ_i n_i (ȳ_i − ȳ)²          df = k − 1
SS_within  = Σ_i Σ_j (y_ij − ȳ_i)²       df = N − k
F = MS_between / MS_within,   R² = SS_between / (SS_between + SS_within)
```

#### Numerical method
Group and grand means use compensated summation with a correction pass, and
both sums of squares are accumulated from centered values (two-pass), never
as `Σy² − (Σy)²/n`, which loses every significant digit when the data have a
large common offset (the NIST SmLs datasets are built to expose exactly that).

- `struct GroupSummary`: Summary of one group.
- `struct OneWayAnova`: Result of a one-way ANOVA.
- `fn one_way_anova`: One-way ANOVA of `groups` (each a slice of observations).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/best_subsets.rs`

Best-subsets regression: the best models of each size among all subsets
of the candidate effects (Furnival & Wilson 1974, *Technometrics* 16;
Miller, *Subset Selection in Regression*, 2nd ed., 2002, ch. 3).

Effects are blocks of design columns, as in [`crate::stepwise`]; size
counts effects, and every model has an intercept. Among models of one
size, R², adjusted R², Mallows' Cp, AICc and BIC all order models as the
residual sum of squares does, so the search keeps the `m` smallest RSS of
each size and computes the criteria afterwards:

* `R² = 1 − RSS/TSS`, `R²_adj = 1 − (RSS/(n − p))/(TSS/(n − 1))`, with `p`
  coefficients (intercept included);
* `Cp = RSS/σ̂² − n + 2p` (Mallows 1973), `σ̂²` the mean squared error of
  the model with every candidate;
* `AICc` and `BIC` exactly as [`crate::fit_linear_model`] reports them
  (`AIC = n ln(2π RSS/n) + n + 2(p + 1)`, `AICc = AIC + 2(p+1)(p+2)/(n − p − 2)`,
  `BIC = n ln(2π RSS/n) + n + (p + 1) ln n`).

**Branch and bound.** The search walks the tree of include/exclude
decisions effect by effect. Every model below a node contains the effects
included so far (`I`) and lies inside `I ∪ U` (`U` the undecided effects),
so its RSS is at least `RSS(I ∪ U)`: adding columns never increases the
residual sum of squares. A node is pruned when, for every size it can
still reach, the list of best models of that size is full and its worst
RSS is at most that bound. This is the bound of Furnival & Wilson's
"leaps and bounds"; the result is the same as exhaustive enumeration.

Forced effects are in every model. With heredity, a model is admitted only
when each interaction or power has all (strong) or one (weak) of its
parent effects. Models that are not estimable (aliased columns, or no
residual degrees of freedom) are skipped.

- `struct BestSubsetsOptions`: Options for [`best_subsets`].
- `struct SubsetModel`: One model found by [`best_subsets`].
- `enum SubsetCriterion`: A criterion for choosing among sizes.
- `struct BestSubsetsResult`: Result of [`best_subsets`].
- `fn best_subsets`: The best `options.models_per_size` models of each size for `y` from the columns of `x`, where effect `i` occupies columns `effects[i]` and has parent effects `parents[i]` (pass empty lists for no hierarchy).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/design.rs`

Model terms and design matrices, including categorical predictors and
interaction and polynomial effects.

A **continuous** predictor contributes one column, its values. A
**categorical** predictor with levels `L₁ < L₂ < … < L_k` (sorted, numerically
when every label is a number) contributes `k − 1` columns, one for each level
other than the first. In a model with main effects only, they are reference
indicators (1 at that level, 0 elsewhere; Draper & Smith, *Applied
Regression Analysis*, 3rd ed., ch. 14), so each coefficient is a difference
from the first level. A model mixing continuous and categorical predictors
is an analysis of covariance.

#### Higher-order effects
[`ModelDesign::with_effects`] builds any set of **effects**, each a product
of predictors raised to powers: `A*B` (interaction), `x^2` (polynomial),
`A*x` (separate slopes). An effect's columns are the products of its
factors' columns (every combination for categorical factors). In
higher-order effects, continuous predictors are **centred** at their mean
over the rows used, `(x − x̄)^p`, so that main effects keep their meaning
(the effect at the average of the other predictors) and polynomial columns
are far less collinear (Montgomery, Peck & Vining, *Introduction to Linear
Regression Analysis*, §7.1). When a categorical predictor appears in a
higher-order effect, all categorical predictors switch to **sum-to-zero**
coding (level `j > 1`: 1 at that level, −1 at the first level, 0 elsewhere),
the coding under which the partial F-tests below are the standard "Type III"
tests (Searle, *Linear Models for Unbalanced Data*, §8). Predictions and
fit statistics do not depend on either choice.

[`effect_tests`] gives one partial F-test per effect — all of its columns
together — comparing the full model with the model that omits that effect:
`F = [(SSE_reduced − SSE_full)/df_effect] / MSE_full`.

- `const MAX_POWER`: Highest power accepted for a continuous predictor in an effect.
- `enum PredictorValues`: One predictor's values for every row of a dataset.
- `struct Predictor`: A named predictor.
- `enum TermKind`: How a predictor enters the design.
- `struct ModelTerm`: One predictor (factor) of the model.
- `struct ModelEffect`: One effect of the model: a product of predictors raised to powers.
- `enum CategoricalCoding`: How categorical predictors are coded.
- `enum TermValue`: A setting of one predictor, for encoding a single prediction point.
- `struct ModelDesign`: The coding of a set of predictors and effects into design-matrix columns.
- `fn main_effects`: The main effects of `k` predictors: `[[(0, 1)], [(1, 1)], …]`.
- `fn effect_name`: Effect name such as `A × B` or `x²`.
- `fn spline_effect_name`: Name of the effect of a predictor entered as a spline, e.g.
- `struct EffectTest`: Partial F-test of one term.
- `fn effect_tests`: One partial F-test per effect of `design`, given the full fit to `x`, `y`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/group_tests.rs`

Comparisons of groups beyond the classical one-way ANOVA: tests that do not
assume equal variances, tests of equal variances, and rank-based tests.

#### Definitions
* **Two-sample t (pooled and Welch).** Difference of means `ȳ₁ − ȳ₂` with
  standard error `s_p√(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)` on `n₁ + n₂ − 2` df (pooled), or
  `√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)` on the Welch–Satterthwaite df
  `(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)² / [(s₁²/n₁)²/(n₁−1) + (s₂²/n₂)²/(n₂−1)]`.
* **Welch ANOVA** (Welch 1951, *Biometrika* 38): weights `wᵢ = nᵢ/sᵢ²`,
  `ȳ_w = Σwᵢȳᵢ/Σwᵢ`, `A = Σwᵢ(ȳᵢ − ȳ_w)²/(k−1)`,
  `λ = Σ(1 − wᵢ/W)²/(nᵢ − 1)`, `F = A / (1 + 2(k−2)λ/(k²−1))` on
  `k − 1` and `(k² − 1)/(3λ)` df. For two groups it equals the Welch t².
* **Levene** (1960): one-way ANOVA F on `|yᵢⱼ − ȳᵢ|`; **Brown–Forsythe**
  (1974): the same on `|yᵢⱼ − medianᵢ|`, robust to non-normality.
* **Bartlett** (1937): `χ² = [(N−k) ln s_p² − Σ(nᵢ−1) ln sᵢ²] / C`,
  `C = 1 + (Σ 1/(nᵢ−1) − 1/(N−k)) / (3(k−1))`, on `k − 1` df.
* **Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann–Whitney** (two groups): `U₁ = R₁ − n₁(n₁+1)/2`
  from mid-ranks; normal approximation with tie correction
  `σ² = n₁n₂/12 · [(N+1) − Σ(t³−t)/(N(N−1))]` and a continuity correction of ½.
* **Kruskal–Wallis** (1952): `H = [12/(N(N+1)) Σ Rᵢ²/nᵢ − 3(N+1)] / (1 − Σ(t³−t)/(N³−N))`,
  chi-square on `k − 1` df.

- `struct MeanDifference`: A t-test of a difference of two means.
- `struct TwoSampleTests`: Pooled-variance and Welch two-sample t-tests.
- `struct FTest`: An F test.
- `struct ChiSquareTest`: A chi-square test.
- `struct VarianceTests`: Tests that the group variances are equal.
- `struct RankSumTest`: Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney) test, normal approximation.
- `fn two_sample_t_tests`: Pooled and Welch t-tests of `mean(a) − mean(b)`, with `level` confidence intervals.
- `fn welch_anova`: Welch's ANOVA for equality of means without assuming equal variances.
- `fn variance_tests`: Levene, Brown–Forsythe and Bartlett tests of equal variances.
- `fn rank_sum_test`: Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney) test of `a` against `b`.
- `fn kruskal_wallis`: Kruskal–Wallis rank test that all groups come from the same distribution.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/hierarchy.rs`

Model hierarchy (effect heredity): an interaction or power should come
with the lower-order effects it is built from — `A*B` with `A` and `B`,
`x^2` with `x`, `A*x^2` with `A*x`, `x^2`, `A` and `x`.

Without them the higher-order effect's estimate and test change with the
origin of continuous predictors and the coding of categorical ones (Peixoto,
"Hierarchical variable selection in polynomial regression models", *The
American Statistician* 41(4), 1987; Nelder, "A reformulation of linear
models", *JRSS A* 140, 1977). In designed experiments the same idea appears
as **effect heredity**: an interaction is rarely active unless its parent
factors are (Hamada & Wu, *J. Quality Technology* 24, 1992; Chipman,
*Canadian J. Statistics* 24, 1996). *Strong* heredity asks for every parent,
*weak* heredity for at least one.

An effect is a product of predictors raised to powers, `[(predictor,
power), …]`; its **ancestors** are its proper divisors (every effect whose
factors it contains to at least the same powers) and its **parents** the
ancestors one step lower: drop one first-power factor or lower one power by
one.

- `type Effect`: An effect: `(predictor, power)` factors.
- `fn parents`: The parents of `effect` (empty for a main effect).
- `fn is_ancestor`: `true` when `a` is an ancestor (proper divisor) of `d`.
- `fn ancestors`: Every ancestor of `effect`, lowest order first.
- `fn hierarchical_closure`: `effects` with every missing ancestor added before the effects that need it (existing effects keep their order).
- `fn hierarchy_violations`: Effects of `effects` whose parents are not all present, each with its missing parents (empty when the model is hierarchical).
- `fn parent_indices`: For each effect, the indices (into `effects`) of its parents that are in the list.
- `fn set_effect`: Turn `effect` on (adding its ancestors when `keep_hierarchy`) or off (removing its descendants when `keep_hierarchy`) in `effects`.

#### stat-linear

Linear models built on [`stat_core`]: [`one_way_anova`] for comparing group means,
[`group_tests`] (Welch, equal-variance and rank tests), [`design`] (continuous and
categorical predictors, interaction and polynomial effects, effect tests), [`stepwise`]
selection by p-values, AIC or BIC, `best_subsets` regression by branch and bound,
and ordinary least squares
multiple regression ([`fit_linear_model`]) with parameter estimates, standard
errors, t-tests, confidence intervals, an ANOVA table, R²/adjusted R²,
AIC/AICc/BIC, residual diagnostics and predictions with intervals;
[`method_comparison`] (Deming and Passing–Bablok regression) and [`stability`]
(shelf life from stability data by ICH Q1E poolability tests); [`nonlinear`]
least-squares regression (library forms or any model function) with
asymptotic and profile t intervals and delta-method bands; [`manova`]
(multivariate analysis of variance: Wilks, Pillai, Hotelling–Lawley and
Roy tests of each effect, canonical analysis, contrasts, Box's M).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/manova.rs`

Multivariate analysis of variance: several continuous responses on the
effects of one linear model.

#### Model
The multivariate linear model `Y = X B + U` has `n` rows, `p` responses
(the columns of `Y`) and `k` design columns (the intercept plus the
columns of [`crate::ModelDesign`]); the rows of `U` are independent
`N_p(0, Σ)`. Each response's coefficients are its own least-squares fit,
`B̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY`, computed from one pivoted Householder QR of `X`.

#### Hypothesis and error matrices
The **error SSCP matrix** is `E = (Y − XB̂)ᵀ(Y − XB̂)` with `ν = n − k`
degrees of freedom; it is accumulated from the trailing `n − k`
components of `QᵀY`, so it is exactly symmetric and as accurate as the
QR. The **hypothesis SSCP matrix** of an effect (all its design columns)
is the increase in the error SSCP when the effect is dropped,
`H = E_reduced − E`, the multivariate extra-sum-of-squares principle; its
diagonal holds each response's partial (Type III, under the design's
sum-to-zero coding) sum of squares. A general linear hypothesis `L B = 0`
(a contrast, `h` rows of `L`) has `H = (LB̂)ᵀ [L(XᵀX)⁻¹Lᵀ]⁻¹ (LB̂)`
(Rencher & Christensen, *Methods of Multivariate Analysis*, 3rd ed.,
§10.4 and §6.1.4).

#### Test statistics
With `λ₁ ≥ … ≥ λ_s` the nonzero eigenvalues of `E⁻¹H`, `s = min(p, h)`,
`m = (|p − h| − 1)/2` and `N = (ν − p − 1)/2`:

* **Wilks' Λ** `= |E| / |E + H| = Π 1/(1 + λᵢ)`, with Rao's (1951) F:
  `t = √((p²h² − 4)/(p² + h² − 5))` (1 when the denominator is not
  positive), `df₁ = ph`, `df₂ = t[ν − (p − h + 1)/2] − (ph − 2)/2`,
  `F = (1 − Λ^{1/t})/Λ^{1/t} · df₂/df₁`; exact when `min(p, h) ≤ 2`.
* **Pillai's trace** `V = Σ λᵢ/(1 + λᵢ)`:
  `F = (2N + s + 1)/(2m + s + 1) · V/(s − V)` on `s(2m + s + 1)` and
  `s(2N + s + 1)` df (Pillai 1955).
* **Hotelling–Lawley trace** `U = Σ λᵢ`: for `N > 0` McKeon's (1974)
  approximation `b = (p + 2N)(h + 2N)/[2(2N + 1)(N − 1)]`,
  `df₂ = 4 + (ph + 2)/(b − 1)`, `c = (df₂ − 2)/(2N)`,
  `F = (df₂/(ph)) · U/c` on `ph`, `df₂` df; otherwise Pillai & Samson's
  (1959) `F = 2(sN + 1)U / [s²(2m + s + 1)]` on `s(2m + s + 1)`,
  `2(sN + 1)` df.
* **Roy's largest root** `θ = λ₁`: with `r = max(p, h)`,
  `F = θ (ν − r + h)/r` on `r`, `ν − r + h` df, an upper bound on the
  true F, so its p-value is a lower bound.

When `s = 1` the four statistics are equivalent and every F above is
replaced by the exact `F = λ₁ (ν − r + h)/r` (Hotelling's T² for
`h = 1`, the univariate F for `p = 1`). These are the forms of Rencher &
Christensen §6.1 and of the SAS/STAT documentation's "Multivariate
Tests" section.

#### Canonical analysis
The eigenvectors `aᵢ` of `E⁻¹H`, scaled so `aᵢᵀ(E/ν)aᵢ = 1`, are the
**canonical variates** of the effect: `aᵢᵀy` has unit error variance and
the largest ratio of hypothesis to error variation after the earlier
ones; `√(λᵢ/(1 + λᵢ))` is its canonical correlation.

#### Equal covariance matrices
[`box_m_test`] tests `Σ₁ = … = Σ_g` across groups (Box 1949):
`M = (n − g) ln|S_p| − Σ(nᵢ − 1) ln|Sᵢ|`,
`c = [Σ 1/(nᵢ − 1) − 1/(n − g)] (2p² + 3p − 1)/[6(p + 1)(g − 1)]`,
`χ² = (1 − c)M` on `p(p + 1)(g − 1)/2` df.

- `enum MultivariateStatistic`: One of the four multivariate test statistics.
- `struct MultivariateTest`: A multivariate test statistic with its F approximation.
- `struct UnivariateTest`: A univariate F-test of one response within a hypothesis.
- `struct HypothesisTest`: The test of one hypothesis (a model effect or a contrast).
- `struct ManovaFit`: A fitted multivariate linear model with its effect tests.
- `fn fit_manova`: Fit the multivariate linear model and test each effect.
- `fn multivariate_tests`: Wilks' Λ, Pillai's trace, the Hotelling–Lawley trace and Roy's largest root, with their F approximations, from the nonzero eigenvalues of `E⁻¹H` for `p` responses, `h` hypothesis and `nu` error degrees of freedom (formulas in the module documentation).
- `struct BoxMTest`: Box's M test of equal covariance matrices across groups.
- `fn box_m_test`: Box's (1949) M test that `g` groups share one covariance matrix.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/marginal.rs`

Least-squares (estimated marginal) means, comparisons within the slices
of an interaction, and comparisons of slopes across groups, for any model
whose fixed effects follow a [`ModelDesign`].

#### Least-squares means
The least-squares mean of a combination of levels is the model's
prediction there, averaged with equal weight over the levels of every
other categorical predictor, with each continuous predictor at its mean
over the rows fitted (Searle, Speed & Milliken, "Population marginal
means in the linear model", *Am. Stat.* 34, 1980). It is a linear
function `ℓᵀβ` of the coefficients; [`marginal_row`] gives `ℓ` (with a
leading 1 for the intercept).

#### Slices of an interaction
For an interaction `A × B`, the slice of `B` at level `b` compares the
least-squares means of `A`'s levels with `B` fixed at `b`
(Milliken & Johnson, *Analysis of Messy Data*, vol. 1, 2nd ed., §10.4).
The test of `A` within the slice is the joint Wald test of the `k − 1`
differences from `A`'s first level, `F = (Lβ̂)ᵀ(L V Lᵀ)⁻¹(Lβ̂)/r` on
`r = rank(L V Lᵀ)` and the model's error degrees of freedom (a χ² test,
reported as `F` on `r` and ∞ df, when the model has no error df, as for
a GLM). Pairwise differences of `A`'s levels within the slice are
`t = (ℓ₁ − ℓ₂)ᵀβ̂ / SE` with `SE² = (ℓ₁ − ℓ₂)ᵀ V (ℓ₁ − ℓ₂)`, adjusted
within each slice by [`PairAdjust`].

#### Slopes
In a model with separate slopes of a continuous `x` for the levels of a
categorical `G` (the effect `G × x`), each level's slope is the
derivative of its least-squares mean with respect to `x` at `x̄`
(computed by a central difference, exact for terms up to `x²`), again
averaged over the other categorical predictors (Milliken & Johnson,
vol. 3, 2002, ch. 3). The test of equal slopes is the joint test of the
differences from the first level's slope; pairwise slope differences are
adjusted like the pairs of a slice.

#### Adjustments
Tukey (Tukey–Kramer for unequal precision): `p = P(Q_{k,ν} ≥ |t|√2)`
with `k` the number of means compared and `ν` the error df, intervals
`±q_{k,ν,1−α}/√2 · SE`; Bonferroni: `p·m` (capped at 1), intervals at
`1 − α/m`; Holm's step-down p-values with Bonferroni intervals (Holm's
procedure has no matching intervals); or none.

- `enum PairAdjust`: How pairwise comparisons in one family are adjusted.
- `struct ContrastEstimate`: A linear function `ℓᵀβ` of the coefficients with its standard error.
- `struct JointTest`: A joint test of several linear functions being zero.
- `trait ContrastInference`: What comparisons need from a fitted model: estimates and joint tests of linear functions of its coefficients (intercept first).
- `struct WaldInference`: Wald inference from coefficients and their covariance, with `df` error degrees of freedom (t and F tests) or none (normal and χ² tests).
- `fn wald_from`: Joint Wald test from `M = L V Lᵀ` and `Lβ̂`, through the eigenvalues of `M` (dropping directions with no variance, so dependent rows count once).
- `fn marginal_row`: The row `ℓ` (intercept first) of the least-squares mean with the predictors in `fixed` set as given: other categorical predictors averaged with equal weight over their levels, other continuous ones at their mean.
- `struct MarginalEstimate`: One least-squares mean (or slope).
- `struct PairDifference`: One pairwise difference within a family.
- `struct Slice`: The comparisons of one factor's levels within one slice.
- `fn pairwise`: Every pair of `rows` (labelled by `levels`), adjusted as one family.
- `fn slices`: Comparisons of factor `a`'s levels within each level of factor `b` (both categorical predictors of `design`), with pairwise differences adjusted by `adjust` within each slice (`None` for no pairs).
- `struct SlopeComparison`: Separate slopes of a continuous predictor across a factor's levels.
- `fn group_slopes`: Slopes of continuous predictor `x` for each level of factor `group` at the mean of `x`, with the test of equal slopes and pairwise differences adjusted by `adjust`.
- `fn slope_pairs`: Pairs `(categorical, continuous)` of predictors in an effect `G × x` of `design`, so separate slopes of `x` across `G` can be compared.
- `fn interaction_pairs`: Pairs `(a, b)` of categorical predictors in an effect `A × B` of `design` (two-factor interactions only).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/method_comparison.rs`

Regression for method-comparison studies, where both measurements carry
error: Deming regression and Passing–Bablok regression.

#### Deming regression
With `xᵢ = ξᵢ + δᵢ`, `yᵢ = α + βξᵢ + εᵢ` and a known ratio
`λ = Var(ε)/Var(δ)` of the error variances of `y` and `x`, the maximum
likelihood slope (Deming 1943, *Statistical Adjustment of Data*; Cornbleet
& Gochman 1979, *Clin. Chem.* 25) is

`β̂ = [S_yy − λS_xx + √((S_yy − λS_xx)² + 4λS_xy²)] / (2S_xy)`,

`α̂ = ȳ − β̂x̄`, with `S` the centred sums of squares and products. With
`λ = 1` this is orthogonal regression (the first principal axis); as
`λ → ∞` it tends to ordinary least squares of y on x. Standard errors and
confidence intervals come from the jackknife (Linnet 1990, *Clin. Chem.*
36; Linnet 1993, *Clin. Chem.* 39): with the leave-one-out estimates
`θ₍₋ᵢ₎`, `se = √((n − 1)/n · Σ(θ₍₋ᵢ₎ − θ̄₍.₎)²)` and the interval
`θ̂ ± t_{1−α/2, n−2} · se`.

#### Passing–Bablok regression
A non-parametric, outlier-resistant estimate (Passing & Bablok 1983,
*J. Clin. Chem. Clin. Biochem.* 21). The slopes `Sᵢⱼ = (yⱼ − yᵢ)/(xⱼ − xᵢ)`
of all pairs `i < j` are formed, leaving out pairs with both differences
zero and slopes of exactly −1 (a tied `x` gives ±∞ by the sign of the `y`
difference). With `N` slopes sorted and `K` of them below −1, the slope is
the median shifted by `K`: `S₍(N+1)/2+K₎` for odd `N`, otherwise the mean
of `S₍N/2+K₎` and `S₍N/2+1+K₎`. Its confidence limits are `S₍M₁+K₎` and
`S₍M₂+K₎` with `C = z_{1−α/2} √(n(n − 1)(2n + 5)/18)`,
`M₁ = round((N − C)/2)` and `M₂ = N − M₁ + 1`. The intercept is
`median(yᵢ − β̂xᵢ)`, with limits `median(yᵢ − β̂_U xᵢ)` and
`median(yᵢ − β̂_L xᵢ)`. The method assumes the two measurements are
linearly related; Passing & Bablok's cumulative-sum test checks it: with
`l` points above and `L` below the line, points above score `√(L/l)`,
points below `−√(l/L)`, points on it 0; ordered by their projection
`Dᵢ = (yᵢ + xᵢ/β̂ − α̂/β̂)/√(1 + 1/β̂²)` onto the line, the largest absolute
cumulative sum divided by `√(l + L)` is compared with the Kolmogorov
distribution (critical value 1.36 at α = 0.05). With these scores the
cumulative sum after `k` points is `√(lL)·(F₊(k) − F₋(k))`, where `F₊` and
`F₋` are the empirical distribution functions of the points above and below
the line, so the statistic is Smirnov's two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov
statistic `√(lL/(l + L))·D`. (The divisor is often printed `√(L + 1)`; that
form rejects a linear relation far more often than the nominal level, about
19% at α = 0.05 for 20 points on each side.)

- `struct ComparisonEstimate`: An estimate with its standard error (when one exists) and confidence limits.
- `struct DemingFit`: A Deming regression fit.
- `fn deming_regression`: Deming regression of `y` (test method) on `x` (comparison method) with error-variance ratio `variance_ratio = Var(error of y)/Var(error of x)` (1 for orthogonal regression), with jackknife standard errors and t-based confidence limits on `n − 2` df.
- `struct LinearityTest`: Passing–Bablok's cumulative-sum test of linearity.
- `struct PassingBablokFit`: A Passing–Bablok fit.
- `fn passing_bablok`: Passing–Bablok regression of `y` (test method) on `x` (comparison method), with the cumulative-sum linearity test.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/assay.rs`

Derived quantities and acceptance checks for assay curves.

The assay curve templates (receptor binding, enzyme kinetics,
pharmacological dose–response, immunoassay standard curves, growth and
survival) are ordinary nonlinear regressions ([`super::fit_nonlinear`]);
this module holds what they report beyond the parameter estimates.

#### Derived quantities
A quantity `q = g(θ)` of the fitted parameters has the delta-method
standard error `se(q̂) = √(∇gᵀ Σ ∇g)`, `Σ` the covariance of the estimates
and `∇g` the gradient at `θ̂` (central differences), and the Wald interval
`q̂ ± t·se` ([`delta_method`]; Seber & Wild, *Nonlinear Regression*, Wiley
1989, §5.1). When `q` is a monotone function of a single parameter its
interval is that parameter's interval mapped through `g`
([`map_interval`]), which keeps the asymmetry of a profile interval and
never leaves the quantity's range (for example a dissociation constant
from a log concentration stays positive). The standard formulas:

* inhibition constant from a competition curve (Cheng & Prusoff,
  *Biochem. Pharmacol.* 22, 1973): `Ki = IC50 / (1 + [L]/Kd)`, `[L]` the
  labelled ligand's concentration and `Kd` its dissociation constant
  ([`cheng_prusoff_ki`]);
* the concentration giving `F`% of the maximal effect of a logistic curve
  with slope `h`: `EC_F = EC50·(F/(100 − F))^{1/h}` ([`ec_f`]);
* half-life of a first-order process with rate constant `k`:
  `t½ = ln 2 / k` ([`half_life`]);
* equilibrium dissociation constant from binding kinetics:
  `Kd = koff / kon` ([`kinetic_kd`]);
* relative potency of a test preparation against a standard from
  parallel log-dose curves (Finney, *Statistical Method in Biological
  Assay*, 3rd ed., Griffin 1978, ch. 4): `ρ = 10^(log EC50_S − log EC50_T)`,
  its interval `10^` of the t interval of the difference
  ([`relative_potency`]).

#### Standard curves (ligand-binding assays)
* **Back-calculation:** each calibration standard's response is read off
  the fitted curve and compared with its nominal concentration,
  `recovery = 100·x̂/x`. ICH M10 *Bioanalytical Method Validation and Study
  Sample Analysis* (2022), §7.2.1 (ligand-binding assays): back-calculated
  standards within ±20% of nominal (±25% at the lowest and highest
  standards, the LLOQ and ULOQ), at least 75% of them, and at least six
  concentration levels, meeting it ([`standard_curve_acceptance`]; the
  limits are settings, so the chromatographic ±15%/±20% can be used).
* **Precision profile:** the coefficient of variation of a concentration
  read off the curve from one response, `CV(c) = 100·sd(x̂)/c` with
  `sd(x̂) = √(s²/w(c) + se(f(c))²) / |f′(c)|` (Ekins, "The precision
  profile: its use in assay design, assessment and quality control", in
  *Immunoassays for Clinical Chemistry*, 1983; Findlay & Dillard,
  *AAPS J.* 9, 2007). The working (quantitation) range is the widest
  stretch of concentrations, within the standards, where `CV ≤` a limit
  (20% by default) ([`quantitation_range`]).

#### Failure modes
A quantity that cannot be computed at the estimates (a division by zero,
a logarithm of a negative value) or whose gradient cannot be formed is
returned as NaN with a NaN standard error; callers show it as missing.

- `struct DerivedValue`: A quantity computed from the estimates, with its uncertainty.
- `fn delta_method`: Delta-method standard error and Wald interval `q̂ ± t·se` of `q = g(θ)` at `theta` with covariance `covariance` (`P × P`; NaN rows and columns for parameters held at a bound are treated as zero variance).
- `fn map_interval`: The interval of a monotone function `g` of one parameter: `g` applied to each limit, ordered (an open limit, NaN, stays NaN).
- `fn cheng_prusoff_ki`: Inhibition constant `Ki = IC50 / (1 + [L]/Kd)` (Cheng & Prusoff 1973), for a competitor's `ic50` against a labelled ligand at concentration `ligand` with dissociation constant `kd` (same units).
- `fn ec_f`: `EC_F = EC50·(F/(100 − F))^{1/h}`: the concentration giving `f_percent` of the way from the bottom to the top of a logistic curve with Hill slope `hill` (`0 < F < 100`, `h ≠ 0`; NaN otherwise).
- `fn half_life`: Half-life `ln 2 / k` of a first-order rate constant `k` (NaN for `k ≤ 0`).
- `fn kinetic_kd`: Equilibrium dissociation constant `koff / kon` (NaN for `kon ≤ 0`).
- `fn relative_potency`: Relative potency `ρ = 10^(d)`, `d = log EC50_standard − log EC50_test`, with its interval `10^(d ± t·se(d))`, `se(d)² = Var_S + Var_T − 2·Cov_ST` (Finney 1978, ch.
- `struct AcceptanceLimits`: Limits of [`standard_curve_acceptance`].
- `struct BackCalculated`: One calibration standard read back off the curve.
- `struct Acceptance`: Verdict of [`standard_curve_acceptance`].
- `fn standard_curve_acceptance`: Back-calculated standards checked against `limits`.
- `fn quantitation_range`: The widest stretch of a precision profile where `CV ≤ limit`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/compare.rs`

Comparing two least-squares fits of the same data.

#### Extra sum-of-squares F test (Bates & Watts 1988, §3.10; Draper & Smith,
*Applied Regression Analysis*, 3rd ed., §24.3)
For a simpler model nested in a more complex one (the simpler is the
complex model with some parameters fixed or set equal), with residual sums
of squares `S₀ > S₁` on `ν₀ > ν₁` residual degrees of freedom,
`F = ((S₀ − S₁)/(ν₀ − ν₁)) / (S₁/ν₁)` on `(ν₀ − ν₁, ν₁)` df; a small p
says the extra parameters reduce the sum of squares by more than chance.
For nonlinear models the F distribution is approximate (exact when the
models are linear). It is not valid for models that are not nested.

#### AICc (Burnham & Anderson, *Model Selection and Multimodel Inference*,
2nd ed., Springer 2002, §2.4 and §2.9)
For a least-squares fit with `P` estimated parameters to `n` observations,
`K = P + 1` (the error variance counts) and
`AICc = n·ln(S/n) + 2K + 2K(K + 1)/(n − K − 1)`. The model with the lower
AICc is better supported; with `Δ = AICc₀ − AICc₁`, the probability that
model 1 is the better of the two is `e^{Δ/2} / (1 + e^{Δ/2})` (Akaike
weights). Unlike the F test it does not need nested models, but both fits
must use the same observations (and the same weights).

- `struct FitScore`: One fit's summary for a comparison.
- `struct ExtraSumOfSquares`: An extra sum-of-squares F test.
- `fn extra_sum_of_squares`: The extra sum-of-squares F test of `simple` against `complex` (module documentation).
- `fn aicc_probability`: Probability (Akaike weight) that model `b` is the better of `a` and `b` by AICc; `NaN` when either AICc is undefined.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/forms.rs`

A library of common one-predictor nonlinear model forms, each with
analytic derivatives and automatic starting values.

| Form | `f(x; θ)` |
|---|---|
| Exponential | `Scale·exp(Rate·x)` |
| Exponential with asymptote | `Asymptote + Scale·exp(Rate·x)` |
| Logistic (3 parameters) | `Asymptote / (1 + exp(−Rate·(x − Midpoint)))` |
| Logistic (4 parameters) | `Lower + (Upper − Lower) / (1 + exp(−Rate·(x − Midpoint)))` |
| Gompertz | `Asymptote·exp(−exp(−Rate·(x − Inflection)))` |
| Michaelis–Menten | `Vmax·x / (Km + x)` |
| Power | `Scale·x^Exponent` |
| Rational (linear / linear) | `(a + b·x) / (1 + c·x)` |
| Straight line | `Intercept + Slope·x` |
| Dose–response, log dose | `Bottom + (Top − Bottom) / (1 + 10^((LogEC50 − x)·HillSlope))` |
| Dose–response, dose | `Bottom + (Top − Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / x)^HillSlope)`, `x ≥ 0` |
| Asymmetric logistic (5 parameters) | `Bottom + (Top − Bottom) / (1 + 10^((LogC − x)·HillSlope))^Asymmetry` |
| Weibull growth | `Asymptote − (Asymptote − Initial)·exp(−(Rate·x)^Shape)`, `x ≥ 0` |
| Beta growth | `Ymax·(1 + (End − m)/(End − Peak))·(m/End)^(End/(End − Peak))`, `m = min(x, End)`, `x ≥ 0` |
| Segmented line | `Intercept + Slope1·x + (Slope2 − Slope1)·max(x − Breakpoint, 0)` |
| Sum of two exponentials | `Plateau + Span1·exp(−Rate1·x) + Span2·exp(−Rate2·x)` |
| Gaussian peak | `Baseline + Height·exp(−(x − Center)² / (2·Width²))` |
| Lorentzian peak | `Baseline + Height / (1 + ((x − Center) / HalfWidth)²)` |

The dose–response forms are the four-parameter Hill (log-logistic) curve,
on the log₁₀ dose scale or the dose scale; a negative `HillSlope` gives a
falling (inhibition) curve, whose midpoint is then an IC50. The
asymmetric logistic is the five-parameter logistic of Gottschalk & Dunn
("The five-parameter logistic: a characterization and comparison with the
four-parameter logistic", *Anal. Biochem.* 343, 2005) on the log-dose
scale; `Asymmetry = 1` gives the four-parameter curve. Weibull growth is
from Ratkowsky (*Handbook of Nonlinear Regression Models*, 1990); the beta
growth function, rising from 0 at `x = 0` to its maximum `Ymax` at
`x = End` with its fastest growth at `x = Peak` (`0 ≤ Peak < End`) and
constant after `End`, is from Yin, Goudriaan, Lantinga, Vos & Spiertz ("A
flexible sigmoid function of determinate growth", *Annals of Botany* 91,
2003). The segmented line is continuous at its breakpoint (Muggeo,
"Estimating regression models with unknown break-points", *Stat. Med.* 22,
2003); its derivative in `Breakpoint` is `−(Slope2 − Slope1)` for
`x > Breakpoint` and 0 otherwise.

#### Starting values
Every form is conditionally linear: given its nonlinear parameters (a rate,
midpoint, Km, exponent or `c`) the others enter linearly and follow from a
small linear least-squares problem. The starting values are the best point
of a grid over the nonlinear parameters, scaled to the data (rates
`±k / range(x)` for `k` on a log grid from 0.01 to 30, midpoints at
quantiles of `x`, Km from 0.01 to 10 times the largest `x`, exponents from
−3 to 3; Hill slopes `±rate / ln 10` for the log-dose forms, ±0.2 to 8 on
the dose scale with EC50 on a geometric grid over the positive `x`;
asymmetries 0.2 to 5; Weibull shapes 0.3 to 8; beta-growth ends at upper
quantiles of `x` and up to three times its maximum, with peaks at 0 to 95%
of the end; breakpoints between each pair of adjacent distinct `x` values
that leave two values on each side; rate pairs `Rate1 > Rate2 > 0`; peak
centers at quantiles of `x` and widths 0.01 to 1 times its range), each
with its conditionally optimal linear parameters — the
idea of separable (variable projection) least squares (Golub & Pereyra,
"The differentiation of pseudo-inverses and nonlinear least squares
problems whose variables separate", *SIAM J. Numer. Anal.* 10, 1973),
used here only to start the full fit.

- `enum CurveForm`: One of the library forms.
- `struct FormModel`: A library form evaluated at fixed predictor values, as a [`ModelFunction`] with analytic derivatives.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/global.rs`

Global (shared-parameter) fitting: several data sets fitted together, each
with its own copy of some parameters and one common value of the others
(Motulsky & Christopoulos, *Fitting Models to Biological Data Using Linear
and Nonlinear Regression*, Oxford University Press 2004, ch. 37–38).

#### Model
Data set `g` has `n_g` observations and a model `f_g(x; φ_g)` with the
same `K` parameters. The global parameter vector `θ` holds each shared
parameter once and each unshared one once per data set; `φ_g = M_g θ`
picks data set `g`'s values (`map[g][k]` is the index in `θ` of its
`k`-th parameter). The data sets are stacked, so the fit minimises
`Σ_g Σ_i (y_gi − f_g(x_gi; M_g θ))²` and every statistic of
`fit_nonlinear` — standard errors, profile
intervals, bands — refers to `θ`, with one residual variance for all
data sets. The Jacobian is `∂f_g/∂θ = (∂f_g/∂φ_g) M_g`: analytic when
every data set's model has analytic derivatives.

Sharing every parameter fits one curve to all the data; sharing none fits
the data sets separately but with a pooled variance (the same estimates as
separate fits).

- `struct GlobalModel`: Several data sets' models over one global parameter vector.
- `type Owner`: The parameter a global position belongs to, and its data set (`None` when shared).
- `fn layout`: The global parameter layout for `n_groups` data sets of a model with `shared.len()` parameters: `(map, owner)` where `map[g][k]` is the global index of data set `g`'s parameter `k`, and `owner[i]` is `(k, None)` for a shared global parameter `i` or `(k, Some(g))` for data set `g`'s copy.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/implicit.rs`

Implicit models `F(x, y; θ) = 0` fitted by orthogonal distance.

#### Model
The observations `(xᵢ, yᵢ)` lie on the curve `F(x, y; θ) = 0` up to
independent errors of equal variance in both coordinates. The estimates
minimise the sum of squared orthogonal (geometric) distances
`Σ dᵢ(θ)²`, `dᵢ` the distance from `(xᵢ, yᵢ)` to the nearest point of the
curve (Boggs, Byrd & Schnabel, "A stable and efficient algorithm for
nonlinear orthogonal distance regression", *SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput.*
8, 1987; Ahn, Rauh & Warnecke, "Least-squares orthogonal distances fitting
of circle, sphere, ellipse, hyperbola, and parabola", *Pattern
Recognition* 34, 2001). The model is passed to
`fit_nonlinear` as a [`ModelFunction`] whose value
for observation `i` is the signed distance `dᵢ` (the sign of
`F(xᵢ, yᵢ)`), fitted to a response of zeros. The error of an observation
normal to the curve has the variance `σ²` of each coordinate, so
`s² = Σdᵢ²/(n − P)` estimates `σ²`, and the standard errors follow from
the Jacobian of the distances.

#### Foot points
The nearest point `q` of the curve to `p = (xᵢ, yᵢ)` starts as the Newton
projection of `p` onto the curve (`z ← z − F(z)∇F(z)/‖∇F(z)‖²` until
`|F|/‖∇F‖ ≤ 10⁻¹²·scale`). It then moves along the tangent `t` by the
tangential part of `p − q`, `(p − q)·t`, and is projected back onto the
curve; the move is halved until the distance falls, and the steps stop
when the tangential part is below `10⁻¹⁰·scale`. At the end `F(q) = 0`
and `p − q ∥ ∇F(q)`, the conditions for a stationary distance.
The gradient `∇F` is a central difference with step `ε^{1/3}·max(|q|,
scale)`, `scale` the spread of the data.

#### Failure modes
`F` undefined near an observation, a vanishing gradient (a singular point
of the curve), or a projection that does not converge make the model
uncomputable at that `θ` (the solver then shortens its step).

- `type ImplicitFunction`: `F(x, y; θ)` for observation `i` at the point `(x, y)`, or `None` where undefined.
- `struct ImplicitModel`: Signed orthogonal distances to the curve `F = 0` as a [`ModelFunction`].

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/inverse.rs`

Inverse prediction (calibration): reading an unknown predictor value off a
fitted curve from an observed response (Draper & Smith, *Applied
Regression Analysis*, 3rd ed., Wiley 1998, §3.2; Eisenhart, "The
interpretation of certain regression methods and their use in biological
and industrial research", *Ann. Math. Statist.* 10, 1939; Seber & Wild,
*Nonlinear Regression*, Wiley 1989, §5.12).

#### Method
For an observed response `y₀`, the estimate `x̂₀` solves `f(x̂₀; θ̂) = y₀`
within the calibration range `[a, b]` (normally the range of the
standards). The interval is the set of `x` whose prediction interval for
one new observation contains `y₀`:
`{x : |y₀ − f(x; θ̂)| ≤ t·√(se(x)² + s²/w₀)}`, with `se(x)` the
delta-method standard error of the fitted mean and `w₀` the weight of the
new observation (for a straight line this is the classical
Fieller-type interval of Draper & Smith eq. 3.2.6, exactly). The limits
are the crossings nearest `x̂₀` on each side.

Roots are bracketed on a grid of 400 intervals over `[a, b]` and refined
by bisection to `10⁻¹²·(b − a)`.

#### Failure modes
* `y₀` not reached by the curve within `[a, b]`: no estimate.
* More than one solution (a curve that is not monotone): the one nearest
  `a` is reported and [`InversePrediction::several_solutions`] is set.
* A limit beyond `[a, b]` (a flat curve or a response near an asymptote):
  that side of the interval is open (`None`).

- `struct InversePrediction`: One inverse prediction.
- `fn inverse_predict`: Inverse prediction of `y0` on `[a, b]`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/robust.rs`

Robust nonlinear fitting and outlier identification (Motulsky & Brown,
"Detecting outliers when fitting data with nonlinear regression – a new
method based on robust nonlinear regression and the false discovery rate",
*BMC Bioinformatics* 7:123, 2006).

#### Robust scale
The robust standard deviation of the residuals is
`RSDR = P₆₈ · N/(N − K)`, where `P₆₈` is the 68.27th percentile of the
absolute (weighted) residuals (linear interpolation between order
statistics) — for normal errors about one standard deviation — and the
factor corrects for the `K` fitted parameters.

#### Robust fit (Cauchy / Lorentzian loss)
The estimates minimise `Σ ln(1 + (rᵢ/RSDR)²)`, the negative
log-likelihood of Cauchy-distributed errors, so a point far from the curve
has bounded influence. The minimum is found by iteratively reweighted
least squares: at a fixed scale the normal equations of the loss are
those of weighted least squares with `wᵢ = 1/(1 + (rᵢ/RSDR)²)`, so each
step refits with these weights (times any given weights) and recomputes
`RSDR` from the new residuals, as the paper does, until the estimates
stop changing (relative change below 10⁻⁷). Standard errors from the last
weighted fit treat the robust weights as known, so they are approximate.

#### Outliers (the paper's false-discovery-rate rule)
With the absolute residuals of the robust fit sorted from smallest to
largest (`i = 1..N`), each of the largest 30% (from `i = ⌊0.7N⌋`) is
given `tᵢ = |rᵢ|/RSDR` and a two-sided p-value `Pᵢ` from the t
distribution on `N − K` df. Moving up from the smallest of these, the
first `i` with `Pᵢ < αᵢ = Q(N − (i − 1))/N` marks that point and every
point further from the curve as outliers (a Benjamini–Hochberg threshold:
the largest residual is tested at `Q/N`). `Q` (1% recommended) bounds the
expected fraction of identified outliers that are false discoveries. The
paper then removes the outliers and refits by ordinary (or weighted)
least squares.

- `fn robust_sd`: `RSDR = P₆₈ · N/(N − K)` of residuals `r` with `k` fitted parameters (module documentation); `NaN` when `N ≤ K`.
- `fn outliers`: Indices of the outliers among residuals `r` of a fit with `k` parameters, by the false-discovery-rate rule at level `q` (module documentation), most extreme last.
- `struct RobustFit`: A robust fit.
- `fn fit_robust`: Fit `y = f(x; θ)` with the Cauchy loss (module documentation), from `start`, with the settings of `options` (its weights, if any, multiply the robust ones).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear.rs`

Nonlinear least-squares regression with inference.

#### Model
`yᵢ = f(xᵢ; θ) + εᵢ`, `εᵢ` independent `N(0, σ²)`, for a model function
`f` with `P` parameters `θ`. The estimates minimise
`S(θ) = Σ (yᵢ − f(xᵢ; θ))²` ([`stat_core::optimize::levenberg_marquardt`]).
The model is given as a [`ModelFunction`]: either one of the library
forms in [`forms`] (analytic derivatives and automatic starting values),
or any function of the parameters (central-difference derivatives).

#### Inference (Bates & Watts, *Nonlinear Regression Analysis and Its
Applications*, Wiley 1988, ch. 2 and 6)
With `V = ∂f/∂θ` (`n × P`) at `θ̂`, `s² = S(θ̂)/(n − P)` and
`(VᵀV)⁻¹` from the QR decomposition of `V`. Here `P` counts the
*estimated* parameters: one fixed by equal lower and upper bounds is a
known constant of the model, not estimated, so it uses no degree of
freedom (the fit equals the fit of the model with that constant written
in):

* standard errors `se(θ̂ⱼ) = s·√[(VᵀV)⁻¹]ⱼⱼ`, `t = θ̂ⱼ / se`, two-sided
  p-values on `n − P` df, and linearisation (Wald) intervals
  `θ̂ⱼ ± t(n − P; α/2)·se`;
* the correlation of the estimates from `(VᵀV)⁻¹`;
* profile t intervals (§6.1): with `S̃(θⱼ)` the least sum of squares when
  `θⱼ` is held fixed and the other parameters re-estimated,
  `τ(θⱼ) = sign(θⱼ − θ̂ⱼ)·√(S̃(θⱼ) − S(θ̂))/s`, and the interval is
  `{θⱼ : |τ(θⱼ)| ≤ t(n − P; α/2)}`. This is the likelihood-ratio (F-test)
  interval `S̃(θⱼ) − S(θ̂) ≤ s²·F(1, n − P; α)`; unlike the Wald interval it
  follows the curvature of the model and need not be symmetric;
* the fitted mean at a point with gradient `g = ∂f/∂θ` has delta-method
  standard error `s·√(gᵀ(VᵀV)⁻¹g)`; confidence limits for the mean are
  `f ± t·se`, prediction limits for a new observation
  `f ± t·√(se² + s²)` ([`NonlinearFit::mean_interval`],
  [`NonlinearFit::prediction_interval`]).

#### Weights
With weights `wᵢ > 0` ([`NonlinearOptions::weights`]) the estimates
minimise `S(θ) = Σ wᵢ (yᵢ − f(xᵢ; θ))²`: the problem is solved for the
scaled residuals `√wᵢ (f − yᵢ)` and every statistic above uses the scaled
Jacobian `W^{1/2}V` (Bates & Watts §1.3.2 / Seber & Wild, *Nonlinear
Regression*, Wiley 1989, §2.2.2), so `s²` estimates the variance of an
observation of weight 1, `Var(yᵢ) = σ²/wᵢ`. Prediction limits for a new
observation of weight `w₀` are `f ± t·√(se² + s²/w₀)`
([`NonlinearFit::prediction_interval_weighted`]).

#### Curvature diagnostic (Hougaard 1985)
The asymptotic skewness of each estimate (Hougaard, "The appropriateness of
the asymptotic distribution in a nonlinear regression model in relation to
curvature", *J. R. Statist. Soc. B* 47, 1985; in the form of Ratkowsky,
*Handbook of Nonlinear Regression Models*, Dekker 1990, §2.5): with
`L = (VᵀV)⁻¹`, `Hₖₗ = ∂²f/∂θₖ∂θₗ` and `Wⱼₖₗ = Σᵤ Vᵤⱼ Hᵤₖₗ`,
`E(θ̂ᵢ − θᵢ)³ ≈ −s⁴ Σⱼₖₗ Lᵢⱼ Lᵢₖ Lᵢₗ (Wⱼₖₗ + Wₖⱼₗ + Wₗⱼₖ)` and the
standardised skewness is `g₁ᵢ = E(θ̂ᵢ − θᵢ)³ / (s² Lᵢᵢ)^{3/2}`. Ratkowsky's
guide: `|g₁| < 0.1` the estimator is very close to linear, `0.1–0.25`
reasonably close, above `0.25` the nonlinearity is apparent, and above 1
it is considerable. Second derivatives are central differences of the
model values (step `ε^{1/4}·max(|θ|, 10⁻⁸)`), whatever the first
derivatives.

#### Failure modes
* **No convergence** — the iteration limit is reached or no step lowers
  `S`: the fit is still returned, with [`NonlinearFit::termination`] saying
  why and a warning; its estimates and statistics are those of the last
  iterate and should not be relied on. Try other starting values.
* **Singular Jacobian** at the solution (parameters not separately
  identifiable, e.g. a redundant parameter or a rate whose curve is flat
  over the data): [`StatError::RankDeficient`].
* **Parameter at a bound** — it is reported as such, held fixed for the
  inference (no standard error; the residual df still count it, since it
  was estimated and the data put it there), and a warning says so.
* **Parameter fixed by equal bounds** — not estimated: no standard error,
  not counted in `P`, and a warning says so.
* Fewer observations than estimated parameters + 1, or non-finite responses:
  [`StatError::InsufficientData`] / [`StatError::NonFiniteInput`].

- `trait ModelFunction`: A model function `f(xᵢ; θ)` evaluated at every observation.
- `struct NonlinearOptions`: Settings of [`fit_nonlinear`].
- `struct ProfileInterval`: A profile t interval; a side is `None` when `|τ|` did not reach the critical value inside the parameter's bounds and the search range (the interval is open on that side).
- `struct NonlinearParameter`: One estimated parameter.
- `struct NonlinearFit`: A fitted nonlinear regression.
- `fn fit_nonlinear`: Fit `y = f(x; θ) + ε` by least squares from `start` and compute the inference described in the module documentation.
- `fn numeric_gradient`: Central-difference gradient `∂f/∂θ` of a scalar model value at `theta` (used for bands of models without analytic derivatives).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/ols.rs`

Ordinary least squares multiple regression.

#### Model
```text
y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + β_p x_p + ε,     ε ~ N(0, σ² I)
```
(the intercept β₀ is optional). The estimate `β̂ = argmin ‖y − Xβ‖²` and every
derived statistic follow the standard textbook definitions, e.g. Draper & Smith,
*Applied Regression Analysis* (3rd ed., 1998), chs. 4–5, and the NIST/SEMATECH
e-Handbook of Statistical Methods §4.4.

#### Numerical method
Accuracy is the priority, so the normal equations `XᵀX β = Xᵀy` are never
formed (that would square the condition number). Instead:

1. **Centering.** With an intercept, each predictor and the response are
   centered at their (compensated) means. The slopes are invariant to this
   shift, and removing the constant direction is the single largest
   improvement in conditioning for typical data (e.g. calendar years).
2. **Power-of-two column scaling.** Each centered column is divided by the
   power of two nearest its Euclidean norm. Scaling by powers of two is exact
   in binary floating point, yet equilibrates the columns so the pivoted QR's
   rank test is scale-invariant.
3. **Householder QR with column pivoting** of the scaled, centered design.
4. **Iterative refinement.** The residual `r = y − Xβ̂` is recomputed with
   compensated dot products and the correction `δ = argmin ‖r − Xδ‖` is added
   to `β̂` (Björck, *Numerical Methods for Least Squares Problems*, 1996, §2.9).
5. **Inference without cancellation.** Standard errors come from row norms of
   `R⁻¹`, and the intercept variance from `‖R⁻ᵀ x̄‖²`, both sums of squares.

#### Conventions
* **R² without an intercept** is the *uncentered* R² = Σŷ² / Σy², with the
  ANOVA sums of squares likewise uncentered. This matches the convention of the
  NIST StRD certified values (datasets NoInt1/NoInt2).
* **Information criteria** use the Gaussian maximum log-likelihood
  `ℓ = −(n/2)(ln 2π + ln(RSS/n) + 1)` and count σ² as a parameter, so with `k`
  coefficients `AIC = −2ℓ + 2(k+1)`, `BIC = −2ℓ + (k+1) ln n` and
  `AICc = AIC + 2(k+1)(k+2)/(n−k−2)` (Hurvich & Tsai 1989, Biometrika 76).

- `const INTERCEPT_NAME`: Name used for the intercept term in [`ParameterEstimate::name`].
- `struct OlsOptions`: Options controlling [`fit_linear_model`].
- `struct ParameterEstimate`: Estimate and inference for one model coefficient.
- `struct AnovaRow`: One row of an analysis-of-variance table.
- `struct AnovaTable`: Regression analysis-of-variance table.
- `struct FitSummary`: Overall goodness-of-fit summary.
- `struct ResidualDiagnostics`: Per-observation regression diagnostics.
- `struct Prediction`: Predicted mean response with confidence and prediction intervals.
- `struct LinearModelFit`: A fitted ordinary-least-squares model.
- `fn fit_linear_model`: Fit `y = Xβ (+ β₀) + ε` by ordinary least squares.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/spline.rs`

Regression spline bases: a continuous predictor expanded into the columns
of a B-spline or natural cubic spline basis, so a model can fit a smooth
curve in it with ordinary least squares or a GLM.

#### B-splines
For degree `d` (order `d + 1`), boundary knots `a < b` and interior knots
`a < t₁ < … < t_m < b`, the knot sequence repeats each boundary knot
`d + 1` times. The `m + d + 1` B-spline functions follow the Cox–de Boor
recursion (de Boor, *A Practical Guide to Splines*, 1978, ch. IX):

`B_{j,0}(x) = 1` on `[u_j, u_{j+1})`, and
`B_{j,q}(x) = (x − u_j)/(u_{j+q} − u_j) B_{j,q−1}(x)
           + (u_{j+q+1} − x)/(u_{j+q+1} − u_{j+1}) B_{j+1,q−1}(x)`.

The first function is dropped (the model's intercept takes its place), so
the basis has `m + d` columns. Outside `[a, b]` each function continues
the polynomial of the nearest interval. With these conventions the columns
are exactly those of R's `splines::bs(x, knots, degree, Boundary.knots)`.

#### Natural cubic splines
A natural cubic spline is cubic between knots and linear beyond the
boundary knots (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, *Elements of Statistical
Learning*, 2nd ed., §5.2.1; Harrell, *Regression Modeling Strategies*,
2nd ed., §2.4.5). Its basis is built from the cubic B-splines (without
the first) by removing the two directions in which the second derivative
at `a` or `b` is not zero: with `C` the `2 × (m + 3)` matrix of second
derivatives at the boundary knots and `Q` the orthogonal factor of the
Householder QR of `Cᵀ`, the basis is `B Q` without its first two columns,
`m + 1` columns. Beyond the boundary knots each column continues linearly
(value and slope at the knot). The Householder convention is LINPACK's,
so the columns equal those of R's `splines::ns`.

#### Default knots
[`SplineSpec::Count`] places `m` interior knots at the quantiles
`k/(m + 1)`, `k = 1…m`, of the values (linear interpolation, Hyndman–Fan
type 7), as R's `bs(x, df)` and `ns(x, df)` do; the boundary knots are
the smallest and largest value.

- `const MAX_KNOTS`: Most interior knots accepted.
- `const MAX_DEGREE`: Highest B-spline degree accepted.
- `enum SplineKind`: The kind of spline basis.
- `enum SplineKnots`: Where the interior knots go.
- `struct SplineSpec`: A spline term as requested: its kind and knots.
- `struct SplineBasis`: A spline basis with fixed knots: evaluates the columns at any `x`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/stability.rs`

Shelf-life estimation from stability data of several batches (ICH Q1E,
*Evaluation for Stability Data*, 2003; Chow, *Statistical Design and
Analysis of Stability Studies*, 2007, ch. 3).

#### Batch poolability
The response (e.g. assay, % of label claim) of batch `j` at time `t` is
modelled by analysis of covariance, `yᵢⱼ = αⱼ + βⱼtᵢⱼ + εᵢⱼ`, fitted by
[`fit_linear_model`] with batch indicators and batch-by-time products. Two
extra-sum-of-squares F tests decide how far the batches can be pooled,
each at the significance level 0.25 that ICH Q1E sets (a high level, so
that a real batch difference is not pooled away):

1. equal slopes: `F = [(RSS_c − RSS_s)/(k − 1)] / [RSS_s/(n − 2k)]`, the
   separate-lines model `s` against the common-slope model `c`;
2. if slopes are not rejected, equal intercepts:
   `F = [(RSS_p − RSS_c)/(k − 1)] / [RSS_c/(n − k − 1)]` against the single
   pooled line `p`.

Rejecting equal slopes gives separate lines (the error variance still
pooled from the full model); rejecting only equal intercepts gives
parallel lines; otherwise one line for all batches.

When the separate-lines model leaves no residual degrees of freedom
(`n = 2k`, e.g. every batch measured at only two times) the slope test is
impossible: the slopes are assumed common, with a note, and the intercept
test decides between parallel lines and one line. An F test whose extra
sum of squares is negligible (below 10⁻¹² of the total) gives F = 0 and
p = 1, even when the larger model fits exactly; a real extra sum of squares
over an exact fit gives F = ∞ and p = 0.

#### Shelf life
For an attribute with a lower acceptance limit the shelf life is the
earliest time at which the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound for the
mean, `ŷ(t) − t_{0.95, df} · se(ŷ(t))`, falls to the limit (an upper limit
uses the upper bound); with both limits the two-sided 95% bounds are
compared with both (ICH Q1E §2.4). With separate or parallel lines the
shortest batch shelf life applies. The search runs from time 0 to a
horizon (default twice the longest time observed).

#### Extrapolation limit
ICH Q1E (Appendix A, for long-term data analysed statistically with no
significant change at accelerated conditions) allows a proposed shelf life
of at most twice the period covered by long-term data, `X`, and no more
than 12 months beyond it: `min(2X, X + 12 months)`. The 12-month part needs
the unit of the time column, [`ShelfLifeOptions::time_unit`]; without one
only the `2X` part is applied. [`ShelfLifeResult::supported_shelf_life`]
is the estimated shelf life cut back to that limit.

- `struct ShelfLifeOptions`: Options for [`shelf_life`].
- `enum StabilityTimeUnit`: Unit of the time values in a stability study.
- `enum ExtrapolationRule`: Which rule sets [`ShelfLifeResult::extrapolation_limit`].
- `enum PoolingModel`: The model chosen by the poolability tests.
- `struct PoolingTest`: One extra-sum-of-squares F test.
- `struct BatchLine`: A batch's fitted line and shelf life under the chosen model.
- `struct ShelfLifeResult`: Result of [`shelf_life`].
- `fn shelf_life`: Estimate the shelf life from stability data.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/stepwise.rs`

Stepwise selection of model effects (Efroymson 1960; Draper & Smith,
*Applied Regression Analysis*, 3rd ed., ch. 15; Venables & Ripley, *Modern
Applied Statistics with S*, §6.8).

Effects are blocks of design columns (all of a categorical effect's columns
enter or leave together); the intercept is always in the model.

* **p-value criterion** — an effect enters when its partial F-test against
  the current model has `p < α_enter` (the smallest such p first) and leaves
  when its test within the current model has `p > α_remove` (the largest
  first). `F = [(RSS_without − RSS_with)/df] / [RSS_with/(n − p_with)]`.
* **AIC / BIC** — `n·ln(RSS/n) + k·p`, with `p` the number of coefficients
