nested or crossed factors, to see which "family" of variation — within a
piece, from piece to piece, or over time — dominates.

Factors are given outermost first. The observations are grouped into the
cells of every leading set of factors that occurs in the data (factor 1;
factors 1–2; …), so nested factors (levels unique within their parent)
and crossed factors are handled alike. For each cell the mean, extremes,
range and standard deviation are computed.

Two summaries accompany the chart:

* **Variation by factor**: for factor `d`, the range of the means of its
  levels within each cell of the factors above it (the spread a
  multi-vari chart shows as the length of the connecting lines), averaged
  over those cells; and, within the innermost cells, the average range and
  the pooled standard deviation `√(Σ (nᵢ − 1) sᵢ² / Σ (nᵢ − 1))`.
* **Range limits**: the ranges of the innermost cells charted with 3-sigma
  limits (Montgomery, *Introduction to Statistical Quality Control*,
  section 6.2): `σ̂ = mean(Rᵢ / d₂(nᵢ))`, centre `d₂(nᵢ) σ̂`, limits
  `max(0, d₂(nᵢ) − 3 d₃(nᵢ)) σ̂` and `(d₂(nᵢ) + 3 d₃(nᵢ)) σ̂`, which for
  equal cell sizes are `R̄`, `D₃ R̄` and `D₄ R̄`.

- `const MAX_MULTI_VARI_FACTORS`: The most factors a multi-vari chart takes.
- `struct MultiVariCell`: One cell: the observations sharing the levels of the leading factors.
- `struct FactorVariation`: Spread of one factor's level means within the cells of the factors above it.
- `struct CellRangeLimits`: Range-chart limits of one innermost cell.
- `struct MultiVari`: A computed multi-vari breakdown.
- `fn multi_vari`: Group `values` by the factors `factors` (outermost first; `factors[d][i]` is observation `i`'s level code of factor `d`).

### `crates/stat-quality/src/multivariate.rs`

Multivariate control charts for several correlated quality
characteristics measured on the same items (Montgomery, *Introduction to
Statistical Quality Control*, 7th ed., ch. 11).

Every chart takes the first `m` points (subgroups, or single
observations) as the **reference** sample that estimates the in-control
mean vector and covariance matrix; points after it are **monitored**
against those estimates. Without a separate reference the whole sample is
the reference (a phase I study).

* **Hotelling T²** (Hotelling 1947). Subgroups of size `n ≥ 2`:
  `T²ⱼ = n(x̄ⱼ − x̿)ᵀ S̄⁻¹ (x̄ⱼ − x̿)` with `S̄` the average within-subgroup
  covariance matrix; reference points have the upper limit
  `p(m − 1)(n − 1)/(mn − m − p + 1) · F_α(p, mn − m − p + 1)` and monitored
  points `p(m + 1)(n − 1)/(mn − m − p + 1) · F_α(p, mn − m − p + 1)`
  (Montgomery eqs. 11.19–11.20; Alt 1985). Individual observations:
  `T²ᵢ = (xᵢ − x̄)ᵀ S⁻¹ (xᵢ − x̄)` with the sample covariance `S`; reference
  points follow a scaled beta distribution, with upper limit
  `((m − 1)²/m) · B_α(p/2, (m − p − 1)/2)` (Tracy, Young & Mason 1992,
  *J. Quality Technology* 24), and monitored points
  `p(m + 1)(m − 1)/(m(m − p)) · F_α(p, m − p)` (Montgomery eqs. 11.23–11.24).
  `F_α` and `B_α` are upper-`α` quantiles. There is no lower limit.
* **Contributions** of each variable to a point's T²:
  `dⱼ = T² − T²₍₋ⱼ₎`, where `T²₍₋ⱼ₎` leaves variable `j` out (its row and
  column of the covariance matrix and its deviation); a large `dⱼ`
  (compare with `χ²_α(1)`) marks a variable that drives the signal (Runger,
  Alt & Montgomery 1996, "Contributors to a multivariate statistical
  process control chart signal", *Communications in Statistics — Theory
  and Methods* 25; Montgomery §11.3.2).
* **Generalized variance** `|Sⱼ|` (Alt 1985, "Multivariate quality
  control", *Encyclopedia of Statistical Sciences* 6; Montgomery
  §11.3.3): with `b₁ = Π_{i=1}^p (n − i) / (n − 1)^p` and
  `b₂ = Π_{i=1}^p (n − i) / (n − 1)^{2p} · [Π_{j=1}^p (n − j + 2) − Π_{j=1}^p (n − j)]`,
  `E|S| = b₁|Σ|` and `Var|S| = b₂|Σ|²`; estimating `|Σ|` by `|S̄|/b₁`, the
  limits are `|S̄|/b₁ · (b₁ ± 3√b₂)` around the center `|S̄|`, with a
  negative lower limit set to zero. Needs `n > p`.
* **MEWMA** (Lowry, Woodall, Champ & Rigdon 1992, "A multivariate
  exponentially weighted moving average control chart", *Technometrics*
  34): `Zᵢ = λ(xᵢ − x̄) + (1 − λ)Zᵢ₋₁`, `Z₀ = 0`, plotted as
  `T²ᵢ = Zᵢᵀ Σ_{Zᵢ}⁻¹ Zᵢ` with the exact covariance
  `Σ_{Zᵢ} = λ/(2 − λ) · [1 − (1 − λ)^{2i}] · S`, against an upper limit `H`.
  `H` is given, or found for a target in-control average run length by
  simulation ([`mewma_limit_for_arl`]).

#### Failure modes
An empty sample, observations of unequal length, unequal subgroup sizes, a
reference too small for the limits (`m > p + 1` for individuals,
`mn − m − p + 1 > 0` for subgroups, `n > p` for `|S|`), a singular
covariance matrix, `α ∉ (0, 1)`, `λ ∉ (0, 1]` or `H ≤ 0` are errors.

- `enum ChartPhase`: Whether a point belongs to the reference sample that estimated the limits, or is monitored against them.
- `struct MultivariatePoint`: One plotted point of a multivariate chart.
- `fn t2_contributions`: Contributions `dⱼ = T² − T²₍₋ⱼ₎` of each variable to `T² = scale · dᵀ Σ⁻¹ d` (see the module notes).
- `struct HotellingChart`: A Hotelling T² chart.
- `fn hotelling_t2_chart`: Hotelling T² chart of subgroups (`subgroups[j][obs][variable]`; subgroups of one observation give the individuals chart), with the first `reference` points as the reference sample (all when `None`).
- `fn generalized_variance_constants`: The constants `(b₁, b₂)` of the generalized variance for subgroups of size `n` and `p` variables (see the module notes).
- `struct GeneralizedVarianceChart`: A generalized variance (|S|) chart.
- `fn generalized_variance_chart`: Generalized variance chart: each subgroup's `|Sⱼ|` against limits `|S̄|/b₁ · (b₁ ± width·√b₂)` (width 3 in Alt's chart).
- `enum MewmaLimit`: How the MEWMA upper limit is set.
- `struct MewmaChart`: A MEWMA chart.
- `fn mewma_chart`: MEWMA chart of individual observations (`observations[i][variable]`) with the first `reference` observations estimating the mean and covariance (all when `None`).
- `const MEWMA_SIMULATION_RUNS`: Most simulated in-control runs used by [`mewma_limit_for_arl`].
- `const MEWMA_MIN_SIMULATION_RUNS`: Fewest simulated in-control runs used by [`mewma_limit_for_arl`] (at the largest run length, [`MEWMA_MAX_ARL`]).
- `const MEWMA_MAX_ARL`: Largest in-control average run length [`mewma_limit_for_arl`] accepts, so that the simulation stays interactive.
- `fn mewma_limit_for_arl`: The MEWMA limit `H` whose in-control average run length is `arl`, for `p` variables and weight `λ`, by simulation: `R` in-control runs (independent standard normal vectors, as the statistic is invariant to the mean and covariance) from a fixed seed, each followed for up to `10·arl` points, with `…

### `crates/stat-quality/src/nonnormal.rs`

Capability of non-normal processes: percentile-based performance indices
from a distribution fitted to the data, a Johnson transformation, or the
empirical percentiles.

The normal-theory indices put the natural process spread at `6σ`, the
width between the 0.135% and 99.865% points of a normal distribution.
Clements (1989), "Process capability calculations for non-normal
distributions", *Quality Progress* 22(9), and ISO 22514-2 replace those
points by the percentiles `X₀.₀₀₁₃₅`, `X₀.₅` and `X₀.₉₉₈₆₅` of the process
distribution:

```text
Pp  = (USL − LSL) / (X₀.₉₉₈₆₅ − X₀.₀₀₁₃₅)
Ppl = (X₀.₅ − LSL) / (X₀.₅ − X₀.₀₀₁₃₅)
Ppu = (USL − X₀.₅) / (X₀.₉₉₈₆₅ − X₀.₅)
Ppk = min(Ppl, Ppu)
```

which reduce to the normal-theory `Pp`, `Ppk` (with the sample standard
deviation) for a normal fit. The expected nonconforming fractions are
`F̂(LSL)` and `1 − F̂(USL)` under the fitted distribution `F̂`, and the
*equivalent* `Ppk` is the normal-theory index with the same worse-side
fraction, `min(−Φ⁻¹(p_L), −Φ⁻¹(p_U)) / 3` (ISO 22514-2, the "Z" method).

Percentiles come from:

* a maximum-likelihood fit of one family ([`stat_core::distribution_fit`]),
  or of whichever of the fourteen families has the smallest AIC;
* a Johnson transformation `z = γ + η·g((x − ε)/λ)` (Slifker–Shapiro
  percentile fit; Chou, Polansky & Mason 1998, "Transforming non-normal
  data to normality in statistical process control", *Journal of Quality
  Technology* 30(2)): `X_p = g⁻¹(Φ⁻¹(p))`, `p_L = Φ(z(LSL))`;
* the sample itself (Hyndman–Fan type 6 percentiles, `p(n + 1)`-th order
  statistic, interpolated and clamped to the sample): with fewer than 740
  values the outer percentiles are the sample extremes, so these indices
  are only rough guides for small samples, and the expected rates are the
  observed ones.

- `enum CapabilityModel`: How the process distribution is modelled.
- `const REFERENCE_PROBABILITIES`: The probabilities of the lower, middle and upper reference percentiles.
- `enum PercentileSource`: What the percentiles were taken from.
- `struct PercentileCapability`: Result of [`percentile_capability`].
- `fn percentile_capability`: Percentile-based capability of `values` against `limits` under `model` (see the module documentation).
- `struct BootstrapIntervals`: Bootstrap percentile intervals for the indices of a [`PercentileCapability`] (see [`bootstrap_percentile_intervals`]).
- `const MIN_BOOTSTRAP_RESAMPLES`: Smallest number of usable resamples for which intervals are reported.
- `fn bootstrap_percentile_intervals`: Bootstrap percentile intervals (Efron & Tibshirani 1993, *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*, ch.

### `crates/stat-quality/src/pareto.rs`

Pareto analysis of defect categories (Juran's "vital few and trivial
many"; Juran & Godfrey, *Juran's Quality Handbook*, 5th ed., 1999,
section 5; Montgomery, *Introduction to Statistical Quality Control*,
section 5.4).

Each observation names a category and carries a weight (1 for a count of
rows, or a frequency). Categories are ranked by their totals, largest
first, and each gets its share of the grand total and the cumulative
share up to and including it:

```text
share_k      = T_k / Σ_j T_j
cumulative_k = Σ_{j ≤ k} share_j
```

Categories whose share falls below a threshold can be pooled into one
"Other" bar, which is placed last whatever its size (Juran's convention),
so the ranking of the named categories stays readable.

- `struct ParetoOptions`: Options of [`pareto_table`].
- `struct ParetoCategory`: One ranked category of a [`ParetoTable`].
- `struct ParetoTable`: Categories ranked by total, largest first ("Other" last).
- `fn pareto_table`: Rank categories by total weight.

### `crates/stat-quality/src/pca_chart.rs`

Multivariate monitoring from a principal-components model of a reference
period: Hotelling's T² on the retained component scores and the squared
prediction error (SPE, also written Q) of the part of each observation the
model does not explain (Jackson & Mudholkar 1979; Nomikos & MacGregor
1995, "Multivariate SPC charts for monitoring batch processes",
*Technometrics* 37; Kourti & MacGregor 1996, "Multivariate SPC methods for
process and product monitoring", *J. Quality Technology* 28).

The first `m` observations (rows of `p` variables) are the **reference**
sample. Its columns are centred on their means and, for a correlation
model, divided by their standard deviations, giving standardized rows `z`
for every observation (the same reference means and scales apply to later,
**monitored**, observations). A principal component analysis of the
reference rows ([`stat_multivariate::principal_components`]) gives
eigenvalues `λ₁ ≥ … ≥ λ_p` and unit loadings `P` (`p × A` for the `A`
retained components). For each observation:

* scores `t = Pᵀz` and `T² = Σₐ tₐ²/λₐ`. Reference points have the
  scaled-beta upper limit `((m − 1)²/m) · B_α(A/2, (m − A − 1)/2)` and
  monitored points `A(m + 1)(m − 1)/(m(m − A)) · F_α(A, m − A)` (Tracy,
  Young & Mason 1992), as for a T² chart of `A` variables;
* residual `e = z − P t` and `SPE = Σⱼ eⱼ²`. With
  `θₖ = Σ_{j>A} λⱼᵏ` (k = 1, 2, 3) and `h₀ = 1 − 2θ₁θ₃/(3θ₂²)`, the
  **Jackson–Mudholkar** upper limit is
  `Q_α = θ₁ [z_α √(2θ₂h₀²)/θ₁ + 1 + θ₂h₀(h₀ − 1)/θ₁²]^{1/h₀}` with `z_α`
  the upper-α standard normal point (Jackson & Mudholkar, "Control
  procedures for residuals associated with principal component analysis",
  *Technometrics* 21, 1979); the **scaled χ²** limit is
  `g χ²_α(h)` with `g = θ₂/θ₁` and `h = θ₁²/θ₂` (Box 1954; Nomikos &
  MacGregor 1995). When the bracket of the first is not positive the
  second is used.

**Contributions** split each statistic over the variables. For T²,
variable `j` contributes `cⱼ = zⱼ Σₐ (tₐ/λₐ) pⱼₐ`, and the `cⱼ` sum to T²
(a variable can contribute negatively); for SPE it contributes `eⱼ²`
(Miller, Swanson & Heckler 1998, "Contribution plots: a missing link in
multivariate quality control", *Applied Mathematics and Computer Science*
8; Westerhuis, Gurden & Smilde 2000, *Chemometrics and Intelligent
Laboratory Systems* 51).

**Choosing `A` by cross-validation** ([`pca_cross_validation`]) follows
the element-wise "EKF" scheme of Bro, Kjeldahl, Smilde & Kiers (2008),
"Cross-validation of component models: a critical look at current
methods", *Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry* 390: the reference rows
are split into `k` folds by venetian blinds (row `i` in fold `i mod k`);
each fold's rows are left out in turn and the model refitted on the rest;
for every left-out row and variable `j`, the scores are estimated from the
other variables by least squares, `t̂ = (P₋ⱼᵀP₋ⱼ)⁻¹P₋ⱼᵀz₋ⱼ`, and `zⱼ` is
predicted as `pⱼᵀt̂`. The prediction error sum of squares (PRESS) over all
rows and variables is computed for `A = 1, 2, …` and the `A` with the
smallest PRESS is chosen. Leaving out the predicted variable is what makes
PRESS rise again once components fit noise (naive row-wise PRESS can only
fall as `A` grows).

**Change point** ([`mean_change_point`]): for a sequence of `n` vectors
`y₁, …, y_n` with common covariance, the likelihood-ratio statistic for a
single shift of the mean after observation `τ` is
`Λ_τ = −n ln(1 − τ(n − τ)/n² · dᵀ S⁻¹ d)`, where `d` is the difference of
the means before and after `τ` and `S` the covariance of all `n` vectors
about their mean (divisor `n`); the estimate is the `τ` that maximizes
`Λ_τ` (Sullivan & Woodall 2000, "Change-point detection of mean vector or
covariance matrix shifts using multivariate individual observations",
*IIE Transactions* 32; Srivastava & Worsley 1986). Its p-value is from a
permutation test of the maximum (the vectors are exchangeable when there
is no shift, and `S` does not change under permutation).

#### Failure modes
Fewer than two variables, observations of unequal length, non-finite
values, a reference too small (`m ≤ A + 1`) for the limits, a constant
variable in a correlation model, `A` outside `1 … min(p, m − 1)`,
`α ∉ (0, 1)` and fewer than two folds are errors. With `A = p` every SPE
is zero and there is no SPE limit (`NaN`).

- `enum ComponentChoice`: How many principal components the model keeps.
- `enum SpeLimitMethod`: Which approximation sets the SPE limit.
- `struct PcaChartOptions`: Settings of a principal-components monitoring chart.
- `struct PcaChart`: A fitted principal-components monitoring chart.
- `fn spe_limit`: The SPE limit of `method` from the residual eigenvalues `λ_{A+1}, …`; `None` when the residual variance is zero, and for Jackson–Mudholkar when its bracket is not positive.
- `fn pca_t2_limits`: The T² limits `(reference, monitoring)` for `a` components and `m` reference observations.
- `fn pca_cross_validation`: Cross-validated PRESS of principal-components models with `1, 2, …, max_components` components (element-wise EKF scheme with venetian-blind folds; see the module notes).
- `fn pca_chart`: Fit the principal-components model on the first `reference` observations (all when `None`) and chart T² and SPE for every observation.
- `struct ChangePoint`: A likelihood-ratio estimate of a single shift in the mean vector.
- `fn mean_change_point`: The likelihood-ratio change-point estimate for a single shift in the mean of `y` (rows of equal length), with a permutation p-value from `permutations` shuffles drawn with `seed` (see the module notes).

### `crates/stat-quality/src/phased.rs`

Control charts with phases and subgroups of varying size.

The charts of [`crate::charts`] need equal subgroups and one set of
limits. Here each subgroup may have its own size and belongs to a
**phase** (a block of time such as "before" and "after" a process change);
every phase gets its own center line, process σ and limits, computed from
that phase's points only, and run rules restart at each phase boundary.

Within a phase, with subgroup sizes `nᵢ`, means `x̄ᵢ`, ranges `Rᵢ` and
standard deviations `sᵢ` (Montgomery, *Introduction to Statistical Quality
Control*, §6.3.1 on variable sample sizes; NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook §6.3.2):

| chart | σ̂ | center | limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| X̄ | (from R or S) | x̿ = Σnᵢx̄ᵢ / Σnᵢ | x̿ ± 3σ̂/√nᵢ |
| R | mean of Rᵢ/d₂(nᵢ) | d₂(nᵢ)σ̂ | max(0, d₂ − 3d₃)σ̂, (d₂ + 3d₃)σ̂ |
| S | mean of sᵢ/c₄(nᵢ) | c₄(nᵢ)σ̂ | max(0, c₄ − 3√(1 − c₄²))σ̂, (c₄ + 3√(1 − c₄²))σ̂ |
| Individuals | M̄R/d₂(2) | x̄ | x̄ ± 3σ̂ |
| Moving range | | M̄R | 0, D₄(2)M̄R |

With equal sizes these are exactly the usual `A₂R̄`, `D₃R̄`, `D₄R̄`, `A₃s̄`,
`B₃s̄`, `B₄s̄` limits. Moving ranges are taken within a phase (the first
point of each phase has none). The moving-average, three-way, zone and
short-run charts build on these; their formulas are in [`crate::extended`].

**Options** ([`ChartSettings`], individuals, X̄–R and X̄–S charts only;
Montgomery §6.2 and §6.4, Wheeler 1995):

- limits at `k`σ instead of 3σ: every `3` above becomes `k` (the zones of
  the run rules stay at 1σ and 2σ);
- a moving range over `w` consecutive values, `MRᵢ = max − min` of
  `xᵢ₋w₊₁ … xᵢ`, with `σ̂ = M̄R/d₂(w)` and moving-range limits
  `M̄R · max(0, 1 − k d₃(w)/d₂(w))` and `M̄R · (1 + k d₃(w)/d₂(w))` (the first
  `w − 1` points of a phase have none);
- **standard (historical) values** `μ₀`, `σ₀` in place of the estimates:
  center `μ₀`, location limits `μ₀ ± kσ₀/√nᵢ`, and dispersion center and
  limits `d₂σ₀`, `(d₂ ± k d₃)σ₀` (R), `c₄σ₀`, `(c₄ ± k√(1 − c₄²))σ₀` (S)
  or `d₂(w)σ₀`, `(d₂(w) ± k d₃(w))σ₀` (moving range), lower limits clipped
  at zero.

**Run rules** on limits that vary from point to point are applied to the
standardized values `zᵢ = (yᵢ − CLᵢ)/σ_zᵢ` with `σ_zᵢ = (UCLᵢ − CLᵢ)/k`,
which have constant zones; rule 1 uses each point's actual limits, so a
lower limit clipped at zero is honoured. With constant limits this gives
exactly the results of [`crate::rules::check_rules`].

- `struct VaryingChart`: One chart whose limits may change from point to point.
- `struct PhaseSummary`: One phase of a [`PhasedChart`].
- `struct PhasedChart`: Location and dispersion charts over one or more phases.
- `struct ChartSettings`: Settings of the charts that need more than the data.
- `struct StandardValues`: Known (standard, historical) process center and standard deviation.
- `fn varying_violations`: Run-rule violations of `values` against per-point `limits`, with patterns restarting at each `(start, end)` span (see the module documentation).
- `fn varying_violations_at`: [`varying_violations`] for limits at `multiple` σ: the zones are `(UCL − CL)/multiple` wide.
- `fn phased_chart`: Location and dispersion charts of `subgroups` (in time order), with `phases[i]` the phase number of subgroup `i`: consecutive subgroups with the same number form one phase.
- `fn phased_chart_with`: Charts of any [`ChartKind`] over phases (see [`phased_chart`] and [`crate::extended`]).

### `crates/stat-quality/src/rules.rs`

Run rules for detecting non-random patterns on control charts.

The eight tests of Nelson (1984), "The Shewhart Control Chart — Tests for
Special Causes", *Journal of Quality Technology* 16(4), 237–239. Zones are
measured from the center line in units of the plotted statistic's standard
deviation σ_z = (UCL − CL)/3 ([`ControlLimits::zone_sigma`]):

| rule | pattern |
|---|---|
| 1 | one point beyond a control limit |
| 2 | nine points in a row on the same side of the center line |
| 3 | six points in a row steadily increasing or decreasing |
| 4 | fourteen points in a row alternating up and down |
| 5 | two of three points in a row more than 2σ_z from center, same side |
| 6 | four of five points in a row more than 1σ_z from center, same side |
| 7 | fifteen points in a row within 1σ_z of center (either side) |
| 8 | eight points in a row more than 1σ_z from center (either side) |

#### Conventions
* A violation is reported at the point that **completes** the pattern; while a
  pattern continues, each further point is reported too.
* Rules 5 and 6 report a point only if that point is itself one of the
  points beyond the zone boundary (on the same side).
* Comparisons are strict: a point exactly on the center line belongs to neither
  side; a tie between consecutive points breaks a trend or an alternation.
* Rule 1 uses the actual limits (so a lower limit clipped at zero is honoured).
* A missing value (`None`, e.g. the first moving range) breaks every pattern.

- `enum RunRule`: One of Nelson's eight run rules.
- `struct RuleViolation`: A rule broken at a point.
- `fn check_rules`: Apply `rules` to a sequence of chart values.

### `crates/stat-quality/src/time_weighted.rs`

Time-weighted control charts, which accumulate information across samples
and so detect small sustained shifts sooner than Shewhart charts
(Montgomery, *Introduction to Statistical Quality Control*, ch. 9; NIST/SEMATECH
e-Handbook §6.3.2.3–6.3.2.4).

* **EWMA** (Roberts 1959): `zᵢ = λxᵢ + (1 − λ)zᵢ₋₁`, `z₀ = μ₀`, with limits
  `μ₀ ± Lσ √(λ/(2 − λ) · [1 − (1 − λ)^{2i}])` that widen to their
  steady-state value.
* **Tabular CUSUM** (Page 1954): `Cᵢ⁺ = max(0, xᵢ − (μ₀ + K) + Cᵢ₋₁⁺)` and
  `Cᵢ⁻ = max(0, (μ₀ − K) − xᵢ + Cᵢ₋₁⁻)`, with reference value `K = kσ` and
  decision interval `H = hσ`. Each signal also reports the number of
  consecutive non-zero sums, which estimates when the shift began.

When `σ` is not given it is estimated from the average moving range,
`σ̂ = MR̄ / d₂` with `d₂ = 2/√π ≈ 1.128` for spans of two.

- `struct ProcessTarget`: In-control process mean and standard deviation.
- `struct EwmaPoint`: One point of an EWMA chart.
- `struct EwmaChart`: An EWMA chart.
- `struct CusumPoint`: One sample of a tabular CUSUM.
- `struct CusumChart`: A tabular CUSUM chart.
- `fn moving_range_sigma`: `σ̂ = MR̄ / d₂` from the moving ranges of consecutive observations.
- `fn resolve_target`: The target to use: `target` if given, otherwise the sample mean and the moving-range estimate of `σ`.
- `fn ewma_chart`: EWMA chart of individual observations.
- `fn cusum_chart`: Tabular CUSUM of individual observations with `K = kσ`, `H = hσ`.

Test files: `attribute/tests.rs`, `extended/tests.rs`, `monitoring_limits/tests.rs`, `nonnormal/tests.rs`, `pca_chart/tests.rs`, `phased/tests.rs`.

## Crate `stat-reliability` (`crates/stat-reliability`)

Survival and reliability analysis: Kaplan–Meier product-limit estimates with Greenwood confidence bands, the log-rank test, and censored maximum-likelihood life-distribution fits with right, left and interval censoring, the Turnbull estimate, reliability growth, repairable systems and test plans.

Dependencies: `stat-core`, `stat-mixed`.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/censored_count.rs`

Maximum-likelihood fits of count distributions to censored counts:
counts reported only as "below the detection limit" (left-censored),
"too numerous to count" (right-censored) or within a range
(interval-censored), alongside exact counts (Helsel, *Statistics for
Censored Environmental Data Using Minitab and R*, 2nd ed., 2012, ch. 6;
Cameron & Trivedi, *Regression Analysis of Count Data*, 2nd ed., 2013,
§3.3 and ch. 4 on censored counts).

#### Data
Each [`CountObservation`] states that the count `X` satisfies
`lower ≤ X ≤ upper` (integers, `upper` may be `+∞`), with a frequency
weight. An exact count has `lower = upper`; a count below a detection
limit `d` is `0 ≤ X ≤ d − 1`; a count of at least `c` is
`c ≤ X ≤ +∞`.

#### Families
* **Poisson** with mean `λ`: `P(X = x) = λˣ e^{−λ} / x!`.
* **Negative binomial** with mean `μ` and size (dispersion) `k`:
  `P(X = x) = Γ(x + k) / (Γ(k) x!) · pᵏ (1 − p)ˣ`, `p = k / (k + μ)`, so
  `Var X = μ + μ²/k`; it tends to the Poisson as `k → ∞`. This is the
  "NB2" parametrization (Cameron & Trivedi §3.3).

#### Likelihood
`ℓ = Σ w ln P(lower ≤ X ≤ upper)`. Exact counts use the probability
function; ranges of up to 1 000 values sum it (in log space), so
left-censored counts are exact; other tails use the regularized incomplete
gamma function (`P(X ≥ a) = P(a, λ)` for the Poisson) and the regularized
incomplete beta function (`P(X ≤ b) = I_p(k, b + 1)`,
`P(X ≥ a) = I_{1−p}(a, k)` for the negative binomial), taking the
difference in whichever tail is smaller.

#### Estimation and intervals
The log-likelihood is maximized over the log parameters (`ln λ`, or
`ln μ` and `ln k`) by damped Newton steps. Standard errors come from the
observed information on the log scale; Wald limits are
`exp(ln θ̂ ± z · se)` and the reported standard error of `θ̂` is
`θ̂ · se(ln θ̂)` (delta method). Likelihood-ratio limits are the set
`{θ : 2[ℓ̂ − ℓ_p(θ)] ≤ χ²₁(level)}`, with the other parameter
re-maximized (Meeker & Escobar 1998, §8.3); a limit more than a factor
`e²⁰` from the estimate is reported as unbounded (`0` or `+∞`), which
happens to the size `k` of nearly Poisson counts.

- `enum CountFamily`: A count distribution.
- `struct CountObservation`: A possibly censored count: `lower ≤ X ≤ upper`.
- `struct CountFit`: A count distribution fitted to censored counts.
- `fn fit_censored_counts`: Fit a Poisson or negative binomial distribution to censored counts by maximum likelihood (see the module docs), with intervals at confidence `level`.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/censored_fit.rs`

Maximum-likelihood fits of life distributions to censored data: exact
failures with right-, left- and interval-censored observations, for the
fourteen families of [`stat_core::distribution_fit`] (exponential,
Weibull, lognormal, log-logistic, gamma, normal, logistic, smallest and
largest extreme value, and the threshold forms), plus the Weibull with a
known shape for data with few or no failures.

#### Likelihood
With the family's density `f`, distribution function `F` and survival
function `S = 1 − F` (taken from [`FittedDistribution`], so the family
definitions are shared with distribution identification and capability),
observations weighted by their frequencies `wᵢ` contribute

```text
ℓ(θ) = Σ_exact w ln f(t) + Σ_right w ln S(l) + Σ_left w ln F(u) + Σ_interval w ln[F(u) − F(l)]
```

(Meeker & Escobar, *Statistical Methods for Reliability Data*, 1998,
§2.4, ch. 8; Lawless, *Statistical Models and Methods for Lifetime Data*,
2nd ed., 2003, §2.2). `F(u) − F(l)` is computed from whichever of `F`
and `S` is smaller, so long intervals far in either tail keep their
precision.

#### Estimation
The likelihood is maximized over unconstrained parameters — `(μ, ln σ)`
for the location–scale families (on `ln(t − γ)` for the Weibull,
lognormal and log-logistic), `ln θ` for the exponential, `(ln k, ln θ)`
for the gamma — by damped Newton (Levenberg–Marquardt) iterations with
central-difference derivatives, from moment estimates computed as if every
observation were a failure at a representative time (the time itself, the
censoring time, the interval's geometric or arithmetic midpoint).

A threshold `γ` must lie below `m`, the earliest time by which some unit
is known to have failed. As for complete data, the profile likelihood
`ℓ_p(γ)` is searched on `γ = m − r·eᵗ` (`r` the range of the data) over
a grid of `t`, the largest interior local maximum is refined by
golden-section search and then polished jointly. The likelihood can rise
without bound as `γ → m` when that earliest time is an exact failure
(shapes below one); such boundary solutions are not reported. The
exponential with a threshold is the exception: its likelihood rises to a
finite maximum at `γ = m` when `m` is an exact failure, so that boundary
value is the estimate (with no standard error).

#### Intervals
The covariance of the estimates is the inverse of the observed
information `−∇²ℓ` (central differences). **Wald** intervals are formed
on the scale where the estimate is unconstrained: `exp(ln θ̂ ± z·SE)` for
positive parameters and quantiles, `logit⁻¹(logit F̂ ± z·SE)` for
probabilities, the delta method supplying the standard error.
**Likelihood-ratio (profile)** intervals are the sets
`{c : 2[ℓ(θ̂) − max_{g(θ)=c} ℓ(θ)] ≤ χ²₁(1 − α)}` (Meeker & Escobar §8.3,
Appendix B.6.6; Cox & Hinkley 1974, §9.3): for a parameter the other
parameters are re-maximized with it held fixed; for the quantile `t_p`,
and for the failure probability `F(t)` (the quantile constraint read the
other way round), the location (or the gamma scale) is solved from the
constraint and the rest re-maximized. Each end is located by bracketing
from the Wald interval and Illinois-modified regula falsi.

#### Weibull with known shape
With the shape `β` known, `T^β` is exponential with mean `η = α^β`, so for
failures and right-censored times (Nelson 1985, "Weibull analysis of
reliability data with few or no failures", *J. Quality Technology* 17,
140–146; also Abernethy, *The New Weibull Handbook*) the estimate is
`η̂ = Σ wᵢ tᵢ^β / r` with `r` failures, and the chi-square limits for an
exponential mean give `η_L = 2Σ wᵢ tᵢ^β / χ²(C; 2r + 2)` (a one-sided lower
bound with confidence `C`, defined even when `r = 0`) and
`η_U = 2Σ wᵢ tᵢ^β / χ²(1 − C; 2r)`. The scale limits are `η^{1/β}`;
percentiles `α(−ln(1 − p))^{1/β}` and reliabilities `exp(−(t/α)^β)` follow
from the scale bound.

- `fn censored_log_likelihood`: The censored-data log-likelihood of `d` (see the module docs); `−∞` when an observation is impossible under `d`.
- `struct CensoredFit`: A maximum-likelihood fit to censored data.
- `struct IntervalEstimate`: An estimate with its standard error and Wald and likelihood-ratio limits.
- `fn fit_censored`: Fit `family` to censored life data by maximum likelihood (see the module docs).
- `struct NestedComparison`: A likelihood-ratio comparison of a family with one it contains.
- `const NESTED_FAMILIES`: Pairs `(reduced, full)` where the first family is a special or limiting case of the second: the exponential is the Weibull with `β = 1` and the gamma with `k = 1`; each two-parameter form is its threshold form with `γ = 0`.
- `fn nested_comparison`: The likelihood-ratio test of `reduced` within `full`: `2(ℓ_full − ℓ_red)` referred to χ² with the difference in parameter counts (Wilks 1938).
- `struct KnownShapeWeibull`: A Weibull fit with a known shape (see the module docs).
- `fn weibull_known_shape`: Fit a Weibull with known shape `β` to failures and right-censored times (Nelson 1985; see the module docs).

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/competing_risks.rs`

Competing risks: units that can fail from one of several causes (failure
modes), the first of which ends their life, with right censoring.

* [`aalen_johansen`] — the cumulative incidence function of each cause,
  `F_j(t) = P(T ≤ t, cause = j)`, by the Aalen–Johansen estimator with the
  delta-method (Greenwood-type) variance and log(−log) pointwise limits.
* [`gray_test`] — Gray's (1988) K-sample test that one cause's cumulative
  incidence is the same in every group.
* [`fine_gray`] — Fine & Gray's (1999) proportional subdistribution hazards
  regression with inverse-probability-of-censoring weights, robust
  (sandwich) covariance and predicted cumulative incidence.
* [`fit_failure_modes`] and [`SeriesSystem`] — for engineering data, a
  parametric life distribution per failure mode (the other modes treated as
  censoring) combined into the system's failure distribution
  `F_sys(t) = 1 − Π_j (1 − F_j(t))` with delta-method limits (Meeker &
  Escobar, *Statistical Methods for Reliability Data*, 1998, ch. 15).

#### Data
Each [`CompetingObservation`] is a time, the index of the cause that ended
the unit's life (`None` when the unit was still running at that time) and
a frequency weight. At a tied time, failures are taken to happen before
censoring.

#### Aalen–Johansen estimator
With distinct failure times `t_i`, `n_i` units at risk just before `t_i`,
`d_ji` failures from cause `j` and `d_i = Σ_j d_ji` from any cause, and
`Ŝ` the Kaplan–Meier estimate of surviving every cause,

```text
F̂_j(t) = Σ_{t_i ≤ t} Ŝ(t_{i−1}) d_ji / n_i
```

(Kalbfleisch & Prentice, *The Statistical Analysis of Failure Time Data*,
2nd ed., 2002, §8.2; Klein & Moeschberger, *Survival Analysis*, 2nd ed.,
2003, §2.7). The causes' incidences add up to `1 − Ŝ(t)`. The variance is
the delta-method (Greenwood-type) estimate (Marubini & Valsecchi 1995,
*Analysing Survival Data from Clinical Trials and Observational Studies*,
§10.2; Collett, *Modelling Survival Data in Medical Research*, 3rd ed.,
2015, §12.2):

```text
Var F̂_j(t) = Σ_{t_i ≤ t} { [F̂_j(t) − F̂_j(t_i)]² d_i / (n_i (n_i − d_i))
                         + Ŝ(t_{i−1})² d_ji (n_i − d_ji) / n_i³
                         − 2 [F̂_j(t) − F̂_j(t_i)] Ŝ(t_{i−1}) d_ji / n_i² }
```

and the pointwise limits are formed on the log(−log) scale,
`exp(−exp(ln(−ln F̂) ± z·SE/(F̂ |ln F̂|)))`, which keeps them inside (0, 1).

#### Gray's test
For cause 1 (any cause can play that part) and groups `k = 1…K`, let
`R_k(t) = Y_k(t) [1 − F̂_1k(t−)] / Ŝ_k(t−)` be the estimated number in
group `k` still exposed to cause 1 in the subdistribution sense (units at
risk, plus those that failed from another cause, reweighted). The scores
compare the observed cause-1 failures with their share of the pooled ones,

```text
z_k = Σ_t [ d_1k(t) − R_k(t) d_1·(t) / R_·(t) ],
```

which is Gray's (1988, *Annals of Statistics* 16, 1141–1154) statistic
with weight `L(t) = 1` (the default `ρ = 0` of his class). The
covariance is the one of his §2, from the asymptotic representation of
`z` as a sum of integrals over each group's cause-specific counting-process
martingales, with the group-specific cause-specific hazards estimated by
`d/Y`; ties are handled by the exact linearization of the product-limit
estimator (denominators `Y − d`), and the multinomial covariance of the
failures at a time. The statistic `zᵀ V⁻ z` over `K − 1` groups is
referred to χ² with `K − 1` degrees of freedom.

#### Fine–Gray regression
The subdistribution hazard of cause 1 is modelled as
`λ₁(t | Z) = λ₁₀(t) exp(βᵀZ)` (Fine & Gray 1999, *JASA* 94, 496–509), so
`F₁(t | Z) = 1 − exp(−Λ₁₀(t) e^{βᵀZ})`. Units that failed from another
cause stay in the risk set after their failure with weight
`w_j(t) = Ĝ(t−)/Ĝ(X_j−)`, where `Ĝ` is the Kaplan–Meier estimate of the
censoring distribution (censored rows as its events); units at risk have
weight 1. β maximizes the weighted partial likelihood (Breslow's handling
of ties) by Newton–Raphson with step halving; the baseline cumulative
subdistribution hazard is the Breslow-type estimate
`Λ̂₁₀(t) = Σ_{t_i ≤ t} d_1i / Σ_j w_j(t_i) e^{β̂ᵀZ_j}`.

The robust covariance is the sandwich `I⁻¹ (Σ_i (η_i + ψ_i)(η_i + ψ_i)ᵀ) I⁻¹`
of Fine & Gray (1999, §3): `η_i` is unit `i`'s weighted score residual and
`ψ_i` accounts for estimating `Ĝ` (each unit's censoring martingale
acting through the weights of units that failed from other causes). With
no censoring `ψ ≡ 0` and the fit is Cox regression on the subdistribution
risk set with the Lin–Wei robust covariance.

#### Failure modes of a series system
Each mode's life distribution is fitted by maximum likelihood with
`fit_censored`, failures from the
other modes being right-censored at their times (valid when the modes act
independently). The system fails at its first mode failure, so
`F_sys(t) = 1 − Π_j (1 − F̂_j(t))`. Because the modes' estimates come from
separate likelihoods they are independent, and the delta method gives
`Var F̂_sys(t) = Σ_j [Π_{k≠j} (1 − F̂_k(t))]² Var F̂_j(t)`; limits are formed
on the logit scale (Meeker & Escobar 1998, §15.3).

- `struct CompetingObservation`: One unit (or a frequency of identical units) in a competing-risks study.
- `struct IncidenceStep`: The estimates at one distinct failure time.
- `struct CumulativeIncidence`: The Aalen–Johansen estimates of every cause's cumulative incidence.
- `fn aalen_johansen`: The Aalen–Johansen cumulative incidence of each of `n_causes` causes, with delta-method variances (see the module docs).
- `struct GrayTest`: Gray's K-sample test of one cause's cumulative incidence.
- `fn gray_test`: Gray's test that the cumulative incidence of `cause` is equal in the `n_groups` groups (`groups[i]` is the group of `obs[i]`); see the module docs.
- `struct FineGrayFit`: A Fine–Gray proportional subdistribution hazards fit.
- `struct HazardRatioEstimate`: One coefficient with its robust standard error, Wald test and the subdistribution hazard ratio's interval.
- `fn fine_gray`: Fit the Fine–Gray model for `cause` with covariates `x` (one row of `p` values per observation, already coded: indicators for categorical factors).
- `fn mode_life_data`: The life data of failure mode `mode`: its failures exact, every other unit right-censored at its time.
- `fn fit_failure_modes`: Fit `family` to each of `n_modes` failure modes separately, the other modes' failures treated as censoring (see the module docs).
- `struct SystemProbability`: The system's failure probability at a time, with its delta-method standard error and logit-scale limits.
- `struct SeriesSystem`: A series system of independently acting failure modes, each with its own fitted life distribution.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/degradation.rs`

Degradation analysis: life information from measurements of a
performance characteristic that drifts towards a failure threshold
(Meeker & Escobar, *Statistical Methods for Reliability Data*, 1998,
ch. 13; Lu & Meeker 1993, "Using degradation measures to estimate a
time-to-failure distribution", *Technometrics* 35, 161–174).

#### Repeated measures: paths per unit
Each unit `i` is measured at times `tᵢⱼ`; its path is one of

* **linear** on transformed scales, `g(y) = a + b·h(t)`, with `g` and `h`
  each the identity, natural log or square root (so exponential growth is
  `g = ln`, a power law `g = h = ln`);
* **asymptotic**, `D(t) = D∞(1 − e^{−kt})` (a first-order chemical
  reaction approaching `D∞`; Meeker & Escobar §13.2);
* **power**, `D(t) = a·tᵇ`,

fitted to each unit by least squares (the nonlinear forms exactly, by
a one-dimensional search over `k` or `b` with the linear coefficient
solved in closed form). A unit fails when its path reaches the threshold
`D_f` (rising to it, or falling to it). The **approximate method**
(Meeker & Escobar §13.6–13.7) solves each fitted path for its crossing
time, the unit's *pseudo failure time*; a path that never reaches the
threshold, or is moving away from it, gives a unit right-censored at its
last measurement, and one already past the threshold at time zero a unit
left-censored at its first. A life distribution (or a life–stress model,
with a stress per unit) is then fitted to the pseudo failure times by
[`crate::censored_fit`] or [`crate::life_stress`].

#### Repeated measures: random-effects path model
With the linear path, the units' intercepts and slopes may instead be
treated as random: `g(yᵢⱼ) = (β₀ + b₀ᵢ) + (β₁ + b₁ᵢ) h(tᵢⱼ) + εᵢⱼ` with
`(b₀ᵢ, b₁ᵢ) ~ N(0, Σ)` and `εᵢⱼ ~ N(0, σ²)`, fitted by REML (or ML) with
`stat_mixed`. The fraction of the population whose actual path
`D(t) = β₀ + b₀ + (β₁ + b₁) h(t)` is beyond the transformed threshold
`g(D_f)` at `t` is

```text
F(t) = Φ( ±(β₀ + β₁h(t) − g(D_f)) / √(Σ₀₀ + 2Σ₀₁h(t) + Σ₁₁h(t)²) )
```

(`+` for a rising failure direction), computed exactly (Meeker & Escobar
§13.5; Lu & Meeker 1993). Pointwise intervals for `F(t)` and its
quantiles come from a parametric bootstrap with a fixed seed: new
data are simulated from the fitted model at the observed design, the model
refitted, and the percentiles of the bootstrap values taken (Meeker &
Escobar §13.7).

#### Destructive degradation
When measuring a unit destroys it, each unit gives one value. The
transformed response is modelled as a location–scale regression
(normal, logistic or extreme value) with constant `σ` and location
`μ(t) = β₀ + β₁ h(t)`, or with a stress `s` acting on the degradation rate,
`μ(t, s) = β₀ + β₁ exp(β₂ [x(s) − x(s_U)]) h(t)`, `x(s)` the transformed
stress (Arrhenius `1/kT`, inverse power `ln s`, …) and `s_U` the use
condition, so that `β₁` is the rate at use conditions and, for Arrhenius,
`−β₂` the activation energy of the rate in eV (Escobar, Meeker, Kugler &
Kramer 2003, "Accelerated destructive degradation tests: data, models
and analysis", in *Mathematical and Statistical Methods in Reliability*,
World Scientific; Meeker & Escobar §13.9). The parameters are estimated
by maximum likelihood (damped Newton from a grid over `β₂` with `β₀, β₁`
by least squares), the covariance from the observed information. The
time-to-threshold distribution at stress `s` is
`F(t) = Φ((g(D_f) − μ(t, s))/σ)` for a falling response (`1 − Φ(·)`
rising), and its `p` quantile solves `μ(t_p, s) = g(D_f) − σ w`,
`w = Φ⁻¹(p)` falling or `Φ⁻¹(1 − p)` rising. Intervals are Wald, on log
time for quantiles and the logit for probabilities, from the delta method.

- `enum ScaleTransform`: A monotone transform of a response or time scale.
- `enum PathModel`: The form of each unit's degradation path.
- `enum FailureDirection`: Which way the response moves towards failure.
- `enum Crossing`: How a unit's pseudo failure time is known.
- `struct UnitPath`: One unit's least-squares path.
- `fn fit_unit_path`: Fit one unit's path and find its pseudo failure time.
- `struct UnitSeries`: One unit's measurements.
- `struct RandomPathFit`: The random-effects linear path model and its implied life distribution.
- `fn fit_random_paths`: Fit `g(y) = (β₀ + b₀ᵢ) + (β₁ + b₁ᵢ) h(t) + ε` with correlated random intercepts and slopes per unit (see the module docs).
- `struct BootstrapBands`: Pointwise bootstrap limits.
- `struct DestructiveModel`: A destructive degradation model.
- `struct DestructiveData`: One measurement per unit.
- `struct DestructiveFit`: A fitted destructive degradation model.
- `fn fit_destructive`: Fit a destructive degradation model (see the module docs).

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/fatigue.rs`

Stress–life (S–N) curves for fatigue tests: cycles to failure `N` of
specimens cycled at a stress amplitude `S`, with run-outs (specimens
still unbroken when the test was stopped) as right-censored
observations, fitted by maximum likelihood with
[`crate::life_regression`].

#### Model
Log life is a location–scale variable,

```text
ln N = μ(S) + σ(S) ε,
```

with `ε` standard normal (lognormal life), smallest extreme value
(Weibull) or logistic (log-logistic), and one of four curves for the
location (ASTM E739-10, *Standard Practice for Statistical Analysis of
Linear or Linearized Stress-Life and Strain-Life Fatigue Data*; Meeker &
Escobar, *Statistical Methods for Reliability Data*, 1998, ch. 17;
Pascual & Meeker 1999, "Estimating fatigue curves with the random
fatigue-limit model", *Technometrics* 41, 277–290):

| Form | `μ(S)` |
|---|---|
| Basquin (1910) | `β₀ + β₁ ln S` |
| Semi-log | `β₀ + β₁ S` |
| Quadratic log–log | `β₀ + β₁ ln S + β₂ (ln S)²` |
| Endurance limit (Stromeyer 1914) | `β₀ + β₁ ln(S − E)`, `0 ≤ E < min S` |

The scale `σ` is constant, or optionally `ln σ = γ₀ + γ₁ ln S` (for every
form, including the endurance limit, the scale covariate is `ln S`), as
fatigue lives usually scatter more at low stress (Meeker & Escobar §17.5).

#### Endurance limit
For a fixed `E` the endurance-limit form is a Basquin curve in `S − E`,
so `E` is estimated by profile likelihood: `ℓ_p(E)` = the maximum of the
log-likelihood with `E` held fixed. The profile is evaluated on a grid of
`v = −ln(1 − E / min S)` (which spreads the grid towards `min S`), the
best grid point is refined by golden-section search, and the result is
polished by maximizing the full likelihood jointly over `(E, β, γ)`. When
the profile is largest at `E = 0` the estimate is `0` (no endurance limit
is supported by the data). The likelihood-ratio interval is
`{E : 2[ℓ_p(Ê) − ℓ_p(E)] ≤ χ²₁(level)}` within `[0, min S]`: a limit
that reaches `0` or `min S` means the profile does not fall far enough
before the end of the admissible range.

The coefficients' covariance, and every interval for quantiles and
failure probabilities of the endurance form, are **conditional on `Ê`**:
`E` is treated as known, so they do not include the uncertainty of the
endurance limit and are somewhat too narrow.

#### Likelihood
Failures contribute `w ln f(N)` (the density of `N`, including the
`1/N` Jacobian) and run-outs `w ln S(N)` (see [`crate::life_regression`]).

- `enum SnForm`: The curve relating log life to stress.
- `struct FatigueModel`: The fatigue model: curve, life distribution and scale form.
- `struct FatigueData`: Cycles to failure (or run-out) with the stress of each specimen.
- `struct EnduranceLimit`: The estimated endurance limit.
- `struct FatigueLevel`: Specimens tested at one stress.
- `struct FatigueFit`: A fitted S–N curve.
- `fn fit_fatigue`: Fit an S–N curve by maximum likelihood (see the module docs).

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/growth.rs`

Reliability growth: the power-law nonhomogeneous Poisson process (the
Crow–AMSAA model) fitted to the failure times of one developing system.

#### Model
Failures of a system under development, at cumulative operating times
`t₁ < t₂ < … < tₙ`, follow a Poisson process with intensity

```text
u(t) = λ β t^(β−1),      E N(t) = λ t^β,
```

so `β < 1` means failures arrive ever more slowly (reliability is
growing) and `β = 1` is a constant failure rate. The instantaneous mean
time between failures is `M(t) = 1/u(t)` (Crow 1974, "Reliability
analysis for complex, repairable systems", in *Reliability and
Biometry*, SIAM; MIL-HDBK-189C, *Reliability Growth Management*, 2011,
§5.2).

#### Estimation
For a test **time-terminated** at `T` (`T ≥ tₙ`) or **failure-terminated**
at `T = tₙ` the maximum-likelihood estimates are

```text
β̂ = n / Σ ln(T/tᵢ),      λ̂ = n / T^β̂
```

(the term for `tₙ = T` is zero). Conditional on `n`, `2nβ/β̂` is χ² with
`2n` degrees of freedom (time-terminated) or `2(n − 1)` (failure-
terminated), which gives exact intervals for `β` and the unbiased
estimates `β̄ = (n − 1)β̂/n` and `β̄ = (n − 2)β̂/n` respectively (Crow 1974).
With the unbiased estimate, `λ̄ = n/T^β̄`.

A **phase** that starts at `s > 0` (after design changes, with the
cumulative clock running on) is fitted to the failures in `(s, T]` with
the left-truncated likelihood
`ℓ = n ln λ + n ln β + (β − 1) Σ ln tᵢ − λ(T^β − s^β)`; `β̂` solves the
(monotone) profile score equation by bisection, and only the maximum-
likelihood estimate applies.

#### Intervals for intensity and MTBF
Wald intervals on the log scale from the observed information of
`(a, β)` with `a = ln λ + β ln T` (time measured in units of `T`, which
keeps the information well conditioned): with `r = s/T` and
`c = r^β/(1 − r^β)`,

```text
J = n [ 1          −c ln r          ]
      [ −c ln r    1/β² − c ln² r   ]
```

and `Var ln û(t) = gᵀ J⁻¹ g` with `g = (1, 1/β + ln(t/T))`. For `s = 0`
this gives `Var ln M̂(T) = 2/n`.

#### Goodness of fit
The Cramér–von Mises statistic of MIL-HDBK-189C (§5.2.5) for a phase
starting at zero, with `M = n` (time-terminated) or `M = n − 1`
(failure-terminated, the last failure left out) and the unbiased `β̄`:

```text
C²_M = 1/(12M) + Σᵢ₌₁ᴹ [ (tᵢ/T)^β̄ − (2i − 1)/(2M) ]².
```

Under the model the ratios `(tᵢ/T)^β` are ordered uniform values, and in
both cases `β̄ = (M − 1)/Σ ln(T/tᵢ)`, so the statistic's null distribution
depends on `M` only. Its p-value and critical value are simulated
(20 000 seeded replicates) rather than read from a table.

- `enum Termination`: How a growth test (or phase) ended.
- `enum BetaEstimator`: Which estimate of the shape `β` the fitted curve uses.
- `struct CramerVonMises`: The Cramér–von Mises goodness-of-fit test of the power-law model.
- `struct PowerLawProcess`: A power-law (Crow–AMSAA) process fitted to one phase.
- `fn fit_power_law`: Fit the power-law process to the failure times of one phase.
- `fn cramer_von_mises_statistic`: `C²_M` for ordered ratios `tᵢ/T` (`M ≥ 2`), with the unbiased shape `β̄ = (M − 1)/Σ ln(T/tᵢ)`.
- `fn cramer_von_mises_test`: The Cramér–von Mises test for ordered ratios `tᵢ/T` (`M ≥ 2`), with the critical value at significance level `alpha` and the p-value simulated from the statistic's null distribution for this `M`.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/kaplan_meier.rs`

The Kaplan–Meier product-limit estimator and the log-rank test.

#### Product-limit estimate
Let `t₁ < t₂ < … < t_m` be the distinct observed times, `nⱼ` the number of
units **at risk** just before `tⱼ` (observed time `≥ tⱼ`) and `dⱼ` the number
of events at `tⱼ`. Kaplan & Meier (1958, *JASA* 53:457) estimate the survival
function `S(t) = P(T > t)` by

```text
Ŝ(t) = ∏_{tⱼ ≤ t} (1 − dⱼ / nⱼ).
```

A unit censored at `tⱼ` counts as at risk at `tⱼ` (censoring is taken to
happen just after any events at the same time), so ties between events and
censorings are handled in the conventional way.

#### Greenwood standard error
Greenwood's formula (1926) estimates the variance

```text
Var[Ŝ(t)] = Ŝ(t)² · Σ_{tⱼ ≤ t} dⱼ / (nⱼ (nⱼ − dⱼ)).
```

#### Pointwise confidence bands
With `σ(t)² = Σ dⱼ/(nⱼ(nⱼ−dⱼ))` and `z` the standard normal quantile
([`BandTransform`]; Kalbfleisch & Prentice, *The Statistical Analysis of
Failure Time Data*, 2nd ed., §1.4; Klein & Moeschberger §4.3):

* plain: `Ŝ ± z Ŝ σ`, clipped to `[0, 1]`;
* log: `Ŝ · exp(± z σ)`, clipped at 1;
* log–log: `Ŝ^{exp(± z σ / |ln Ŝ|)}` — always inside `[0, 1]` and the most
  accurate in small samples (Borgan & Liestøl 1990).

#### Quantiles and median survival
The `p`-quantile (the time by which a fraction `p` has failed) is the
smallest time with `Ŝ(t) ≤ 1 − p`; when `Ŝ` equals `1 − p` exactly over an
interval the midpoint of that interval is used. It is undefined (`None`) if
`Ŝ` never falls that far. The confidence interval of Brookmeyer & Crowley
(1982, *Biometrics* 38:29) is the set of times whose pointwise band contains
`1 − p`: its lower limit is the first time the band's lower curve reaches
`1 − p`, its upper limit the first time the upper curve does.

#### Log-rank test
For `g` groups, at each distinct event time the observed events of group `k`
are compared with their expectation `eₖⱼ = dⱼ nₖⱼ / nⱼ` under equal hazards,
with hypergeometric covariance
`Vₖₗ = Σⱼ dⱼ (nⱼ − dⱼ)/(nⱼ − 1) · (nₖⱼ/nⱼ)(δₖₗ − nₗⱼ/nⱼ)`. The statistic
`(O − E)ᵀ V⁻¹ (O − E)` over the first `g − 1` groups is referred to χ² with
`g − 1` degrees of freedom (Mantel 1966; Peto & Peto 1972).

- `enum BandTransform`: How pointwise confidence limits for `S(t)` are constructed.
- `struct ProductLimitStep`: The estimate at one distinct observed time.
- `struct KaplanMeier`: A Kaplan–Meier survival estimate.
- `fn kaplan_meier`: Kaplan–Meier estimate from observed `times` and event indicators (`events[i]` is `true` for an event, `false` for a right-censored time).
- `struct LogRankTest`: Result of a log-rank test.
- `struct LogRankTrend`: Log-rank test for trend across ordered groups.
- `fn log_rank_test`: Log-rank test that `n_groups` groups share one survival function; `groups[i] < n_groups` is observation `i`'s group.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-reliability

Time-to-event (survival, reliability) analysis with right censoring. An
observation is either an **event** (failure, death, relapse) at its time, or
**censored**: the unit was still running when observation stopped, so its
event time is only known to exceed the recorded time.

* `kaplan_meier` — the nonparametric product-limit
  estimate of the survival function, Greenwood standard errors, pointwise
  confidence bands, quantiles (median survival) with Brookmeyer–Crowley
  intervals, and the log-rank test comparing groups.
* [`parametric`] — maximum-likelihood fits of the two-parameter Weibull and
  lognormal life distributions to censored data, with the observed-information
  covariance matrix, parameter intervals and fitted survival curves.
* [`censored_fit`] — maximum-likelihood fits of every family in
  `stat_core::distribution_fit` (including threshold forms) to data with
  exact, right-, left- and interval-censored times; Wald and profile
  likelihood intervals for parameters, percentiles and failure
  probabilities; likelihood-ratio tests of nested forms; and the
  known-shape Weibull scale limits (Nelson 1985).
* [`competing_risks`] — competing risks: Aalen–Johansen cumulative
  incidence per cause, Gray's K-sample test, Fine–Gray subdistribution
  hazards regression, and failure modes combined into a series system.
* [`warranty`] — warranty returns: shipment and return counts as
  interval- and right-censored life data, and forecasts of future returns
  with prediction limits.
* [`life_data`] — censored life data, Turnbull's nonparametric estimate
  (which reduces to Kaplan–Meier for right censoring) and the censored
  Anderson–Darling distance of a fit from it.
* [`growth`] — reliability growth: the power-law (Crow–AMSAA) process for
  one developing system, time- or failure-terminated, with exact and
  unbiased shape estimates, intensity and MTBF intervals, the
  Cramér–von Mises test and phases.
* [`repairable`] — repairable systems: Nelson's mean cumulative function
  with confidence limits, two-population differences, constant-rate and
  power-law fits, and the Laplace and military handbook trend tests.
* [`proportional_hazards`] — Cox proportional hazards regression with
  Efron or Breslow ties and optional strata: hazard ratios with Wald and
  profile-likelihood intervals, likelihood-ratio, Wald and score tests,
  Breslow baseline and predicted survival with limits, Schoenfeld
  residuals and the Grambsch–Therneau test of proportional hazards,
  martingale and deviance residuals.
* [`survival_regression`] — accelerated failure time models (Weibull,
  lognormal, log-logistic, exponential) with covariates for exact, right-,
  left- and interval-censored times: maximum likelihood with Wald and
  profile intervals, time ratios, quantile and failure-probability
  predictions, Cox–Snell residuals.
* [`test_plans`] — demonstration plans for a Weibull shape, sample sizes
  for a percentile's precision under censoring, and optimum and
  compromise accelerated life test plans.
* [`life_regression`] — censored location–scale regression (location and
  log scale linear in covariates) with Wald and likelihood-ratio intervals.
* [`life_stress`] — life–stress models for accelerated life tests:
  Arrhenius, Eyring, inverse power and exponential relationships in one or
  two stresses, activation energies, acceleration factors, the life
  distribution at use conditions and comparisons with per-level fits.
* [`degradation`] — degradation paths per unit (linear on transformed
  scales, asymptotic, power) with pseudo failure times, the random-effects
  linear path model with its implied life distribution, and destructive
  degradation.
* [`fatigue`] — stress–life (S–N) curves for fatigue tests with run-outs:
  Basquin, semi-log, quadratic log–log and endurance-limit (Stromeyer)
  forms with lognormal, Weibull or log-logistic scatter, the endurance
  limit by profile likelihood, quantile curves and fatigue strength at a
  given life.
* [`censored_count`] — Poisson and negative binomial fits to counts that
  are censored (below a detection limit, too numerous to count, or in a
  range), with Wald and likelihood-ratio intervals.

Results are cross-validated in the tests against published values for the
Freireich et al. (1963) leukemia remission data (Kaplan–Meier estimates and
Greenwood standard errors as tabulated by Klein & Moeschberger, *Survival
Analysis*, 2nd ed., §4.2; log-rank χ² = 16.79) and against independent
numerical maximization of the censored likelihoods.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/life_data.rs`

Life data with exact, right-, left- and interval-censored observations,
Turnbull's nonparametric estimate of the distribution function, and an
Anderson–Darling distance between that estimate and a fitted distribution.

#### Observations
Each observation says that a unit's failure time `T` lies in an interval
and carries a weight (a frequency):

| Kind | Known | Interval |
|---|---|---|
| exact failure | `T = t` | `[t, t]` |
| right-censored | `T > l` (still running at `l`) | `(l, ∞)` |
| left-censored | `T ≤ u` (already failed at the first look) | `(−∞, u]` |
| interval-censored | `l < T ≤ u` (failed between inspections) | `(l, u]` |

#### Turnbull's estimate
The nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimate of `F` for such data puts
all its probability on the **innermost intervals** `[qⱼ, pⱼ]`: intervals
whose left end is an observation's left end and whose right end is an
observation's right end, with no other end point between them (Turnbull
1976, "The empirical distribution function with arbitrarily grouped,
censored and truncated data", *JRSS B* 38, 290–295; Peto 1973). With
`αᵢⱼ = 1` when innermost interval `j` lies inside observation `i`'s
interval and weights `wᵢ`, the masses `sⱼ` maximize
`Σᵢ wᵢ ln Σⱼ αᵢⱼ sⱼ` and satisfy the self-consistency equations

```text
sⱼ = (1/W) Σᵢ wᵢ αᵢⱼ sⱼ / Σₖ αᵢₖ sₖ,      W = Σᵢ wᵢ,
```

which are iterated (an EM algorithm, Dempster, Laird & Rubin 1977) from
equal masses, accelerated by squared extrapolation (SQUAREM; Varadhan &
Roland 2008, *Scand. J. Statist.* 35) with a fall-back to the plain step
whenever the extrapolated step lowers the likelihood. Within an innermost
interval that is not a single point the estimate does not say how the
mass is spread; plots join its ends with a straight line. For exact and
right-censored data the innermost intervals are the failure times (plus
`(l_max, ∞)` when the largest time is censored) and the estimate is the
Kaplan–Meier product-limit estimate (Efron 1967).

#### Anderson–Darling distance
[`censored_anderson_darling`] evaluates the integral form of the
Anderson–Darling statistic (Anderson & Darling 1952, *Ann. Math. Statist.*
23, 193–212)

```text
A² = W ∫ (F̂(t) − F(t))² / [F(t)(1 − F(t))] dF(t)
```

with the empirical distribution function replaced by the nonparametric
estimate, as Koziol & Green (1976, *Biometrika* 63, 465–474) do for the
Cramér–von Mises statistic with the product-limit estimate. The integral
runs over the range where the estimate is determined: up to `u = 1` when
it has placed all its mass at finite times, otherwise up to the largest
finite time in the data (as for Type I censored samples, Pettitt &
Stephens 1976, *Biometrika* 63). Inside an innermost interval the
estimate is taken to rise linearly in `u = F(t)`. On complete data the
statistic equals the usual computing formula
`A² = −n − (1/n) Σ (2i − 1)[ln F(x₍ᵢ₎) + ln(1 − F(x₍ₙ₊₁₋ᵢ₎))]`.
Each piece is integrated exactly: for `F̂ = c + (b + 1)u` on `[u₁, u₂]`,
`∫ (c + bu)²/(u(1 − u)) du = c² ln(u₂/u₁) − (c + b)² ln((1 − u₂)/(1 − u₁)) − b²(u₂ − u₁)`.
Smaller is better; with censoring there is no general null distribution,
so the statistic is used to compare fits on the same data.

- `enum CensorKind`: How an observation's failure time is known.
- `struct LifeObservation`: One observation: the failure time lies in `(lower, upper]` (exactly at `lower` when `lower == upper`), with a frequency weight.
- `struct LifeData`: A validated set of life observations.
- `struct TurnbullInterval`: One innermost interval of Turnbull's estimate with its probability.
- `struct NonparametricEstimate`: Turnbull's nonparametric estimate of the failure-time distribution.
- `fn turnbull`: Turnbull's (1976) self-consistent nonparametric estimate (see the module docs).
- `fn censored_anderson_darling`: The Anderson–Darling distance between the nonparametric estimate and a fitted distribution (see the module docs).

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/life_regression.rs`

Censored location–scale regression: a life (or response) distribution
whose location, and optionally whose log scale, are linear in covariates,
fitted by maximum likelihood to exact, right-, left- and
interval-censored observations with frequencies. It is the engine behind
the life–stress models of [`crate::life_stress`] and the destructive
degradation model of [`crate::degradation`].

#### Model
For observation `i` with location covariates `xᵢ` (first entry 1), scale
covariates `zᵢ` (first entry 1) and a known offset `oᵢ`,

```text
Y = μᵢ + σᵢ ε,   μᵢ = xᵢᵀβ + oᵢ,   ln σᵢ = zᵢᵀγ,
```

where `Y = ln T` for the log-location-scale families (Weibull: `ε` smallest
extreme value; lognormal: normal; log-logistic: logistic; exponential: the
Weibull with `σ = 1`) and `Y = T` for the normal, logistic and extreme-value
families (Meeker & Escobar, *Statistical Methods for Reliability Data*,
1998, ch. 17; Lawless, *Statistical Models and Methods for Lifetime Data*,
2nd ed., 2003, ch. 6; Nelson, *Accelerated Testing*, 1990, ch. 5). The
`p` quantile at a covariate point is `y_p = μ + w_p σ` with `w_p` the
standard quantile of `ε`, so `t_p = exp(y_p)` for the log families.

#### Likelihood
Each observation contributes as in [`crate::censored_fit`]:
`w ln f(t)` for an exact time, `w ln S(t)` right-censored, `w ln F(t)`
left-censored and `w ln[F(u) − F(l)]` interval-censored, with the
observation's own `μᵢ, σᵢ`; the log-likelihood includes the Jacobian `1/t`
of the log families, so it is the likelihood of the times themselves.

#### Estimation
Covariates other than the intercept are centred and scaled internally, so
every coefficient is of order one; the likelihood is maximized over the
standardized coefficients by damped Newton (Levenberg–Marquardt) steps
with central-difference derivatives from least-squares starting values
that treat every observation as a failure at a representative time. The
covariance of the estimates is the inverse observed information, mapped
back to the original coefficients linearly.

#### Intervals
**Wald** limits use the delta-method standard error on the scale where
the quantity is unconstrained (log time for quantiles of the log
families, logit for probabilities). **Likelihood-ratio** limits are the
sets `{c : 2[ℓ̂ − max_{g(θ) = c} ℓ(θ)] ≤ χ²₁(1 − α)}` (Meeker & Escobar
§8.3, §17.4; Cox & Hinkley 1974 §9.3), where for a linear function of the
coefficients one coefficient is solved from the constraint, and for a
quantile or failure probability at a covariate point the intercept is
solved from `μ + w_p σ = y` and the rest re-maximized.

- `enum RegressionFamily`: The distribution of the standardized error of a location–scale regression.
- `struct CovariatePoint`: Covariates of one point: location covariates (first entry 1), scale covariates (first entry 1) and the location offset.
- `struct RegressionData`: Observations with their covariates.
- `struct RegressionFit`: A fitted location–scale regression.
- `fn fit_regression`: Fit a location–scale regression by maximum likelihood (see the module docs).

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/life_stress.rs`

Life–stress models for accelerated life tests: a log-location-scale life
distribution (Weibull, lognormal, log-logistic) or the exponential whose
location depends on one or two stresses through a physical acceleration
relationship, fitted to censored failure times with
[`crate::life_regression`].

#### Relationships
The location of log life is `μ = β₀ + Σ βⱼ xⱼ + o`, where each stress `s`
enters through its transform `x`:

| Relationship | `x` | Offset `o` | Life proportional to |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arrhenius | `1/(k T)` = `11 604.518 / T[K]` | – | `exp(Eₐ/(kT))` |
| Eyring | `1/(k T)` | `−ln T[K]` | `(1/T) exp(ΔH/(kT))` |
| Inverse power | `ln s` | – | `s^(−n)`, `n = −β` |
| Exponential | `s` | – | `exp(β s)` |

with `k = 8.617 333 262 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K` (Boltzmann's constant), temperatures
in °C (`T[K] = °C + 273.15`) or kelvin, so the Arrhenius (or Eyring)
coefficient is the activation energy in electron-volts (Nelson,
*Accelerated Testing*, 1990, ch. 2; Meeker & Escobar, *Statistical Methods
for Reliability Data*, 1998, ch. 18–19; Escobar & Meeker 2006, "A review
of accelerated test models", *Statistical Science* 21, 552–577). Two
stresses give, for example, the temperature–humidity (Peck) model
(Arrhenius in temperature, inverse power in relative humidity) or the
generalized Eyring model (Eyring in temperature, an exponential or inverse
power second stress, optionally with the interaction `x₁x₂`).

#### Scale
The scale `σ` (Weibull shape `β = 1/σ`) is constant across stress by
default; optionally `ln σ` is linear in the transformed stresses
(Meeker & Escobar §17.5). The likelihood-ratio statistic
`2(ℓ_varying − ℓ_constant)` on as many degrees of freedom as stresses
tests a constant scale.

#### Acceleration and use conditions
The acceleration factor of stress `a` relative to `b` is
`AF = exp(μ(b) − μ(a))`, the ratio of the lives at `b` and `a` (with a
constant scale, of every quantile). The life distribution at use
conditions is the fitted distribution at the use stresses, with Wald
and likelihood-ratio limits for its quantiles and failure probabilities.

#### Checking the model
Following Nelson (1990, ch. 5 §4) and Meeker & Escobar (§19.2), the
fit is compared with models for the distinct stress levels:
*individual* fits (a location and scale per level), and a *common scale*
model (a location per level, one scale). Likelihood-ratio tests compare
individual with common scale (equal scales, `L − 1` df), common scale
with the life–stress model (the relationship, `L − 1 − m` df for `m`
stress terms) and individual with the life–stress model. Levels where an
individual fit is impossible (e.g. no failures) are left out of these
comparisons, and the models compared are refitted to the rest.

- `const INVERSE_BOLTZMANN`: `1/k` in kelvin per electron-volt (`k` = Boltzmann's constant, 8.617 333 262 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K).
- `enum StressTransform`: How one stress enters the location of log life.
- `enum TemperatureUnit`: Units of a temperature stress.
- `struct StressVariable`: One stress variable and its relationship.
- `struct LifeStressModel`: The model: a life distribution, its stresses and scale form.
- `struct LifeStressData`: Failure times with the stresses each unit was tested at.
- `struct LikelihoodRatioTest`: A likelihood-ratio test between two nested models.
- `struct StressLevel`: One distinct combination of stresses.
- `struct LevelComparison`: Comparison of the life–stress model with per-level models.
- `struct LifeStressFit`: A fitted life–stress model.
- `fn fit_life_stress`: Fit a life–stress model (see the module docs).
- `fn coefficient_names`: Names of the location coefficients of a model.
- `struct StressParameter`: A stress-related quantity derived from a coefficient.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/parametric.rs`

Maximum-likelihood Weibull and lognormal fits to right-censored data.

Both distributions are **log-location-scale** families: with `y = ln t`,
location `μ`, scale `σ > 0` and `z = (y − μ)/σ`, the survival function is
`S(t) = S₀(z)` for a standard distribution `S₀` (Lawless, *Statistical
Models and Methods for Lifetime Data*, 2nd ed., §1.3, §5.2; Meeker & Escobar,
*Statistical Methods for Reliability Data*, ch. 8):

| Distribution | `S₀(z)` | log density `ln f₀(z)` | parameters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weibull | `exp(−eᶻ)` (smallest extreme value) | `z − eᶻ` | scale `α = e^μ`, shape `β = 1/σ`; `S(t) = exp(−(t/α)^β)` |
| Lognormal | `1 − Φ(z)` | `−z²/2 − ½ ln 2π` | `μ`, `σ` of `ln T`; median `e^μ` |

#### Likelihood
For events `E` and right-censored observations `C`, the log-likelihood on
the time scale is

```text
ℓ(μ, σ) = Σ_E [ln f₀(zᵢ) − ln σ − ln tᵢ] + Σ_C ln S₀(zᵢ).
```

It is maximized by damped Newton iterations (Levenberg–Marquardt) on
`(μ, ln σ)` with analytic first and second derivatives, from moment-based
starting values. The covariance of `(μ̂, σ̂)` is the inverse of the observed
information `−∇²ℓ` at the maximum.

#### Intervals
Wald intervals are formed on scales where the estimates are closer to
normal: `μ̂ ± z·SE`, `σ̂·exp(±z·SE/σ̂)`. For a time quantile
`t_p = exp(μ + σ w_p)` (with `w_p = S₀⁻¹(1 − p)`) the delta method gives
`Var(ln t̂_p) = V_μμ + 2w_p V_μσ + w_p² V_σσ`; for the survival curve,
`Var(ẑ) = (V_μμ + 2z V_μσ + z² V_σσ)/σ̂²` and the limits are `S₀(ẑ ± z·SE)`.

- `enum LifeDistribution`: A two-parameter life distribution.
- `struct ParameterEstimate`: One estimated parameter with its standard error and confidence limits.
- `struct ParametricFit`: A maximum-likelihood life-distribution fit.
- `fn fit_life_distribution`: Fit `distribution` by maximum likelihood to observed `times` (all `> 0`) with event indicators (`false` = right-censored).

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/proportional_hazards.rs`

Proportional hazards (Cox) regression for right-censored times, with
optional strata.

#### Model
The hazard of a unit with covariate row `x` in stratum `s` is
`h(t | x) = h₀ₛ(t) exp(xᵀβ)`: covariates multiply an unspecified baseline
hazard by the **hazard ratio** `exp(xᵀβ)` (Cox 1972, "Regression models
and life-tables", *JRSS B* 34, 187–220). `β` is estimated by maximizing
the partial likelihood, which does not involve `h₀`. With `dⱼ` events at
the distinct event time `tⱼ`, `Dⱼ` the units failing there, `Rⱼ` the units
at risk (time ≥ `tⱼ`, same stratum), `S⁽⁰⁾ = Σ_R exp(xᵀβ)`,
`S⁽⁰⁾_D = Σ_D exp(xᵀβ)` and likewise `S⁽¹⁾`, `S⁽²⁾` with weights `x`,
`xxᵀ`, the log partial likelihood is

```text
Efron (1977):   ℓ(β) = Σⱼ [ Σ_{Dⱼ} xᵀβ − Σ_{l=0}^{dⱼ−1} ln(S⁽⁰⁾ − (l/dⱼ) S⁽⁰⁾_D) ]
Breslow (1974): ℓ(β) = Σⱼ [ Σ_{Dⱼ} xᵀβ − dⱼ ln S⁽⁰⁾ ]
```

(Efron, "The efficiency of Cox's likelihood function for censored data",
*JASA* 72, 557–565; Breslow, "Covariance analysis of censored survival
data", *Biometrics* 30, 89–99). The two agree without tied event times;
Efron's is the default because it is much closer to the exact discrete
likelihood when ties are common (Therneau & Grambsch, *Modeling Survival
Data*, 2000, §3.3). Its score and information follow by differentiating
each term: `U = Σⱼ [Σ_D x − Σₗ aₗ/φₗ]` and
`I = Σⱼ Σₗ [(S⁽²⁾ − cₗS⁽²⁾_D)/φₗ − aₗaₗᵀ/φₗ²]` with `cₗ = l/dⱼ`,
`φₗ = S⁽⁰⁾ − cₗS⁽⁰⁾_D`, `aₗ = S⁽¹⁾ − cₗS⁽¹⁾_D` (Breslow: `cₗ = 0`).
Covariates are centred at their means for the computation (which leaves
`β` unchanged) and the linear predictors shifted by their maximum, so the
exponentials never overflow. Strata have their own risk sets.

#### Estimation and inference
Newton–Raphson from `β = 0` with step halving; the covariance is
`I(β̂)⁻¹`. Each coefficient has a Wald interval `β̂ ± z·SE` and a
**profile-likelihood** interval `{b : 2[ℓ(β̂) − max_{β_j = b} ℓ(β)] ≤ χ²₁}`
(the other coefficients re-maximized at each `b`); hazard ratios are their
exponentials. The global null hypothesis `β = 0` has the likelihood-ratio
test `2[ℓ(β̂) − ℓ(0)]`, the Wald test `β̂ᵀ I(β̂) β̂` and the score
(log-rank-type) test `U(0)ᵀ I(0)⁻¹ U(0)`, each χ² with `p` degrees of
freedom (Klein & Moeschberger, *Survival Analysis*, 2nd ed., 2003, §8.3).
[`ProportionalHazardsFit::drop_columns_test`] refits without a set of
columns for the likelihood-ratio test of an effect.

#### Baseline and predicted survival
Breslow's estimator of the cumulative baseline hazard, at the covariate
means, is `Ĥ₀(t) = Σ_{tⱼ ≤ t} dⱼ / S⁽⁰⁾(tⱼ; β̂)` (per stratum), and the
survival of a unit with covariates `x` is
`Ŝ(t | x) = exp(−Ĥ₀(t) exp((x − x̄)ᵀβ̂))`. Its cumulative hazard has the
variance (Tsiatis 1981; Klein & Moeschberger §8.8)

```text
Var Ĥ(t|x) = exp(2zᵀβ̂) [ Σ_{tⱼ≤t} dⱼ/S⁽⁰⁾(tⱼ)² + qᵀ I(β̂)⁻¹ q ],
q = Σ_{tⱼ≤t} (z − S⁽¹⁾/S⁽⁰⁾) dⱼ/S⁽⁰⁾,   z = x − x̄,
```

and the pointwise limits are formed on the log cumulative-hazard scale,
`Ĥ exp(±z_{α/2} SE/Ĥ)`, then mapped to survival (Klein & Moeschberger
§4.3 for the transformation).

#### Checking proportional hazards
The **Schoenfeld residual** of a unit failing at `tⱼ` is `x − x̄(tⱼ)`, with
`x̄(tⱼ)` the risk-set mean `S⁽¹⁾/S⁽⁰⁾` (Breslow) or its Efron average
`(1/dⱼ) Σₗ aₗ/φₗ` shared by the tied failures (Schoenfeld 1982,
*Biometrika* 69, 239–241). Scaled residuals
`s*ₖ = β̂ + D I(β̂)⁻¹ rₖ` (`D` events) estimate a time-varying coefficient
`β(tₖ)`. With `gₖ = g(tₖ)` a transform of time, the Grambsch & Therneau
(1994, "Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics based on weighted
residuals", *Biometrika* 81, 515–526) score tests of `β_j(t) = β_j + θ_j g(t)`
are, with `u = Σₖ (gₖ − ḡ) rₖ` and `V = I(β̂)⁻¹`,

```text
per covariate:  T_j = D (V u)_j² / (V_jj Σ(gₖ − ḡ)²)   ~ χ²₁
global:         T   = D uᵀ V u / Σ(gₖ − ḡ)²           ~ χ²_p
```

(the approximation using `D·V` for the variance of the scaled residuals,
as in their paper). `g` is `1 − KM(t)` (the default), the rank of `t`
among the failure times, `t` itself, or `ln t`.

#### Residuals
Martingale residuals `Mᵢ = δᵢ − Ĥ₀ₛ(tᵢ) exp((xᵢ − x̄)ᵀβ̂)` and deviance
residuals `sign(Mᵢ) √(−2[Mᵢ + δᵢ ln(δᵢ − Mᵢ)])` (Therneau, Grambsch &
Fleming 1990, *Biometrika* 77, 147–160).

#### Failure modes
[`StatError::InvalidArgument`] for mismatched lengths, non-finite values,
no events, or collinear covariates (singular information);
[`StatError::ConvergenceFailure`] when the estimates diverge, which
happens when a covariate separates the failures from the survivors
(monotone likelihood: no finite maximum).

- `enum TieMethod`: How tied event times enter the partial likelihood.
- `enum TimeTransform`: The transform of time in the test of proportional hazards.
- `struct ProportionalHazardsData`: Right-censored times with covariates and optional strata.
- `struct ProportionalHazardsOptions`: Settings of a proportional hazards fit.
- `struct HazardCoefficient`: One coefficient of the fit.
- `struct BaselineStep`: One distinct failure time of the Breslow baseline (one stratum).
- `struct PredictedSurvival`: Predicted survival at one time, with pointwise limits.
- `struct SchoenfeldResidual`: The Schoenfeld residual of one failure.
- `struct ProportionalityTest`: Grambsch–Therneau tests of proportional hazards.
- `struct ProportionalHazardsFit`: A fitted proportional hazards model.
- `fn fit_proportional_hazards`: Fit the proportional hazards model to `data`.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/repairable.rs`

Repairable systems: recurrent failures (repairs) of several systems, each
observed from age 0 to its own end of observation.

#### Mean cumulative function
Nelson's nonparametric estimate of the mean number of repairs per system
by age `t` (Nelson 2003, *Recurrent Events Data Analysis for Product
Repairs, Disease Recurrences, and Other Applications*, SIAM, ch. 2–3):
at each distinct repair age `u_j`, with `d_j` repairs among the `r_j`
systems still observed (end of observation `≥ u_j`),

```text
M̂(t) = Σ_{u_j ≤ t} d_j / r_j.
```

Its variance is estimated either robustly, without assuming a Poisson
process (Lawless & Nadeau 1995, *Technometrics* 37, 158–168; Nelson 2003,
§3.3):

```text
V̂(t) = Σ_i [ Σ_{u_j ≤ t, i at risk} (d_ij − d_j/r_j) / r_j ]²,
```

or under a Poisson process, `V̂(t) = Σ_{u_j ≤ t} d_j / r_j²`. Pointwise
limits are `M̂ ± z·SE` (normal) or `M̂·exp(±z·SE/M̂)` (log, never
negative). Two populations are compared through the difference
`M̂₁(t) − M̂₂(t)` with variance `V̂₁ + V̂₂` (Nelson 2003, §3.5): where its
limits exclude zero, the populations differ at that age.

#### Parametric fits
A homogeneous Poisson process (constant rate `ρ = n/ΣT_j`, with the exact
interval `[χ²_{α/2}(2n), χ²_{1−α/2}(2n + 2)]/(2ΣT_j)`) and the power-law
process `u(t) = λβt^(β−1)` shared by every system, fitted by maximum
likelihood (Crow 1974): `λ = n/ΣT_j^β` and `β` solves
`n/β + Σ ln t_ij − n ΣT_j^β ln T_j / ΣT_j^β = 0`. The likelihood-ratio
test of `β = 1` compares them.

#### Trend tests
For each system observed to `T_j` with `m_j` repairs (a system whose
observation ended at a repair drops that repair and uses its age as
`T_j`):

* **Laplace**: `U = [Σ t_ij − Σ m_j T_j/2] / √(Σ m_j T_j²/12)`, standard
  normal under a constant rate; `U > 0` suggests deterioration.
* **Military handbook** (MIL-HDBK-189): `χ² = 2 Σ ln(T_j/t_ij)` with
  `2Σ m_j` degrees of freedom; small values suggest deterioration, large
  values improvement.

Both p-values are two-sided (Ascher & Feingold 1984, *Repairable Systems
Reliability*; Meeker & Escobar 1998, §16.5).

- `struct SystemHistory`: One system's repair history.
- `enum McfVariance`: How the variance of the mean cumulative function is estimated.
- `enum McfLimits`: How pointwise limits are formed.
- `struct McfStep`: The estimate at one distinct repair age.
- `struct MeanCumulativeFunction`: Nelson's mean cumulative function.
- `fn mean_cumulative_function`: Estimate the mean cumulative function of `systems`.
- `struct McfDifferenceStep`: The difference of two mean cumulative functions at one age.
- `fn mcf_difference`: `M̂₁ − M̂₂` at every repair age of either population up to the earlier of the two ends of observation, with normal pointwise limits at `confidence`.
- `struct HppFit`: A homogeneous Poisson process fit.
- `fn hpp_fit`: Fit a constant repair rate.
- `struct PowerLawFit`: The power-law process fitted to several systems.
- `fn power_law_fit`: Fit the power-law process by maximum likelihood.
- `struct TrendTest`: A trend test's result.
- `fn laplace_test`: The Laplace test of a constant repair rate, pooled over systems.
- `fn military_handbook_test`: The military handbook (MIL-HDBK-189) test of a constant repair rate.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/support.rs`

Small numerical helpers shared by the regression models of this crate:
symmetric positive-definite solves and inverses (Cholesky), the normal
quantile, and the outward root search used for profile-likelihood limits.

- `struct ChiSquareTest`: A chi-square test statistic.

### `crates/stat-reliability/src/survival_regression.rs`

Parametric survival regression: accelerated failure time (log-location–
scale) models with covariates, for exact, right-, left- and
interval-censored times.

#### Model
The log of the failure time is linear in the covariates with a standard
error distribution scaled by `σ` (Meeker & Escobar, *Statistical Methods
for Reliability Data*, 1998, ch. 17; Kalbfleisch & Prentice, *The
Statistical Analysis of Failure Time Data*, 2nd ed., 2002, §2.3; Lawless,
*Statistical Models and Methods for Lifetime Data*, 2nd ed., 2003, ch. 6):

```text
ln T = μ(x) + σ W,    μ(x) = β₀ + xᵀβ
```

| distribution of `T` | `W`                       | `F_W(w)`              |
|---------------------|---------------------------|-----------------------|
| Weibull             | smallest extreme value    | `1 − exp(−eʷ)`        |
| exponential         | as Weibull with `σ = 1`   |                       |
| lognormal           | standard normal           | `Φ(w)`                |
| log-logistic        | standard logistic         | `1/(1 + e⁻ʷ)`         |

A covariate change `Δx` multiplies every quantile of `T` by the **time
ratio** (acceleration factor) `exp(Δxᵀβ)`. For the Weibull, the shape is
`1/σ` and the scale `exp(μ(x))`, and the model is also a proportional
hazards model with hazard ratio `exp(−Δxᵀβ/σ)`.

#### Likelihood
With `z = (ln t − μ(x))/σ`, a unit with frequency `w` contributes
`w[ln f_W(z) − ln σ − ln t]` when it failed at `t` (the density of `T`),
`w ln S_W(z_l)` when still running at `l`, `w ln F_W(z_u)` when found failed
by `u`, and `w ln[F_W(z_u) − F_W(z_l)]` when it failed between inspections
at `l` and `u`. A lower end at or below zero counts as left censoring.
Tail probabilities are evaluated on the log scale, and interval
probabilities from whichever tail is smaller, so extreme observations keep
their precision.

#### Estimation and inference
